Your visual impact can be mitigated given that people who are off the gas grid currently have an oil tank or a Calor gas tank sitting in the garden. There are things that can be done.

PDR needs to be looked at and there needs to be a mechanism that allows it to keep up with the pace of change of the technologies. There are just single letters missing —“ a” heat pump. If you need two, you do not get permitted development rights. Very small things like that could be tweaked, which would make a big difference.

I echo Bean’s comments. It is quite restrictive. Most machines do not need 1 metre of operating clearance, but you have to adhere to that for boundaries. We are trying to get the machines more efficient, which makes them bigger and quieter, and that obviously hinders because of the 0.6 cubic metre restriction. For smaller properties, it becomes a real hindrance because you are limited to outside space for siting equipment. It becomes a real problem.
Q49 Baroness Northover : What arrangements are in place for the disposal, reuse and recycling of old heat systems, and are they adequate?

Currently, what would happen with an old gas boiler system that was taken out and replaced with an alternative is that, typically, installers would strip the boiler of any useful parts and it would just go off to a commercial recycling scheme. They are commercial activities.

Thinking ahead to where we might be from 2030 onwards, when we start to recycle heat pumps as part of their natural life cycle, there is some concern about F gas release because of the effect in magnifying its global warming potential. There are some concerns about how we deal with F gas and F gases being released during recycling, and that is something the industry has to nail down. I know it is looking at it. I know BEIS is looking at it. Because of the global warming potential, it needs to be further addressed.
Baroness Northover : What is F gas?
F gases deliver refrigerant. They are used in the heat pump to compress and use that heat.
N oble Lords : Fluorocarbons?
The global factor for F gases varies according to the type of F gas. There could be F gases that are 2,000 times more dangerous than carbon dioxide in their emission potential.
Are they not used in fridges and freezers at the moment ? This is not a new worry.
It is not new, but it is on a different scale.
Baroness Northover : Lee, do you have any comments?

A similar thing, really; it is like fridges. There is not really a disposable avenue. We as a company do it responsibly, degassing and disposing of them and then making use of the parts—doing what we can do. There is obviously some cost to us in doing that, so we have to factor that in to the customer. If there is another avenue like the disposal of fridges, it would help.

Bean Beanland : There is a mature market in disposal of fridges in terms of F gas. As I said earlier, we are increasingly moving towards low global warming-potential refrigerant gases. The issue of global warming potential will start to decrease with time. Clearly, we will have heat pumps with existing refrigerants in them for the next 20 years , because that is the sort of life cycle we are talking about, but there are mature mechanisms already in place for recovery of F gas.

Of course, those gases have a value. Because they have a value, it is incumbent on industry to want to recover them. You will need to keep other systems running that might need to be re-gassed. There are all sorts of reasons why you would want to recover. I think the industry will rise to that and will borrow a lot of the set-ups that are already in place to deal with fridges, deep freezers, car air-conditioning and any other places where you find F gases, because they are ubiquitous.

This is not a question, but could we have from any of you any detailed points about the machinery of government, particularly what Bean said about the role of the Treasury and the different bits of BEIS? If we had that in detail, it would be helpful.

Those reflections from Mike on BEIS and Bean on the Treasury would be extremely helpful for our comments. I thank our three panellists. It has been really interesting and fascinating to have different perspectives, which will help us in our deliberations on this matter. Thank you, Bean, Lee and Mike for your time today and for sitting in on the first session. It is always helpful when panellists are able to respond to that.

sessions.w: Alex Schoch (Octopus Energy); Mark Robson (OVO)

segs.tx: Environment and Climate Change Committee
C orrected oral evidence: Boiler U pgrade S cheme
Wednesday 23 November 2022
10 am
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Parminter (The Chair); Baroness Boycott; Lord Browne of Ladyton; Lord Colgrain; Lord Lilley; Lord Lucas; Baroness Northover; The Lord Bishop of Oxford; The Duke of Wellington; Lord Whitty.
Evidence Session No. 3 Heard in Public Questions 25 - 3 8
Witnesses
I : Alex Schoch, Head of Flexibility, Octopus Energy; Mark Robson, Commercial Development Director, OVO.
Examination of witnesses
Alex Schoch and Mark Robson.

Q25 Good morning and welcome to this third evidence session of our inquiry into the Government’s B oiler U pgrade S cheme. We are very pleased to have two representatives from the energy suppliers with us today. Thank you very much for joining us.

We have two panels. Our second panel is starting in an hour’s time with other panellists with other industry experience, to give us their understanding. The first two panellists are Alex Schoch, H ead of F lexibility from Octopus Energy, and Mark Robson from OVO Energy. We are very pleased to have you both with us. I remind you that a transcript will be taken, which you will have sight of and can review. This session will go out on p arliamentlive .tv and will subsequently be made available on the parliamentary website.

Without further ado, because we have a tight timeline, I will ask the first question. Clearly, in getting to our low-carbon objectives, a number of actors have different roles to play. Perhaps you could set out what you see as the role of the energy suppliers in the overall move towards low-carbon home heating.
Thank you very much for having me and for giving us the opportunity to give testimony here today.

If we look at where energy suppliers sit in the realm of actors in accelerating the decarbonisation of the energy system, but specifically homes, we see the role of Octopus in accelerating that demand and facilitating the transition for homeowners, in the provision of the actual kit and the actual transition to hardware and the installation of heat pumps, and in combining running costs. That ties into electricity tariffs and helping consumers understand how they can save money and future-proof their home with the electrification of heating.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for the invitation. I am from OVO Energy. I look after a range of businesses that we call zero-carbon living solutions. These cover the hardware in homes but also fixing the fabric of the property and how we go about financing that via, for example, the ECO scheme, and taking payments.

At OVO we have set ourselves quite a precise and ambitious mandate. We call it Plan Zero. We aim to be fully net zero by 2035. That sets our mandate and a lot of the culture within the business, as well as our ways of working. It is hugely challenging to do that. We will have to decarbonise the homes of between 2 million and 3 million customers who are on gas, which is a predominant cause of carbon. Our role here is very top - down. That is not to underestimate the difficulty, as Alex outlined.

First, there is a lot to be said about education and giving customers the right information, especially about air source heat pumps, which are quite a complex heating device, and the hardware. On top of that is the differentiator that energy companies such as OVO and Octopus can bring : we can potentially reduce the running costs. Relevant here is the fabric of the household. I see from prior evidence sessions that that has been talked about. Fixing the fabric of the household and not putting an air source heat pump into an inefficient home is critical. For us, the education piece is the first thing, so that consumers understand how exactly these products work, and the eligibility of the household.

The second piece is around simple products and services. How can we deliver an air source heat pump to a customer ? H ow do we fulfil it , and how do we fix the fabric of that household in the first instance?

The third piece for us , and critical in our Plan Zero agenda, is to leave no customers behind. We have a broad spectrum of customers. Unfortunately, the customers with the lowest affordability levels are biased towards the most inefficient properties. We see it within our mandate to support those customers to finance those houses so that they can have comfortable, warm homes that are supported by green energy.

Q26 Mark, you mentioned the heat pump tariffs. Are there any barriers to further innovation in this market —innovations such as h eat as a s ervice , and areas like that? Do you want to respond to that, Alex?

We have the foundations already in place to enable those types of tariffs, especially smart tariffs. At Octopus we have a long history over the last few years, since our inception, of developing and bringing to market innovative smart tariffs that help consumers save money on their electricity bills by being able to shift demand around, based on when energy is greenest and cheapest, without inconveniencing their lifestyle.

In answer to your question as to whether there are barriers, the core foundation is the rollout of smart meters. That allows us to be able to monitor energy usage and bill actual consumption, not estimates. As the national rollout is continuing to progress, th at core foundation , combine d with the ability to bring to market smart tariffs , will help customers save money. For example, we already see that , on a flat electricity tariff, running an air source heat pump is £200 cheaper per year for the average home than the gas boiler equivalent. There is an even further upside with the introduction of smart tariffs. We already have several in the market and plan to release more imminently.

From a smart tariff perspective, there is a distinction between type of use . Y ou can isolate the hardware : you can isolate the air source heat pump and push a tariff just for that in isolation to that piece of kit. That protects the kilowatt hours in the household, so you can price differentially just for that hardware. On top of that there is flexibility of services, whereby you choose when to import or export power to the household, so you can balance the grid, or pull when electricity is greenest.

The type of use tariff we have in place now for air source heat pumps is part of a trial, and it is fair to say that it is a challenge to derive flexibility services around air source heat pumps because of the way they work and the way you need to keep efficiency optimised. We have a lot of emphasis on batteries and discovery of these tariffs, but I draw a distinction between type of use and flexibility services.

The second thing, especially around heat as a service, is that we would love to solve the problem of giving customers an affordable air source heat pump tariff that brings in the upfront cost, and then the ongoing service, maintenance and actual charge of kilowatt hours. Ideally, as Alex says, that should be below your existing gas usage to make it a rational decision for customers.

The challenge for the industry is in a couple of things. What happens if customers move? What happens to that obligation? I think the Green Deal stepped into that space previously. Should there be a charge on the property? There is a range of considerations. It also plays into the space of having a longer-term relationship with the customer, supporting them with an upfront cost and then having it paid back over time. That is often in their interest, but then you have to play into the factors around switching, and those considerations.

Q27 What are the aftercare deals that you offer people for problems and long-term assistance if anything goes wrong? Do they come back to you, or do they go to the equivalent of Yellow Pages and find a boiler repair man or heat pump repair man?

At the moment we install hundreds of air source heat pumps a year. We do it via local authorities and housing associations. As part of that contract, we are in one of the MCS certification schemes as well. In our engagement with businesses and housing associations we take an aftercare perspective. Because it is an immature market in what we would call the business-to-consumer space, we would approach it similarly to boiler servicing warranties, while meeting the obligations of the MCS accreditation.
Can you give me an idea of how long your involvement would last? Would it be six months, or a year?
It is specified in the MCS. Perhaps I could come back to you on that.
If you could write to us on that, it would be helpful.
Alex, you said that it is £200 cheaper to have a heat pump.
On an annual running cost basis.

Is that something that you can document for us? Can we look at it in terms of the real cost of energy, because the electricity price is such a weird thing at the moment? We are trying to look long term at the real cost of green generation and whether that is a differential that is actually there or is just a creation of the markets. It is not the same as some of the other data that has been provided to us. We would love to look at that. Also, on time shifting, are heat batteries practical? If so, on what sort of timescale?
I would be happy to submit detailed follow-up evidence on the analysis. We can submit that via your office.

On your macro question about the energy cost, if we take a step back and look at the actual generation cost of a renewable electron, we see that it is already substantially cheaper than the fossil fuel equivalent kilowatt hour. On a medium-term timescale, we are already at a 40% renewable energy system. As that climbs to 50% and 60%, the commodity cost on average will continue to go down. Of course, there are challenges in balancing the grid, as Mark mentioned, but we are at the forefront of solving that issue because these things are intertwined. Providing benefits to consumers in how their heat pumps are used, for example, or that overall flexibility, is absolutely crucial.

I do not want to go off at too much of a tangent, but just last night we had the second event of the new demand flexibility service called on by National Grid, where home owners are able to participate via their suppliers or third-party aggregators. In the first session, which we ran last week, Octopus customers alone reduced over 100 megawatts-worth of power for an hour, which is the equivalent of Leicester shutting down for an hour. That was just showing the potential for consumers of being part of a flexible, cheaper, greener energy system, and is part and parcel of how we think about the electrification of the home and the electrification of heating.
Can you share that with us, too?
Absolutely.
Are heat batteries a practical technology?

There is a wide range of technologies under the electrification of heat banner. Heat batteries definitely have a place. Our area of focus is air source heat pumps, as we see that as a viable, ready-to-use technology that can be deployed today in UK homes across the country.

Mark, you referred to it as complex hardware. We have been told that putting in a pump can take up to two weeks, and that that is one of the things that is putting off some prospective purchasers. Is there any evidence that the hardware is becoming refined and getting smaller , and so will be easier and quicker to fit?

I would say yes, and I would have to think carefully about how I demonstrate the evidence. Certainly from our perspective, we are repeatedly installing air source heat pumps, especially in the same archetype of property, and we do it in what we call an area-based scheme, where the properties have similar fabric qualities. We fix the fabric first and then we undertake the air source heat pump install. That timeframe is then significantly reduced because you fully understand the piping, the insulation requirements and the siting of the air source heat pump. You have a good understanding of , for example, the existing gas boiler or whether it is electrically heated. You effectively design a project to be undertaken at velocity. The intervention in a customer’s home is obviously the pain point that we need to solve.

Air source heat pumps are becoming smaller. We recently saw the prototype of a potential internal air source heat pump. I will not go into the technical detail, but I can ask people to give you an update on that. On the whole, there is a lot of ambition in the industry to drive down costs, drive up efficiencies and deploy at scale.

Q28 Following this through, for the average householder or landlord it is quite a confusing picture. People are talking about heat pumps, but they are also talking about direct electrification, hydrogen-based solutions and so forth.

What is your view as to what the mix of technologies is going to be? The B oiler U p grade S cheme, which we are focusing on, deals largely with air source heat pumps, partially ground source heat pumps and potentially biomass, but people are being bombarded with alternative solutions for different sorts of propert ies . What is your view as to what the eventual mix will be, and how far is the particular scheme on boiler upgrades appropriate in the majority of premises?

There are a couple of things, fundamentally. If we think about what the challenges are in the transition to decarbonised heating, we have a great opportunity as a country to focus on what is the most efficient and first-principled solution. At Octopus, we took the view of looking at all the solutions that are available in the market or are in various stages of R&D. Our conclusion was that, given the fact that we have this tremendous opportunity to reimagine how heating is done in a decarbonised world, we would go with the most efficient solution. That efficiency is air source heat pumps for the vast majority of UK homes. That is proven by multiple independent scientific journals and studies.

I completely appreciate that there is a lot of noise and a lot of different solutions. There need to be different solutions because everything should be tested. That said, the B oiler U pgrade S cheme is very well constructed in the way that it is focused on enabling, at point of sale, a near-term reduction in the cost as the cost of the hardware comes down and as the all-in installation cost and timeframe comes down, as opposed to schemes that have been implemented in other countries or previous schemes here in the UK. That point-of-sale, direct rebate is simple for consumers to understand. It is a clear endorsement. It helps galvanise the industry to scale - up and that is a very powerful signal to send.

In most cases, you will need to convince the householder that it is the most appropriate for them. They are also being bombarded by people with hydrogen-ready boilers saying t hat they expect the gas system to be translated into a hydrogen blend , and o thers are looking at local networks, and so forth.

We will come to other evidence in the second session on the appropriateness of heat pumps to rather more than a minority of homes; at least , if it is a minority, it is a large minority. That does not seem to be touched by this scheme. For example, others are arguing that , in a terrace of 10 houses, only the end terrace would be appropriate for an air source heat pump. Is that your general view? There are a lot of terraced houses in the country.

We focus specifically on the average UK home and not on the detached or semi-detached home. Therefore, to your point, we have focused our efforts specifically on terraced houses. I myself live in a mid-terraced house and I had my heat pump survey just last week. There is absolutely no issue with the installation of an air source heat pump in a mid-terraced home.
We will interrogate others on that.

I endorse Alex’s comments that, for a scaled solution, air source heat pumps are here now. They are proven and are getting better. Certainly, the B oiler U pgrade S cheme is very supportive in pushing scale.

We acknowledge that we are here to electrify heating and that there are alternatives. For example, we recently launched a trial around a zero-emission boiler that lends itself to flexibility services. Again, it is type of use. You can isolate the hardware and it has flexibility services so that you can access green energy at the right time. It has fewer of the issues around the ongoing heat requirements of an air source heat pump. It is not a perfect solution. It is expensive, or can be, and its efficiency is not yet at the same level as the air source heat pump. It is effectively one for one , whereas an air source heat pump COP can be 2 and 2.5 to 3, and some people say up to 4 . There are alternatives out there, and we will trial them with customers.

On the appropriateness for properties, I also live in a mid-terrace. Unfortunately, it would be hard for us to install an air source heat pump. In the archetypes of UK properties, around 30% are terraces and 30% are semi-detached. They are all in a very different state of disrepair, repair and insulation. It is great that we can install air source heat pumps in terraces, but we have to think very carefully about the siting. We should access as many as possible, but we should remember that there will be some properties that need alternatives.

There are also affordability measures. In some cases — for a vulnerable customer , for example — right now it might be best for them to have a highly efficient boiler for their circumstances. We have to think about it in the mix.
What do you have in your house? Why will the heat pump not work, when it apparently works for Alex’s mid-terraced house?
My home has a glass-fronted back, so the siting of the air source heat pump is the issue. I would like to solve it. I have not given up.
What is wrong with the glass back, except that it would release loads of energy? Is it because you would have to look at the pump, or what?

It could be sited on a roof, for example; i t could be sited on a wall. For my particular persona, when we upgraded our home seven or eight years ago, we did not consider an air source heat pump. Now, I would desperately love to get an air source heat pump into my property. I will try to make it work but it will not be easy.
What kind of heating do you have?
I have an efficient gas boiler.
I thank the witnesses for being prepared to disclose personal information.
I am very happy to.
Sorry. One of you said that it worked and one that it did not.
I considered my house for the zero-emission boiler. I would love to get one of those in my home. I am considering all manner of decarbonisation hardware for my property.
But even you find it quite a difficult decision.
F or my particular property.
That is a particular instance.

I n my particular instance. If I was to go backwards and make again the architectural decisions I did, I would think about designing in an air source heat pump. That is how we need to think about it .
Q29 Sorry, this is slightly diverging from the question, but do OVA and Octopus have dealings with big-scale builders such as Barratt for designing in things like that?

Recently we announced a partnership with ilke Homes, a new home developer , and toge ther w e have developed a proposition called zero builds. These are fully electrified new homes , with a solar battery and an air source heat pump. The home owners are able to have a guaranteed zero electricity bill for the first five years, and that can be extended.
What is the name of the company? I did not catch it.
It is ilke Homes.
It does not sound English.
It is English.
Do you know of any other company that is doing something similar?
Following that announcement, we are in discussion with multiple new home developers across the country for a replication of this scheme.
You are saying it is a proposition that can be put to potential buyers. Does that mean it will be more expensive than a traditional heating system, or not?
The solar battery and air source heat pump are part of the package when you buy the home, and then you have no utility costs. Of course, there is water , because we are not optimising water just yet.
Are any of the builders that you are in contact with one of the big six?
Yes ; p ardon me if I cannot disclose any more.
That is really interesting. Can you send us something about ilke and how it works?
We would be happy to follow up.
It would be really useful.

Q30 Are you monitoring the results of your installations? Do you go back a year later to see how it has worked out, whether the customers are actually saving , and, if not, what you could have done better. Do you have a self-improving system in place, or do you just install and then that is that , and you talk to them again in 10 years’ time?

We have invested up and down the value chain in the electrification of heating , from recently acquiring a heat pump manufacturer in Northern Ireland , called R ED , through to investing £10 million in an R&D and training facility in Slough, where we can train over 1,000 installers a year. We have in-house installation teams that we are currently expanding rapidly across the country.

The re was an earlier question on service plans. We have a five-year minimum warranty on parts and labour, and then incremental warranties and extended warranties available for that. W e think about it on a whole - lifecycle basis and not just a fire and forget, as you imply.
But you are not going back a year afterwards.
We are monitoring their energy consumption , because most of the customers are also an energy customer.
That is feeding into the question: “ H ave we done this right?”
Yes.

I have to say the same. In all our domestic trials we seek to understand the performance of the air source heat pumps — the COP — and the kilowatt - hour usage versus what they were using previously, whether that was gas, oil if they are off-grid , or electric heating sources that are less efficient, and finally the price and cost to the customer.

Q31 I am interested in the degree to which what you are doing is impacting people’s awareness of this particular technology. Th e whole climate change environment is full of what has come to be known as techno-optimism — w e are all going to wait until something turns up, like Mr Micawber used to do . This is tried and tested technology, but surprisingly not well known about. It is a very niche deployment in certain places. Mark , y ou take an area-based approach to this.
You can, yes.

To what extent is that impacting on the community where you are deploying this technology? Is the re growing awareness, increasing demand and increasing understanding ? Are you testing that? Perhaps Octopus does the same thing.

For our area-based schemes, just about all the residents —they are not necessarily OVO customers ; it is open to the area— tend to have affordability issues and poor housing stock. We do not just go in and install an air source heat pump. We fix the fabric of the house and retrofit it. In some cases, it involves solar panels, roofing, double - glazing, doors and an air source heat pump. Sometimes , we remove gas from th e property ; we fully decarbonise th e property, especially when there is solar and an air source heat pump. In other cases, the customer or the resident can be on alternative fuels such as oil. In some cases, they are burning peat for heat, which is very inefficient. When the scheme is designed, it is designed for a certain outcome that is good for the customer and good for the local authority and the housing association. In a lot of those cases, an air source heat pump is the best outcome.
This is a slightly different question. Are people coming and asking for it?
Yes.
Yes.
As a datapoint, we have over 30,000 customers who have requested an air source heat pump, with essentially no marketing.

Q32 Alex, when your boss came and spoke to the Net Zero Scrutiny Group, a rather hostile audience in many ways, he won them over very effectively. He said a couple of things that I would like to get on the record .

First , he gave us some numbers about the proportion of houses that could install heat pumps without insulation; the proportion that would need simple insulation in the roof and cavity walls; the proportion that would need more; and the proportion insulation could not be done at all . If you have figures like that, it would be useful for us to have them, either now or later.

Secondly, he said you were engineering down the cost of heat pumps very substantially. I said that if they are prevalent in Germany and so on, why have the Germans—who are rather good engineers— not engineered down the heat pumps? He said something about the structure of the engineering or the heat pump market, or whatever it is, in Germany that made it uncompetitive. If you could tell us anything about that, i t would be interesting.

Thirdly, when I got home and told my wife that these things were really terrific, she displayed an extraordinary knowledge that I had not realised she possessed , and said, “So you mean you are going to rip up the floorboards and put different diameter pipes through the house , and we’re going to have bigger radiators” . She thought I was about to install them, which I cannot afford. Perhaps I can turn that into a question: is it disruptive to install heat pumps , with the associated radiators?

I will follow up in detail on housing stock numbers . O ur view is that there are already 15 million homes in the UK that can have an air source heat pump installed with minimal incremental fabric work. As the c ommittee members all probably know, the BUS requires a certain level of insulation in homes . That is part and parcel of speeding i t up, but we will definitely follow up with detail on that.

On the engineering question, perhaps I can give a quick background . I spent quite a lot of time scaling - up electric vehicles and battery storage around the world, primarily as a former employee of Tesla. L ook at disruption of existing industries and the core heat pump manufacturers that exist today ; they already have more demand than they can meet. There is zero impetus for them to invest in how to engineer down the cost because their order books are already full for the next two years. In Germany , you cannot get a heat pump for love nor money until sometime late next year, so strong is the demand.

In that case, you can see that there is no strong driver to drive down costs when, in that market specifically, the re is a lready such strong demand. That being said, we see tremendous opportunity. That was the reason for our investment and acquisition of R ED , the heat pump manufacturer in Northern Ireland, so that we can drive down the actual bill for material costs so that they are even more effective for UK homes.
What about disruption internally, if you are having to replace all the radiators and the piping?

Many properties, as Alex says, are air source heat pump ready, and so have limited disruption. If you have underfloor, water-based heating, for example, with a gas boiler, depending on the pipework it could be minimal disruption. It is down to the persona of the property. We are investing a lot of time in trying to understand not just our customers and their eligibility around affordability and access to ECO, for example, but what those properties look like and how we could target customers who are eligible because of their property as well as their personal circumstances.

We are just about to launch a really interesting scheme with a community charity called Hubbub, where we will seek to work with a local community in Glasgow to upgrade all the houses in the ir street. The B oiler U pgrade S cheme will be a fundamental opportunity, assuming eligibility is okay, for those residents potentially to afford air source heat pumps in their property. It will be fascinating to see how we go about undertaking that scheme.
My expert adviser, Lady Lilley, told me that most properties need bigger radiators and bigger pipes. Is that so?

You do not need bigger pipes. The difference is the diameter of the pipes. Generally, properties built after 1990 have microbore piping, so the diameter is smaller, which requires a higher pressure and a higher flow of temperature. I believe one of the next witnesses is an installer, who I am sure will be able to illustrate in detail. We are just finalising our testing on microbore, the smaller diameter, to make sure that it meets our own internal stringent requirements. We expect to be installing early in the new year.
What about the radiators point?

Radiators may need to be upgraded and expanded. That is a subject, as Mark pointed out, on a per property - type basis. It all depends on the age of the property and the last time , if ever, the radiators were changed.

One way that we think about it is this: what is the most efficient, long-term future-proof solution for houses ? Mark made an excellent point that property types are at different stages of fabric and energy efficiency. As we think about the transition to decarbonised heating, it is also about future-proofing housing stock. It is how we think about that, because that is the crux of the matter and why we are so invested in the solution.

Q33 What are your hopes for the B oiler U pgrade S cheme, and to what extent do you expect them to be realised? What are the pros and cons of the current design and administration of the scheme? Is the scale of the scheme appropriate alongside other measures that are in place?

We fully support the scheme. Anything that we can do to help make this hardware more accessible and affordable is essential. If I was to draw a line, I would ask—as I think we have said publicly before —whether rather than having £5,000, it could be increased . There is still a significant outlay for customers. If there was no particular requirement for the home— no need to put in new radiators, et cetera—it is still quite significant but closer to a boiler replacement. However, if you need to address some factors in the home, whatever they might be, it is a significant expenditure.

As ever, we would always ask for more in the scale of the scheme, to help more customers. I think it is equivalent to 30,000 a year. The established low level of demand is around 30,000 a year, so are you generating incremental volume with the scheme? Uptake has perhaps been lower than people anticipated. I hope that the money rolls over each year because of the acceptance of air source heat pumps. As Alex and I have said, they are in demand —w e have consumer demand. It is around getting the right engineers into those properties who have the right skill sets, et cetera. Rolling over the money would be a great outcome.

I have touched on a few points already in previous answers. On the pro side, there is very clear endorsement and support from government to enable the industry, not just companies such as Octopus or OVO but small and medium -sized businesses, to galvanise around this and invest, to create more jobs and drive it across the country. That is a very clear sign of support that will allow the industry to galvanise around it further.

It is simple to understand. The actual ability to explain the scheme is incredibly easy and can be easily packaged into consumer communications, which are very important . That especially true if we compare it to some previous schemes and support systems that could be gamed or that led to potential mis-selling. I think that is a very strong positive.

In addition to what Mark mentioned, we see the funding levels of £5,000 for the air source heat pump as very much a steady-state type of funding. We have talked about vulnerable, fuel-poor customers and lower income households. One thing that could be interesting to explore is how you could apply different subsidy levels based on ability to pay, maybe packaged together with low-interest loans or other solutions. As we get to volumetric install volumes, we should see a cost reduction overall. Therefore, we should be applying the support to the households that need it most. That could be an interesting area to explore.
Q34 Thank you for your evidence. I am sorry I cannot be with you in person.

We have identified four barriers to take-up , and I think you have identified at least two more in your evidence this morning. We have identified public awareness; the availability of installers; the cost; and the hassle , which colleagues have referred to. You referred to the availability of the pumps themselves and investment to enable the scale-up. In your mind, a re there any other barriers that will prevent this massive expansion of the rollout of heat pumps? How can all of those barriers best be overcome as we move forward?
I have a quick response : careful thought about the ongoing running cost, whatever that might be.

I think it is about public awareness. As I mentioned before, we have 30,000 customers who have put themselves down without any marketing. I can point to some independent polls. The PA news agency did a survey for Barclays that found that only 20% of the respondents would not consider an air source heat pump as their next heating solution at the end of life of their current solution. We welcome BEIS’s marketing campaigns that are planned to start in Q1. We also see the role of industry and suppliers, as evidenced in the first question, as market actors to drive awareness and communicate it clearly to the public and their customers.

On the availability of installers, I would flip it around. At our training centre, we can train at least 1,000 engineers a year. That is our first training centre , and w e have had 3,000 applicants since we opened the training centre . W e have already trained hundreds, and they are in the field today. Interestingly, a lot of the engineers who come to us are current boiler engineers who are very keen to be retrained, to be able to future-proof their own livelihood and skills on a go-forward basis.
Could you both identify what you think is the single biggest obstacle at the moment to a smooth rollout?
Do you mean the scale of the rollout?
S caling - up the rollout.
Effectively hitting the Government’s targets.
The number of installations by 2030.
We would point to a 600,000 target , with the availability of engineers, but I am obviously encouraged by Alex’s comments.

The single biggest issue is overall support and the clarity of messaging. What is it that we are trying to achieve as a country? As a country, we are trying to achieve the decarbonisation of heating, with no small tinge of energy security thrown in.
That is really helpful. Thank you.

Q35 This just a bit more on the question of how it gets publicised. Given the fact that the Government have not, as a lot of European countries have, given people advice about cutting back on energy, do you feel that they are not really behind you on this?

I was really interested that Octopus provide s training for up to 1,000 people. How do you feel the Government are doing in training this new workforce? Obviously, if we are going to get to the government target, it is going to need a really big workforce , which presumably you would not be able to supply through your 1,000 engineers a year. It is a two-part question.

I will address the second part of the question. Th ose would be our own installers who are part of our own installation business, Octopus Energy Services. The evidence tends to show that the throughput of one company or entity to train up and provide—
You will provide a completely wraparound, discrete service from, so to speak, cradle to grave of your boiler.
Correct.
Would you expect other companies to do similar things to take over the market from beginning to end?
There is a raft of different business models and commercial decisions that can be made. I do not think it is on us to tell others how to run their business.
Go back to the Government training boiler engineers.

We are working with BEIS on the Clean Heat apprenticeship scheme. We are very encouraged by the Government’s investment and commitment on that. Overall, we see that type of apprenticeship programme scaling very well for the next generation of installers.
What about government information on what is available, and how clear all that is or how extensive?

There is always room for continued iteration That said, it is important that the companies and service providers that provide these services to consumers also provide information and communicate with them.

I come back to the previous example about the new demand flexibility service that National Grid has launched , and how suppliers can communicate the benefits of that to their energy customers, where customers who want to can reduce their energy consumption at specific times and be rewarded for it. Possibly the entity that is the energy supplier is better placed to communicate that value to the consumer than a blanket statement from government.
Three members want to squeeze in, so let us be brief.

Q36 We have heard consistent evidence that the skills and capacity issue in the pump and low-carbon heating industry is probably the biggest barrier to acceleration. Every witness that we have had up until now has said that. It is utterly commendable that Octopus has the capacity to train 1,000 engineers a year and that you are oversubscribed. Is anybody else doing this at this scale, or are you alone?
To be perfectly frank, I do not spend my time scanning the market.
I am certain somebody in your business does.
What I mean is—
We will pick that up with other witnesses. It is a good question, but you may not be the right person to frame it to.
Q37 To answer Lord Browne, Eastbourne and OHM Energy are, and the local college is there on a slightly smaller scale, but it is happening.
Could anything be adjusted about the scheme that would encourage manufacturing investment in this country in the kit needed for air source heat pumps?

Before I address that, I think one scheme improvement, especially for smaller installers in the market, would be to look at the speed at which the vouchers are actually reimbursed. There is a significant cash-flow challenge if vouchers are submitted and then the payment timeframes are not kept up. Fundamentally, if smaller businesses do quite a few jobs a month and are then out £20,000, £30,000 or £40,000 while they are waiting to receive reimbursement, it is a challenge to deal with that kind of cash-flow issue .

Currently the scheme is quite manual, with Excel sheets and PDFs that need to be filled in, scanned and uploaded. We are encouraged that there is an online portal that should be launched by the end of this month , which will speed that up. It is worth stressing that the timeframes for reimbursement of the vouchers is definitely something that should be looked at.
I will come back to you on the question on local heat pump manufacturing, and, if we can, submit a written response in a more comprehensive form.

Q38 Alex, could you help with the basic mathematics? A thousand people being trained a year is a very impressive figure, but how many installations can each engineer do in the course of a year? We are trying to see whether the Government have any hope of meeting their own targets.

What we focus on from an installation capacity perspective is how we continue to optimise the survey and installation workload, and how we can speed it up. We have a stated internal goal of continuously cutting down the amount of time required for the installation team to be on - site to complete the job. Our stated goal is to achieve a two-day installation, which we are already achieving with some of our installations; in and out in two days, and for those two days there are two to three installers, depending on the skill sets—a plumber, an electrician and a lead. They are not all required at the same time.
Where are you at the moment towards that goal?
We are already achieving two-day installations in some of our installs, and overall we are driving it down consistently across the country.
That is really interesting because it is quite different from the timescales that we have been given with previous evidence.
It is a comprehensive effort. It is a non-trivial effort, I should say, but it is part of our commitment to be able to drive down costs for consumers.
Going back to the engineers, three engineers would be involved for two days for one installation. Is that the sort of figure that we should have in mind?
Two and a half to three.
Does that include the survey?
I t does not include the survey.
If you include the survey, which presumably involves the same engineers , h ow long would that take?

In our current operational set-up, we have dedicated, trained surveyors. A survey takes about three hours for the average three-bedroom home , because of the requirements of the BUS for a detailed heat loss analysis of every single home. We are minded to move and to use more technology to see how we could speed that up further. Obviously, that is three hours that we should shave down to one , and then to zero , and do it all via technology , but it is a phased approach.
On that mathematics, 1,000 engineers can do 30,000 installations a year, optimistically. At your rate of training, if you carry that on for a couple of years, there will not be a shortage.
Assuming 100% labour utilisation, with no sickness and no illness.

Thank you. I will bring this session to a close in order for us to prepare for our second panel today. I thank Octopus Energy and OVO very much for sending representatives along, and for your forthright answers , both in a company capacity and indeed your personal reflections, which we really appreciate. Thank you for your time.

segs.tx: Joint Committee on the Draft Mental Health Bill
Joint Committee on t he Draft Mental Health Bill
Oral evidence: Draft Mental Health Bill , HC 696 Wednesday 23 November 20 22
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 23 November 20 22 .
Written evidence from witnesses:
– NHS England [MHB0051]
– Department for Health and Social Care, and Ministry of Justice [MHB00 94]
– Department for Health and Social Care [MHB0095]
Watch the meeting
Members present: Baroness Buscombe (The Chair); Baroness Barker; Baroness Berridge; Lord Bradley; Baroness Hollins; Baroness McIntosh of Hudnall; Dr Dan Poulter; Dr Ben Spencer; Sir Charles Walker.
Questions 1 77 - 202
Witnesses
Panel 1 : Professor Tim Kendall , National Clinical Director for Mental Health, NHS England; Dr Roger Banks , National Clinical Director for Learning Disability and Autism, NHS England.

Panel 2: Maria Caulfield , Minister for Mental Health and Women’s Health Strategy, Department of Health and Social Care; Caroline Allnutt , Deputy Director, Mental Health Act, Serious Mental Illness and Offender Health, Department of Health and Social Care; David Nuttall , Deputy Director, Neurodiversity, Disability and Learning Disability, Department of Health and Social Care; Damian Hinds , Minister of State, Ministry of Justice; Anna Lacey , Deputy Director, Female Offenders and Offender Health Policy, Ministry of Justice.
Panel 1
Witnesses : Professor Tim Kendall , National Clinical Director for Mental Health, NHS England; Dr Roger Banks , National Clinical Director for Learning Disability and Autism, NHS England.

Q177 Good afternoon, everyone. This is the final oral evidence session of this Joint Committee scrutinising the draft Mental Health Bill. The aim of this session will be to hear the views of NHS England and the UK Government on the proposals in the draft Bill, to test out some of the views and proposals the Joint Committee has heard during the inquiry, and particularly to test the Ministers.
In addition to the 14 evidence sessions the committee has held, it is important to note that the committee has also held private events with service users and visited a mental health setting.
Can I begin by welcoming our two first panel members, Professor Tim Kendall and Dr Roger Banks? First of all, could I ask you to set out very quickly who you are and whom you represent?
I am national clinical director for mental health at NHS England. I also work clinically with homeless people with mental health problems in Sheffield.
I am national clinical director for learning disability and autism with NHS England. I am a psychiatrist with the speciality of learning disability by background.

Q178 Good afternoon, gentlemen. This is a very quick and high-level question. It is about the issue of the principles that the independent review set out. As you know, the review recommended that those principles be incorporated in the Bill. The draft Bill does not include them. We would like to know what your view is on that decision.

It is the wrong decision. It would be right to have them in the Bill. I am not underestimating how complex that might be because of legal changes that might need to be made to other parts of the Bill, but this is heralding the beginning of what we hope will be a major change in the way we deliver mental health care and care for people with learning disabilities and autism.

At the centre of this should be choice and autonomy, therapeutic benefit, the principle of least restriction and the person as an individual. These could be taken as just words, but, if the Bill had them solidly in it as principles, it would have a much more powerful effect.

I completely agree with what Professor Kendall has said. We are expecting an important cultural change, particularly in the field of learning disability and autism. We feel the principles should be included to make clear the change we are aiming for, both professionally and culturally.

It certainly would be consistent with the aims of the learning disability and autism programme, which very much align with those principles. We feel it is important to have them in the Act, as a basis for understanding the way in which the Act is applied and the way in which people work with it.
Just to be clear—your answers are very clear—neither of you is convinced that putting the principles into the code of practice, for example, would be a good enough alternative.

It gives a much more powerful message to have them in the Act. A short while ago I was asked to appear in a public session of NHS England’s board following the Edenfield horrors, and I was told that they believed the current model for mental health—the in-patient model with closed communities and an excessive dependence on compulsion—was broken. Now, I do not think it is not entirely broken, but we have to do something about it. This heralds the right message for major cultural change.

I have been involved in recent discussion about this, together with Professor Kendall and others. We believe that the process of putting principles in the Bill would help in how the Bill is refined and amended to ensure that other parts of it are not inconsistent with the principles it is setting out to achieve. It could become almost a test framework for ensuring that the rest of the Bill is operating to support those principles.

That is quite interesting. It is almost diametrically opposite to what the Government have said. They are concerned that placing the principles in the Bill would possibly cause an issue around clarity for practitioners. You do not agree with that.

No. The principles should be at the heart of these changes. I am no great expert on legal matters, but my understanding about having principles in an Act is that they become the lens through which you interpret the rest of the Act. That would be a phenomenal change, in my view.
That is very helpful. Thank you very much indeed.

Q179 You say in your written evidence that it is important that the workforce implications are properly understood and accounted for. We have heard particular concerns raised about the resulting extra workload in three areas: community services, second opinion appointed doctors—SOADs—and tribunals. Have the Government accounted properly for these additional workforce pressures?

This needs to be set in the context of understanding where mental health is. When I first started this role in 2016, we were able to see only one out of four children with a mental health problem. Three out of four did not get seen at all. That was because we had set the bar sufficiently high that those with lesser problems were not seen. There were similar outcomes for adult mental health.

There has been a programme of investment in mental health to try to change that. By the end of next year it will be up at £3.3 billion extra. In that context, you can see there is bound to be a shortfall and there is some pressure on community services. The biggest investment we have made is about £1 billion extra into community mental health. I am convinced that we are going in the right direction, but there is still a treatment gap.

With regard to SOADs and tribunals, the Department of Health, NHS England and Health Education England are working out a plan for how to meet these needs. The implementation of the Act may need to be phased to ensure that we meet those problems.

You mentioned phasing. Are you suggesting that we would need additional full time equivalent hours in, say, the consultant psychiatric workforce and the like in order to meet the tribunal commitments, for example?
We need to grow the workforce. Those specific areas will need specific attention. That is what the workforce plan will address.
Do you have any idea or analysis you could share with us about how many additional full time equivalent hours that would mean in, say, the consultant psychiatric workforce?
I wish I could, but, no, I cannot.
There is still quite a lot of work to do on this
No, indeed. The work between the Department of Health, Health Education England and NHS England is in process. As this unfolds, we will have to meet those needs.
Is it entirely satisfactory that a piece of legislation is going to be put in place before the workforce consequences and the practical consequences have been worked through?

No. They have to be done hand in hand because we do not know the precise endpoint for the Bill. Until we do, it would be hard to work out exactly what the workforce considerations are. It is my view and the view of NHS England that this is a really important step and we need to find the means for supporting it.
Do you think the impact assessment the Government have done accurately or even closely reflects what is needed?
Yes, I do.
Sorry, are you saying that you do think the impact assessment accurately reflects the resources that are going in over the timetable they are setting out?
Yes, but I could not give you the exact number of doctors and second opinion doctors you would need at this point.
The timetable would have to reflect that.
Yes.

Talking about workforce, there is capacity, but there is also quality and capability of workforce. In the learning disability and autism programme, we too are very involved in talking about future workforce in the context of not just the Mental Health Bill but how we continue to develop the appropriate support for people with learning disability or autism where they are.

That is also about the training of that workforce and the different roles that might be required or the different emphasis in roles going forward to be able to support people without reliance on hospital admissions. Workforce impact is not just about quantity; it is also about quality, training and the investment in that.

On the point about the impact assessment and the reality of needs on the ground, if I can call it that, we heard from CQC yesterday that it had real concerns about SOADs and the ability to have sufficient support in that area, for example. Were they right to be concerned? Do you feel, Professor Kendall, they are perhaps too concerned? Is the resource there?

As I say, we have to find a way of doing this because it is too important not to. I could not tell you at this time exactly how we do it. If they have concerns, we need to take those seriously in terms of what training and funding there would be for ensuring we have enough SOADs.

We have been hearing a slightly pessimistic view from some quarters that the community provision is not practicable. This is with respect to learning disability and autism. That might be part of the training you are speaking about, but are you confident that the resourcing will be there?

One of the witnesses yesterday said that it would probably need pump priming and perhaps double funding for a period to enable new services to develop while the traditional services were being wound down. I wondered whether you had any comments about that.

I can understand those concerns. As you will know, there is an ongoing programme of investment in the community. We are investing about £40 million in 2022-23 with an indicative expected budget of £80 million going forward. There are clear ideas and plans for how that should be invested, but one could always do more with more funding.
Thank you very much. We might touch on more of that when we come to that particular question about learning disabilities and autism.

Q180 The issue of the disproportionate impact of mental health legislation on people from black and minority communities is an enduring one. The independent review pointed out to us that there is nothing inherent in mental health law that is discriminatory. It is understood that it is the implementation of the law that leads to problems. That also been reflected in the non-legislative work by the NHS in programmes such as the advancing mental health equalities strategy, the workforce racial equality standard and the long-term plan.
Will those programmes be continued in future? Given the express aim of this legislation, what other workforce strategies will need to be put in place?

This whole area is a major problem that has dogged mental health for years. We are currently in a position where people from black and black British backgrounds are subject to the Mental Health Act about four to five times more than expected. For community treatment orders, that is even worse, where on the latest data it is elevenfold.

I do not underestimate what a big task we have. We are doing some important things at the moment. We have done some pilots on the patient and carer race equality framework in four trusts. The learning from that is that we need to train a workforce that not only matches the population it serves ethnically and culturally, but has co-produced ways of ensuring equality of access and of experience. One of the issues coming out of that is that people need a much better understanding of human rights. In all our work, particularly the quality improvement work that will go around this, we will be focused very much on inequalities.

We heard on our visits yesterday that it is lower-grade staff on the front line who very often bear the brunt of any difficulty in the system at all and that perhaps there is an undue expectation on them. Would you agree with that? Does that understanding of the interface and the dynamic around front-line staff need to go higher up the professional chain?

It is different in different settings. Where I work, on the street, I would be a front-line member of staff. I would see people sometimes in food outlets, sometimes on the street itself and so on. That applies to a number of community-based teams. They are led by more senior people.

I am aware that on in-patient units they find it quite difficult to recruit band 5 and band 6 staff. In some places, they have 40% vacancies. It is a serious issue, and there is not an immediate way of solving this except making in-patient services a more attractive place to work.

Q181 We have been looking at the evidence behind these proposals. One of the few areas, if not the only area, where there is peer review evidence to say that a change would benefit ethnic minority and black communities is that of advance choice documents. They are now not included in the Bill. I was just wondering whether you had a view on that. The Government’s view, if I am fairly saying it, is that they do not want to constrain the procedure in order to do these, but there is very good evidence to say they help reduce detention, particularly in black and minority ethnic communities. What is your view of the lack of ACDs in the Bill?
I would be more in favour of ACDs being in the Bill.

I support that view. Particularly thinking about discrimination and inequality with respect to people from black and ethnic minority groups who have learning disability and autism, advance documents would help.

That is also in the context of other measures to improve how we inform, empower and support people to take a collaborative approach to their care and treatment and to give them a greater opportunity, wherever possible, to question and challenge what they may see as being unfair or unreasonable.
Can I just pick up on the point about advance choice documents, Professor Kendall? Do you feel comfortable that there is the infrastructure to manage the production of advance choice documents?

At this time, no. This would be a major change. The whole Bill sets a tone and an approach to mental health that we really should embed in the system. Advance choice documents are one way in which we could ensure our relationship with patients is much more collaborative, respectful and so on.

In a sense, that is to adhere to the four principles of the independent inquiry. You also mentioned human rights. Do you see that also as part of what should be embedded in the system, more so in terms of people working within the system?
Yes, I do.
That is really helpful.

Could either of you say any more about this issue of collaboration? The Government’s position, as we have so far understood it, on advance choice documents is that creating them and making them statutory means they will trump every other kind of collaborative interface between patient and clinician or patient and supporter.
Is there any validity in that fear? In practice, if there were a statutory requirement to have advance choice documents, is that all there would ever be? Would some people be disadvantaged by that?

I find that very difficult to forecast and project. What I was alluding to in terms of collaboration is that there is a wider sense, not just within the Bill but in healthcare generally, of trying to move towards much greater engagement and choice with identified patients, and dialogue between clinicians and patients about treatment, benefits and outcomes. There would be a concern that, if you have an advance choice document, it may have too rigid an interpretation or application.
I do not hear you saying that is a reason for not having them in the Bill.

No. This is about how you go forward and implement it, how you get people to work with those and how you lay out in a code of practice what would be best practice in working with an advance choice document.

We have heard from previous witnesses that digitisation is making a difference in other spheres. I am looking at Professor Kendall because I know you are very focused on technology and how it can be applied to support the system as a whole. Perhaps that is a way to ease it.

I am sure there are ways of easing this, but I need to be quite clear. Mental health has a Mental Health Act, which no other part of medicine has. That always threatens to make the relationship between the professional and the patient very asymmetric and one that you would rightly consider to be a power relationship. Patients often find that difficult. What this Bill does is transform that relationship. It is our job to embed that in the system, and it will be a big change.
Professor Kendall, would you be suggesting that every patient who came into contact with secondary mental health services should have an advance choice document?
No.
Could you just explain which specific groups or who should have them?
The number of people who are subject to the Mental Health Act is remarkably small by comparison to the number of people coming through mental health services.
You would say that only once the Mental Health Act has been triggered should we be thinking about advance choice documents, in case they were detained a second time.
I am thinking on the hoof here, but in my view it would be people who are likely to be detained.

I am just thinking about the workforce implications, which we come back to again. You could argue that this would affect quite a few people. The threshold for referral to secondary mental health services is fairly high. If someone is taken on to the caseload, there is always going to be a chance that they might be detained. Are we going to end up in a situation where, de facto, anybody who is under the caseload of a community mental health team needs to have an advance document done for them?

No, I do not think so. We would have to think through how to do this and how to put some structure around it. There are people I work with who are homeless, who I do not think are ever likely to be detained, but a small proportion might be. I have detained only six people in 15 years. I would be able to work out reasonably which ones are most likely.
You are saying that is a matter of your clinical judgment. That is much more difficult to put into statute, which is coming back to the point Baroness McIntosh was asking you about.
It is difficult, but I would not say it is impossible.
It is very difficult.
It is probably about how you craft the wording of the statute to keep it broad so you do not fetter too much in terms of detail.
Then you put more detail on how that would be done in the code of practice.

Q182 Your evidence, in common with others, supports the direction of travel with people with learning disabilities and autistic people, and the changes proposed in the draft Bill, while expressing concern about diversion to other routes, especially under Part III. What can be done to minimise these risks, especially the risk of diversion to prison?

In terms of alternatives, you might be thinking about what needs to be commissioned by ICBs, for example, or perhaps for people who are on dynamic support registers. I would be very interested in how you think the risk is going to be minimised.

Just to reiterate, yes, we do support the proposal because it is certainly consistent with the aim of the programme to reduce reliance on hospital admission as a solution to supporting people who are experiencing mental health or behavioural problems and crises.

To mitigate that, what investment is there to support people at the right time and in the right place? How can we intervene early? How can we support people in their own homes and communities? In addition to the general investment into community learning disability teams, we would think about people who might be at risk of offending, early intervention with young people with autism, psychosocial interventions, the work of forensic child and adolescent community teams, the work of forensic teams generally, and increasing awareness and knowledge within the wider health system about learning disability and autism. These are all investments that we are making already and will continue to do so.

There is reference to care, education and treatment reviews, which we regard as important ways of giving some scrutiny and enabling people to look in some detail at the support needs people have, potentially as a way of avoiding admissions.

We made reference to our work on dynamic support registers. Again, the idea of there being registers is raised in the draft Bill. We are about to produce a refreshed policy on care, education and treatment reviews and dynamic support registers, which are there to be pre-emptive, enabling local systems to be aware of people who may be at risk of admission and put in appropriate support, in a timely and proactive way, to try to avoid crises developing where people may need to be admitted or may be at risk of offending.

We already have quite a high number of people with learning disabilities and autism in prison. How worried are you about an increase in people not getting enough support and going to prison? I only ask this question because it has been raised by so many of the people we have spoken to. How worried should we be? Can we be reassured by the measures you are taking through NHS England? Professor Kendall, do you want to come in?

In terms of learning disability and autism, I would have to give way to Roger. With something like this, there is always a risk that you will end up with more people going to prison and that kind of thing. We need to be sure that those unwanted consequences do not happen. We will need a lot of very good data as we go into this.
One should continue to be worried and to act on that worry by scrutinising this. One should continue to look at the evidence, look at the data and find ways of proactively working with that.

It is reassuring to hear from colleagues working in the health and justice system about how much progress is being made within the system on finding ways of supporting people with learning disabilities and autistic people, particularly within prison services, where there are some very interesting developments very specifically aimed at autism, for example.

We need to be vigilant and aware of that, and we need to work closely with those clinical colleagues who, quite rightly, raise concerns about how they may be able to work with a future Act in order to respond appropriately to people who may be at risk of offending or those who have offended. Inevitably, there will be some people with a learning disability for whom a custodial or criminal justice route may be appropriate, but there will also be people who need further help and assistance, and a better assessment of the nature of their offending.

Q183 Professor Kendall, we have heard much evidence about the problems in A&E departments and the gap in the Mental Health Act that covers A&E departments. The staff in those departments are spending a huge amount of time looking after people who are not covered by the Mental Health Act. A huge amount of police time is also taken up with supporting those staff. What is your view about extending the Mental Health Act to cover that gap in A&E departments?

I think it would be a disaster, quite literally. I have a programme of work where we are trying to reduce out-of-area placements and 12-hour waits in A&E for people with mental health problems. We have had some quite good success. We brought down out-of-area placements by 60% to 70% over the last 18 months. I did that in my trust when I was medical director 15 years ago. There are ways of doing it, but you cannot stop. You have to keep working at it.

It amounts to having a really effective urgent and emergency care pathway for mental health with crisis teams, crisis houses and crisis cafés, all as alternatives to admission, so you never end up in a position where you do not have a bed. Then people do not wait. If you introduce a holding power into A&E, one problem is that you will find police take people to A&E far more readily than they perhaps might otherwise.

Secondly, there are people who go to A&E with mental health problems, who have perhaps taken an overdose or self-harmed. They would not go because of the fear they could be detained. The perverse consequence of this would be really unwanted.

You would therefore support Sir Simon Wessely’s view that the way forward is to have increased crisis services and additional facilities away from A&E departments to deal with that crisis point and try to ensure they do not become embedded in the A&E system.

Yes. Because of the pandemic, we advanced setting up crisis lines in every part of England. Everywhere now has them. That was done two years earlier that we otherwise would have done it. We have crisis lines; we have £300 million of additional investment per year into alternatives to admission, including crisis houses, crisis teams and so on. When that works well, you do not have people sitting in A&E for 12 hours.

Sir Simon Wessely also supported increased investment in liaison and diversion services, linking with the teams in police custody. That links also to the point on learning disabilities and autism about early intervention, early assessment and awareness of them, so they do not go down that pathway into the criminal justice system. Would you agree with that?
I would, yes.
Dr Banks, could you say very quickly whether you agree with what we have heard? Do you want to add anything?

I agree, particularly with the last point about liaison and diversion and about supports. This is a problem writ large particularly for people with learning disability and autism. A&E departments, unless appropriately welcoming and reasonably adjusted in terms of the Equality Act, can be very distressing places to be. There is a real risk that you may end up detaining people because of their response to a frightening, overstimulating and unwelcoming environment.

Q184 My question is about supervised discharge. I will keep it very brief and get to the point. It is my understanding that the provision to detain someone of unsound mind but who has decision-making capacity in the community and not in a hospital setting is a new power we have never had in 200 years of mental health law. I just wanted your reflections on crossing that Rubicon and moving from the Mental Health Act being a power that detains in a hospital setting to a piece of legislation that can also detain in the community setting.
Do you mean community treatment orders?

I mean the new supervised discharge power, building on the back of the case of MM in the Supreme Court, whereby somebody is conditionally discharged into an environment that effects a deprivation of liberty. It can be authorised in the context of someone who lacks decision-making capacity under the DoLS, but when someone has decision-making capacity there is a gap in the powers.

As I understand it, the Bill puts greater emphasis on collaboration between the community and the in-patient consultants where these things apply, which would be good and important. They would be more subject to regular review by tribunals.

I am concerned about extending these kinds of powers into the community. When community treatment orders were introduced, a lot of consultants pursued these and had lots and lots of patients on community treatment orders. That is in spite of the fact that there is randomised control trial evidence showing that there is no specific benefit from them. I am keen that we should ensure that supervised discharges of any kind are subject to close scrutiny.

That is a really interesting point because one of the pieces of evidence we have received is that, although it is a change, we should not be so concerned about it because it will affect fleetingly few numbers of people. Yet we have had already in the inquiry—I was not here, but several of our members were—this same discussion about CTOs.

Would you anticipate that there is a danger, with any of these changes, that what might be intended to apply to a fleetingly small number of people opens up a Pandora’s box to become a new form of discharge planning for forensic patients? One could start thinking about these halfway house settings, where one can be discharged through detention in the community under these powers.

I would be very cautious about these things. It is very important that we set up an effective quality improvement programme around all different aspects of the Act. How different consultants use the Act varies hugely. You can have two consultants working in comparable communities with very different rates of detention or supervision et cetera. That needs to be explored and explained, and people need to be able to say why they do it and why others do not. Our response to this has to be to put it into the open air.

Thank you very much. Thank you to both of you very much indeed. I am sorry the time has run out so quickly. We are extremely grateful to you for making time to come to us today. What you have had to say is a really important contribution to our deliberations. Thank you so much.
Panel 2

Witnesses: Maria Caulfield , Minister for Mental Health and Women’s Health Strategy, Department of Health and Social Care; Caroline Allnutt , Deputy Director, Mental Health Act, Serious Mental Illness and Offender Health, Department of Health and Social Care; David Nuttall , Deputy Director, Neurodiversity, Disability and Learning Disability, Department of Health and Social Care; Damian Hinds , Minister of State, Ministry of Justice; Anna Lacey , Deputy Director, Female Offenders and Offender Health Policy, Ministry of Justice.

Q185 Welcome, everyone, to the second session of our final panel. If I may ask each and every one of you just to say who you are and whom you represent, that would be marvellous. We will then go straight into questions. Could I begin with our Ministers, please?
I am the Minister with responsibility for mental health and learning disabilities.
I am the Minister for Prisons and Probation at the Ministry of Justice.
I am a deputy director at the Ministry of Justice responsible for offender health policy and female offenders.
I am deputy director at the Department of Health and Social Care with responsibility for serious mental illness and reform of the Mental Health Act.
Good afternoon. I am the deputy director for neurodiversity, disability and learning disability at the Department of Health and Social Care.

Q186 We will start with Minister Caulfield on this question. When we have been looking at the draft legislation, it has significant impacts on community services, tribunal work and second opinion appointed doctors. We all agree that all three of these things are a step in the right direction, but we have heard from a number of witnesses that this will create resourcing and funding issues.
Are you confident, Minister, that there is not just the funding but the personnel resourcing and the will to deliver these changes when they come into law, as we hope they do?

I want to reassure the committee on that point. Outside of the legislation, this is the direction of travel we want to go in anyway, providing support and care for patients with mental health problems at a much early stage of intervention and making sure that the principles behind the Bill are in everyday practice, not just as part of the legislation, so that patients get treatment where they want it, when they need it, and they have a voice in that. That means investing in resources across the board outside of the legislation. That is why £2.3 billion a year of additional funding is going in from next year, to resource financially the work we are doing.

Sir Charles, you made the point about staffing. We have committed to 27,000 additional mental health workers. We are making good progress on that. By June this year we had 6,900 additional workers. We also have capital programmes at work so that we can improve facilities in the community.
