One is what we call N EU - plus for the existing fleet of reactors that, without being too technical — that is Tim ’ s world—want to increase the burn - up and the cycle of the fuel in the reactor and increase efficiency.

If we move down the path of advanced modular reactors we will need a much higher level of enrichment. We are doing the preparatory w o rk for that , but as a private company , at the moment , there is no market. A lot of design is being discussed. I think the latest count of the I A EA is about 76 different designs. We do not know wh ich will be the winne r. W e do not know when the market will mature or will eventuate.

We find ourselves in a bit of a chicken - and - egg exercise where reactor developers need the fuel to prove their technology , and fuel developers need to have enough demand to be able to make the necessary investment in a categor y 2 facility , which requires significant investment. That is the work we are doing at t he moment , so w e are expecting the G overnment to help us along that path .
Q244 T o be clear for people watching at home, if we were to source uranium we would have to rely on global supply chains, but we have our own uranium enrichment capability here in the UK.

Yes. The UK is one of the only countr ies in the world that has an onshore enrichment capability . There is depleted uranium in the UK as well , but at the moment uranium is mined in Kazakhstan, Canada and Africa. Th ose are the main countries w here you can mine uranium, but in terms of the critical path in enriching uranium the UK has that capabilit y. I n the north - w est of Englan d we have a facility in Capenhurst , close to Cheste r , where we employ about 840 people, plus almost 50% more contractors .
Q245 Professor Abram, is there anything you would like to add ?

O nly to underline the point Lauren t made about the availability of uranium. Please do not be under the illusion that it is a very rare mineral ; it is anything but . It has about the same isotopic abundance in the earth ’ s crust as tin, zinc or other stuff . W e often find it when we are prospecting for other minerals . T here is a lot of uranium in the earth ’ s crust and, as Lauren t said , it is available in a wide range of countries , including many that are politically very stable and easily accessible , like Canada and Australia. T here is not any significant concern about uranium availability . I think that is the take - home.
Q246 More generally, what are the strengths and weaknesses of the UK ’ s uranium supply chain, and how can the weaknesses be overcome?

To start with the positives , th e great strength is U renco . I t really is the jewel in the UK ’ s crown in terms of the nuclear fuel cycle . Laurent can c lose his ears at this point , if he wants to . Its technology is genuinely world-leading; it is very good.

Our weakness , probably , is that the next step in the chain is taking that enriched uranium product and manufacturing it into nuclear fuel. Th at is currently done at a site called Springfield s , to the w est of Preston in n orth - w est England. Most of S pringfield ’ s business is involved in manufacturing fuel for our advanced gas -cooled reactors, the AGRs. As I am sure you are all very well aware , t hree of those stations have already closed ; another two w ill close in 2024 , and the remaining two w ill close in 2028. Therefore, that fuel business based at Springfield s has a very precarious future . I f you put aside our very small naval nuclear fuel manufacturing site that is run by Rolls - Royce, that is our only fuel manufacturing site in the UK .
I can only thank Tim for his nice words about Urenco . Yes, the UK benefits from Urenco being here. The UK also benefits from the existence of the Springfields site and Westinghouse.

When we take natural uranium, we mine it and then there is one step necessary between mining and enriching: conversion. You need to add fuel so that you have a gas; then you can enrich the gas in the centrifuges.

The current world energy crisis is creating a spotlight on the fuel cycle. The UK is uniquely positioned to have all the chains in the fuel cycle: conversion, enrichment and fabrication. We should not undermine that competency. Not only do we do that for the UK market, but we also export it. Urenco sells to 50 different customers in 21 different countries. We are the leader after Rosatom. Rosatom, at the moment , is being disqualified. There is this capability that we can not only use and leverage for the domestic market in the UK but export.
Q247 Forgive me for not understanding the technical details, but what is the average shelf life of a piece of nuclear fuel that is used for a reactor before it becomes nuclear waste?

Once you have made it, the shelf life is, I would say, infinite; it is measured in tens of thousands of years. Using it in a reactor depends on the reactor. In a typical light-water reactor, they operate in 18-month cycles. The fuel sits in the reactor for three of them—so, about four and a half years. Its energy has then been depleted to the point where it is no longer providing useful amounts of power and it is permanently discharged.
Q248 Professor Abram, would it be a problem if we had no manufacturing capability in the UK for nuclear fuel?
That is a very good question that probably requires a more complete answer than I am capable of giving . I will have a go.

Nuclear fuel manufacturing — I take the entire piece; all the stages involved in that — conveys two distinct advantages to the UK. One is it is a valuable economic activity. Clearly, it is one that we make quite a bit of money on. The other is that it bestows upon us a level of energy independence that we do not need to discuss any further. We are well aware of that.

It is absolutely true that uranium is not indigenously sourced. Uranium is easily sourced, as I have said already, from countries where there is no serious prospect of us not being able to get hold of it. A long time ago, when I first started in the industry and everything was controlled by the CEGB, we used to maintain strategic supplies—very large amounts of stored uranium. Those days are long since gone because there is no need to do it.

We heard from previous panels about reactor developers, reactor development. Those reactors will have a life of 60 to 80 years. They will need fuel for those 80 years. When we think about energy dependency — Tim touched on it — it is important to think about, “Okay, I ’ m going to invest that much money in the reactor. How am I going to fuel it?” Developing those skills and capabilities is a good mitigation to shock us into thinking about something happening that we were not foreseeing in developing the whole chain and leveraging the existing capabilities.

The problem is when you stop something. We have seen that with the deployment of the nuclear fleet. You have the supply chain, you have the skills and then you stop and those skills disappear. Then you have to rebuild it again. It is quite critical for the UK to consider the entire supply chain. Again, it has a lot of assets already in-country that should be leveraged.

Q249 Conversations with previous panels included the degree of Government intervention, whether through the financing of new nuclear programmes or the financing of research and development. You heard our exchanges. From what you said, Mr Odeh, should the Government take a view on what it needs to do to secure UK manufacturing capability?

My short answer would be yes, absolutely. Why? At the moment , those developments are still at the start. We have been talking about it for years but you heard about the timeline—are we talking about the 2030s, 2040s? You need to be able to build those capabilities within that timeframe and supply those reactors going forward.

As we do not have a market yet, it is difficult for a private company to make the investment without knowing the size of the price in the market. The way we have been positioning it is to say, “We need a kick - start. We need the support to be able to build, for example, the fuel bank because today we don ’ t know which of the reactors will be the winners and will be able to get licensing going forward.”

If the reactor developers need some certainty on the availability of the fuel, the concept of a fuel bank , w e have enough visibility to make the necessary investment in different capabilities — because today our centrifuge can enrich to that level — but we do not have the security credential s , we do not have the licensing, we do not have all the necessary ancillary systems to make that happen. This is a significant investment and we need to have some kind of certainty about the market size required for us to make those investments.
Q250 Briefly, Professor Abram, do you agree with the analysis that the Government should take a view on the UK manufacture of fuel?

I would like to think that the Government took a view on it, yes. Absolutely, I stand behind everything that Laurent said. From the enrichment side, it is not so much that there is a technology need, because there isn ’ t . Urenco are perfectly capable of taking that technology and designing a plant to produce the more highly enriched material .
It is a classic market failure. The Urenco board, I think, would not be open to the idea of, “Build it and they will come.” They want some financial certainty.

If you move downstream to fuel manufacturing, if we look beyond AGR and ask ourselves, “Are we going to be able to continue to manufacture nuclear fuel indigenously?” , for the large light-water reactors that you discussed earlier, that is a challenge. The market tends to be dominated by very large, existing incumbent players that have very close links to the reactors they sell. For example, the big players are Westinghouse, Framatome in France and Tecnatom in Russia.

There is an interesting opportunity. You were talking in the last session about advanced modular reactors. The dominance of incumbents there does not exist; there are no incumbents. This offers a very interesting opportunity for the UK to get in at the beginning when there are no gigantic players already.
Thank you very much. That is very enlightening.
Q251 Thank you both for coming.

I want to ask about a couple of relatively recent developments and how they have affected the UK ’ s enrichment and fuel manufacturing industry. First, what impact has the Russian invasion of Ukraine had? Russia represents about 20% of global enrichment. Is it good news that we are getting more business? Are there any interventions we have had to make to ensure we have security of supply?

What happened on 24 February created a market imbalance. We were moving from a world where there was significant oversupply in the enrichment market to a world where you have the biggest player that is disqualifying itself. We have seen a different dynamic. We have seen people self-sanctioning, saying, “We will no longer deal with Russia.” That is the decision we made as Urenco ; we terminated our contract with Russia. People came to us to say, “We need additional enrichment services. Can you help?” We are absolutely looking at helping people in eastern Europe heavily reliant on Russian fuel. The Russians were selling the reactors and the fuel that comes with those. So there was a high reliance on the fuel.

If we start thinking about potential expansion, we are moving from a world where there is ample capacity but the biggest player is disqualifying itself. It creates in the western world a shortage of capacity. Before we are able to make those investments in additional capacity, we need to ensure that we have the right policy framework —a t the moment, there is nothing disqualifying Russia from delivering the fuel —and that we have enough support from our utility customers through long-term contracts.

You cannot increase enrichment capacity by flapping fingers. It takes a long time in the making. We have learned from experience. We built an enrichment plant in the UK, starting in 2010 and ending in 2015 [1] . We had to impair that site a couple of times because we were somehow anticipating demand.

At the moment , we are creating opportunity. We are having numerous discussions with policy makers and utility clients. Yes, we stand ready to supply the world and the western world. We believe that is our duty, as a company, because there are only two enrichers in the western world. It is our duty to be ready, but we need enough visibility to do so.
Q252 Urenco would have been disappointed by EDF ’ s decision to use French fuel manufacturers for Hinkley Point C. To what extent does that put the future of your business at risk?
I will not comment on past decisions made by a significant client of ours. We are dealing with 50 different customers in 20 different countries.
Q253 Of course , but l ooking specifically at the UK —

Looking specifically at the UK, we are a significant supplier to EDF globally. Urenco is a significant supplier to EDF and we intend to continue that. Simone came to Capenhurst last week. I am going to Paris after this meeting to meet them. We work closely with EDF. Decisions made in the past are decisions that were made in the past. We are looking forward to the future.

Q254 With regard to Sizewell C, EDF have said they are looking to eliminate the use of freshly mined uranium and do more recycling. How well set up is Urenco to work with that? Do we have the recycling facilities in the UK to generate potentially the fuel for Sizewell? Have any agreements been signed for fuel for Sizewell C yet?

I will not comment on specific deals. What I can say is Urenco is capable of enriching reprocessed uranium. We can do that in our facility in t he Netherlands. We have the technology and we can also easily instal it in the UK if there is a market need to do so.

The big problem for reprocessed uranium is you need the first step before that, which is conversion. That only takes place in Russia. At the moment , as we do not allow transport of UF6 from Russia to any of our sites, we are unable to do that enrichment of the processed uranium, but we have the technical capabilities to do so. If there is a market need, we are willing to consider additional investment there.
Q255 Are you looking at how you can replace that Russian capability with something in Europe?

Our utility customers are responsible for delivering the UF6 to our sites. We know our utility customers are looking at potential options. At the moment , for reprocessed uranium, only Russia is able to provide those services.
Q256 You have answered most of my questions. The one area we have not really approached is the future for thorium as a fuel. Can you give the pros and cons?

Thorium is not in and of itself a fuel. It is not a fissile isotope. The isotope in question is thorium-232. That is not fissile , but if you pack it around the core of a reactor it will absorb neutrons and it will transmute from thorium-232 into uranium-233. That is fissile; uranium-233 does not occur in nature but it is every bit as good a fissile material as uranium-235. It is possible to take thorium and pack it around the core of a reactor and make it into a fuel material.

The nuclear fuel industry in every country in the world, as we speak today, is based essentially on a uranium fuel cycle. That is not to say that an equivalent fuel cycle based on thorium could not be brought into existence. Today, we do not have any industrial capability to do that.

In addition, in order to kick - start such a cycle — I am referring to my earlier point about thorium not being fissile — you would have to use a uranium fissile source to create that first fissile material from thorium. From a global long-term perspective in relation to global energy supplies, it is a very good thing that thorium exists. It may very well come to be an economically viable fuel in the future—probably not today.
Q257 Simply because there has not been the investment; there is nothing inherently difficult about it .

No. It is a little more difficult because, as I said, it is not in and of itself a fissile material; you have to create fissile material from it. Having done that, you have the possibility of either recovering that uranium-233 by reprocessing and manufacturing that into new fuel. Or it is possible to operate, as the German high - temperature reactors used to many years ago, thorium and uranium fuel in tandem. The difficulty there is that that only works from a reactor physics point of view if the uranium is quite highly enriched—above that 20% limit that I was referring to before. Things like that were possible to do in the 1970s; they are very much frowned upon today.
Q258 You may not know the answer to this , but I hope you do . Why have the Indians and Chinese invested in thorium plants?

Two different reasons: China is investing in everything. You point to a nuclear technology that they are not investing in. They are spread betting. If you had their financial resources, you would probably do the same.

India, in common with Norway, is sitting on vast thorium reserves. It is very geographically specific in their case. Even today, even in India, their nuclear power programme is predicated on the uranium fuel cycle.

That concludes this session of the Committee. I am very grateful to Professor Abram and Mr Odeh for joining us today and to all our witnesses. In our next session in this inquiry, we will be looking at the place of nuclear in the green taxonomy , which came up today . To all of our witnesses, thank you very much.
[1] Witness correction: When Mr Odeh referred to a site being built in the UK, he meant to refer to a site in the US.

Witnesses

I : Rt Hon Graham Stuart MP , Minister for Climate at Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy ; and Dr Nicola Higgins, Offshore Wind Programme Director at Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy.
Examination of witnesses
Witness: Graham Stuart and Dr Nicola Higgins.

Q59 G ood morning a nd welcome to this session of the Welsh A ffairs C ommittee. I am d elighted to be joined this morning by the right hon. Graham Stuart MP , from the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy . It is great that you are with us speaking in your capacity as effectively the E nergy M inister . W e are continuing our short inquiry into floating offshore wind in the Celtic S ea . I am delighted to see here as well Dr Nicola Higgins, who leads on offshore wind strategy at the D epartment for BEIS .

We will try and move as quickly as we can through the areas we want to cover. T he re are Wales q uestions later on in the m ain C hamber , so w e all have an interest in moving as briskly as possible.

Can I start , M inister , by asking you about the UK G overnment vision for floating offshore wind? When we last looked at this issue as a C ommittee on 26 October, we heard from several panels of witnesses that included potential developers , t he Crown Estate and Tim P ick , the G overnment ’ s offshore wind champion. We heard a pretty consistent message from them about the enormous low-carbon energy - generating potential of floating offshore wind in the Celtic S ea. We also heard from them about the enormous industrial potential . I s that a vision that is aligned with the UK Government’ s thinking on floating offshore wind ?

T hank you, C hairman , and the other C ommittee members for inviting Nicola and myself to give evidence today. G lobally , 92% — Nicola will correct me , as she may be able to do on a number of technical aspects of my evidence today — of offshore wind capacity is in the floating sector . W e are unusual in a way by having our shallow continental shelf, which has allowed us to lead the world in fixed - bed offshore wind. T here is this gigantic global opportunity , a nd we think that the UK can benefit enormously.

W e are proud of what we have done on the fixed - bed , a l ot of it going on off the coast of my constituency , as it happens . W e brought in the contract for difference scheme and the first allocation round back in 2015 had £ 120 /MW h . They stuck thes e things out into the inhospitable N orth S ea with an aim of driving costs down over time. We did not know how possible that would be but it was a 70% reduction. We have transformed the economics of offshore wind for the world .

W hen I was a T rade Minister , I went from Taiwan to America to other places talking about how the UK supply chain could come in. W hen you see that 92% of it is in floating and you see — reinforced by the illegal invasion of Ukraine by the Russians — the desire all across the world to deliver the stuff , it is a huge potential. R ight now, as you know from your inquiry, we lead the world in floating — in this nascent technology — and the UK G overnment thinks that it is a tremendous opportunity.

H aving sat there in rural east Yorkshire watching that happen in fixed - bed — a tremendous success, but not really seeing the industrial capability in the UK that I would like to have seen going with it —i f I had one personal driver, other than the massive challenges of accelerating the deployment of all these energies to get us on the road to net zero, it would be, with your help , to get the right policies in place s o we maximise the number of jobs and long - term prosperity that we can generate from tackling net zero . It should not be, and for us it does not need to be , a tension between driving net zero and delivering prosperity in the long term. They should go hand in hand , and that is what we want to get right.

Q60 Minister, that is very encouraging to hear. W ould you agree with what we heard previously in our last session on this, which is t hat there is a window of opportunity for the UK to capitalise on first - mover advantage to really develop the industry and lead the world in that ?

Yes , I absolutely would. T he UK currently has 78 MW operational. Hy wind Scotland has 30 MW , Kincardine has 48 MW , a nd they are respectively the world ’ s first and largest floating wind farms. Both of course are located in Scotland , but we are committed to building on the UK’ s world - leading position and placing the UK at the forefront of the development of what is an exciting new secto r.

Q61 Are you satisfied that the targets that the UK G overnment has set specifically for floating offshore wind are ambitious enough, provide enough long ‑ range certainty for this nascent industry and really provide that strong signal that we heard the industry is looking for from G overnment to give it the confidence to unlock the investment and actually start doing this?

T hat is exactly the right question. Again, we saw it with fixed ‑ bottom wind . It was t he pipeline part of it that gi ves sufficient confidence. If you want supply chain to be invested in the UK, you have to give sufficient certainty of future orders while maintaining competitive tensions as well. I t is a balancing act . I t is something we have to constantly question ourselves about, but the pathways to our net zero obligation that BEIS and the Climate Change Committee have set out give pretty high - level confidence on that.

T h e commitment is underlined by our announcement in the British energy security strategy of our ambition to deploy up to 5 GW of floating generation by 2030, which is more than 60 times current installed capacity. I t has come up , and you will doubtless w ant to question me beyond that, but given the nascent status of the technology — we are in 2022 and there are long timelines — the 5 GW does give a pretty good starting point.

W e have set out ambitions for the longer term , in terms of net zero. The Cr own E state, whether in England , Wales or indeed Scotland , are talking about up to 24 GW potentially in the Celtic Sea , but we will continue to look a t how we give the right signals precisely in order to deliver the kind of supply chain confidence that will help deliver the industrial capacity w e would like to s ee .
Q62 I t would be helpful to look again at the targets and see whether they are aligned with what industry needs in terms of building that confidence.

B efore I start bringing in Committee colleagues, Dr Higgins, could you describe how floating offshore wind is being led within G overnment ? We heard from Tim P i ck , who the previous P rime M inister but one , Boris Johnson , appointed as the G overnment's offshore wind champion. H e talked a bit about his role. Does he still have the same role under this latest iteration of the G overnment ? H ow is floating offshore wind being driven as a project within Whiteha ll ?

Ab solutely , Tim P ick is still here and has the same role. Tim was brought in after the publication of the British e n ergy security strategy t o help drive forward the acceleration of offshore wind . I n terms of giving confidence going forward , specifically on floating offshore wind but also more broadly on offshore wind — because a lot of the supply chain for example is the same and t he turbines are the same —w e are working very closely with industry to look at how to commercialise floating offshore wind.

A t the moment it is more expensive than other technologies. As the M inister says, we have had a lot of success using our contracts for differen ce scheme to bring that down. T he first C f D project came forward , and that was in the Celtic S ea in the last C f D round , which was in July . W e are looking to how we industrialise this, how we build a supply chain and how we bring the cost down going forwards.

One of the key things we need to do that is to provide the ports and the manufacturing. We have set up a number of ways in which we work very closely with industry in doing this and also with t he Crown Estate , which is key in giving that future look forwards. As the M inister said, they have s et those 24 GW up to 2045.

A longside the M iniste r , Tim chairs the offshore wind acceleration taskforce , and that looks at various ways to accelerate offshore wind, including looking at the planning and incentive processes which go across the piece. It also has a subgroup on supply chain and infrastructure t hat is specifically looking at how we build the supply chain and the infrastructure needed.

There is also a taskforce with the industry — a floating offshore wind taskforce specifically — which has commissioned a commercialisation and industrialisation road map to see how we get to 2030 in the first instance, and then what we do to build on establishing a mature industry up to 2050 .

T he people on those taskforce s all work very closely together , a nd there is a lot of crossover between those different groups to make sure they focus on specific elements of that journey a nd there is no overlap.
That is very helpful. Thank you very much.

Q63 Beth Winter : T hank you for your time this morning , Minister and Dr Higgins. I just want to ask a bit more about t he Crown Estate . You have touched on it. W e have taken evidence from the Crown Estate and others , and concerns have been raised abou t the targets and request for acceleration of the programme by people like R enewable U K. B y what means , M inister, do you feel t he Crown Estate can be held to account by UK Go vernment for delivery of its programme ?

F irst off , BEIS officials meet regularly with t he Crown Estate , in particular in partnership with t he Crown estate’s offshore wind evidence and change programme — the O WEC programme , another acronym you can add to your list —which is an ambitious strategic research and data - led programme designed to facilitate the sustainable and co - ordinated expansion of offshore wind in the UK .

The Crown Estate is a public corporation with statutory independence , and it operates under the C rown Es tate A ct 1961. I t is charged with maximising the value of its assets and the revenue derived from it. I ts profits are paid over annually to the Exchequer , and the Ac t tasks the T reasury in particular with providing oversight and scrutiny of t he Crown Estate . I should not use language about quasi - independence , but i t has statutory independence.

The Crown Estate operates to a multi-year strategic plan, which is approved by T reasury M inisters. Treasury M inisters also approve targets for th e Crown Estate on a more regular basis , while T reasury officials meet the organisation ’ s executive team very regularly to discuss their results and progress. T he T reasury also oversees appointments to t he Crown Estate’ s governing board , and the CEO is accountable to the Treasury’ s permanent secretary as the principal accounting officer of the T reasury group.

As the Minister said, we talk regularly . I talk to my counterparts on a weekly basis and the directors of m arine on a monthly basis , and t he Crown Estate sit on the offshore wind acceleration taskforce. T hey are a key partner that we work with in this remit.

Q64 Beth Winter : W ere you aware of s ome of the concerns in the industry about the speed with which the Crown Estate is moving and also about the consistency, clarity and transparency? Is that part of your discussions with them?

In t he offshore wind acceleration taskforce , which I co-chair, on every front we are trying to get all these different parts together, some of which are statutor ily independent, some of which are not , and w e have the devolved Administrations . The re are a plethora of taskforces , and i t sounds like a busy institutional landscape , but it is precisely in order to bring people together. T here are frustrations and tensions across the piece , and that is what it exists to do — to accelerate that .

G oing back to wh at the C hairman commented on earlier, we recognise there is window : w e mus t not make the perfect the enemy of the good , and we need to move at speed. W e are trying to get those balances right and make sure , through our engagement with the statutor il y independent Crown E state , that we work in as co - ordinated a fashion as we can, knowing that every single delay costs us in terms of meeting o ur net zero commitments and in terms of our competitiveness globally.

Q65 H opefully , the report from this C ommittee will contribute to that discussion as well in terms of moving forward. W e have also heard that the Scot W ind programme has a competitive advantage over the Celtic Sea programme . Minister, w hat are you doing to establish a level play ing field between the two programmes ?

ScotWind is ahead from that point of view . H av ing come into this job relatively recently , people say, "W e think this is better than that , " but w e pretty much need them all. W e need it all. We need the Celtic S ea. T he nature of floating offshore wind — not that I a m an expert , but fortun ately Nicola is — is the sheer size of this. It makes proximity absolutely fundamental to delivery. O ur view is that Scotland is not going to scoop everything up because it is successful. There is plenty of scope for communities around the Celtic S ea to benefit as well. W e need both , and it is not one or the other.

A follow - up question would be, "I s it going to squeeze out investment? " I do no t think it is . I f we get our frameworks right and w e have our targets and the demand signals right , t here is no reason at all to feel that somehow Wales , and anyone else around the Celtic Sea , is going to be a poor er partner.
Q66 Beth Winter : You are proactively tak ing action to ensure there is a level playing field in terms of the t wo .

Yo u would probably need to identify the way in which it was not level. T he y might be ahead, but as I say, in terms of the Celti c S ea — Nicola may be able to help me out here — we d o not see that there is some significant disadvantage that needs to be overcome.

T he C limate C hange Committee has said that we need aroun d 100 GW of offshore wind to meet net zero by 2050 . W e currently have 11 GW , so there is quite a long way to go. T hat is the challenge in terms of 4 GW or even 17 GW in the recent ScotWind proposal . N either of those alone are going to take us there , so i t is absolutely right that we need both of those .

P articularly for floating offshore wind with the large foundations , w e need the port infrastructure near to those two geographies, because while at least with fixed ‑ bottom wind you can move it large distances across the sea , the huge scale of floating wind foundations makes that harder. Y ou need the ports near Scotland , y ou need the ports in the Celtic S ea as well , and w e need both to deliver the challenge that we have ahead in terms of renewable energy.

Q67 T hank you . Minister, in your opening answer you talked about how, with fixed ‑ bottom offshore wind, we perhaps did not capture as much of that industrial capacity as we should have earlier on. Keeping in mind this question of how much economic value we can hold on for the UK and for Wales from this new industry , h ow concerned are you — you might want to bring in Dr Higgins to help answer the question — t hat t he Crown Estate has the right auction process to really maximise domestic content and help build supply chains?
T hey have asked for local supply plans as part of their programme .
Do those have teeth?

The details of them are still being worked out by the Crown Estate . T he good news is this is the first time they have done it. T hey a re joining us on that journey about trying to encourage supply chain investment at a much earlier stage of the process than we can do with the C f D at the moment. They publish ed their announcement on that in October, and they a re working through the details of that at the moment.

What we have to do is set it up in a way which is compliant with our legal obligations in terms of the World Trade Organisation. Y ou cannot just specify local content, but we do everything we can using all the levers we have within those constraints to encourage and support investment in the UK.

I t is a balancing act between requirements that observe those rules and keep fair competition —a nd thus also help keep prices down for consumer s — while also providing that pipeline certainty, especially in products which are so vast , and use that to make it more likely that more of the supply chain exists in and close to where they a re deployed . I n this case that means in Wales and surrounding communities.

Q68 W elcome to our C ommittee. I was really excited about you both coming, particularly because I have BP Mo na and BP Morgan in my constituency of Ynys Môn. T o put into context h ow transformational that could be , for not only Anglesey but the whole of north Wales and Wales , BP Mo na and BP Morgan will be 1.5 GW e ach . T hat will be £3.5 billion - worth of investment each , a nd that would be 1 , 500 to 2 , 000 construction jobs and around 2 50 to 300 long ‑ term jobs. I t is not actually that far away . W e are looking for the DC O next year — 2023 — a decision on that in 20 25 and FID in 2026. W hat I a m trying to say is it is a really big deal for Wales.

H ow are you going to ensure that local communities like those on Anglesey will actually benefit from these supply chains?

Thank you for your question. As I have already addressed, we are doing everything we can to make sure that we encourage it with the supply chain plans, which we strengthened over time , and learning from the fixed bed to bring to floating. O ne of the reasons for having the offshore wind acceleration taskforce and the floating wind taskforce is to look at any barriers to deployment and enable collaboration with industry, to create the right environment for the investment in Wales to support this. A s part of our contract for difference process, supply chain plans help ensure developers make the investments we need in upgrading supply chain capability, competitiveness and productivity as well.

We recently had the £ 160 million offshore wind manufacturing investment scheme, where the industry did research to identify the gaps in the UK supply chain market. Through this and looking at blades, turbines, monopiles and foundations, we did bring companies in to Great Britain and that was open to Wales. So far none of those companies that we announced are in Wales, but we continue that work. We work closely with the industry and with D IT to see how we can bring more of the supply chain to local communities in the UK.

I have seen numbers specifically for floating, because it is somewhat nascent. By 2030, including our ambition for 50 GW , which includes 5 GW of floating, we believe it will support 90,000 direct and indirect jobs. One of the fortunate aspects of our geography and of where much of the net zero investment and development can take place is that they are the very parts of the country that we want to level up. If we can make this work then we will be bringing well-paid jobs and prosperity to communities which had historically been reliant on high carbon and are currently looking at a bleak future. This brings hope.

Q69 I t is about not only the supply chains for the turbines and the companies like Tratos for the cabling, but also the port infrastructure. As you know, ports like Holyhead are devolved to the Welsh Government . There are ports that need to have this investment so that we can take advantage of these assets. These are huge turbines that do need to be built. T he b reakwater in Holyhead needs an upgrade so that companies like BP Mona can invest there. How are you working with the Welsh Government to ensure that the y i nvest in upgrading these ports?

Shall I speak about how we work with the Welsh Government ? I have talked in governance terms about the groups we set up with industry and Government; the Welsh G overnment sit on those. T he Welsh Government officials sit on the offshore wind acceleration taskforce, the floating taskforce and the supply chain and infrastructure working group . Q70 One last question from me. T omorrow is a very, very important day for Wales because it is the deadline for the Welsh freeport bids. I am sorry to cut across you, but if we are going to capitalise on this I would have thought choosing an initial port to actually start doing these things from should be at the top of your list of things to think about.

Q75 Thank you, Chairman, and thank you, Minister and Dr Higgins , for joining us this morning. As you have already alluded to somewhat in answers to previous questions, I am wondering whether you could perhaps elaborate on some of the lessons that have been learned from the onshore wind rollout and how they may have influenced your approach to offshore wind.

First, you need to send strong signals about the G overnment ’ s desire to see local supply chain, and we do that through plans demonstrating that we have experience, have learned how best to do that and work with industry. That is what the offshore wind acceleration taskforce is a bout. Along with representatives from industry as well as from devolved Governments and others around the country, we discuss the barriers and what it takes. We then understand that cause and it feeds in.

Not only do you have to give the signal, the push and then build the understanding, you also then need to look at the pipeline. How do we make it more programmatic? We try to keep up competitive tension through the round so we can have the lowest price . If people are going to invest here, we want to get the best value for the UK in balance. An area to look at is how we maintain sufficient competition to keep prices low and protect consumers.

We also need to give sufficient confidence that they are going to have contracts for years to come, so that they will invest and that the supply chain will invest in the facilities here in order to deliver. Otherwise, if you have a limited horizon and confidence about winning contracts, the classic thing would be simply to keep buying and expanding an existing facility, perhaps in another jurisdiction, rather than establish one here.

If people knew then what we know now about offshore wind in the UK, many more companies would probably have moved operations here, but they did not. Working our way through that and ensuring we get the right balance is something that we are in the early stages of doing and that w e are challenging the D epartment to look at all the time. From next year w e are moving to our annual rounds of C f Ds. An area I really want to focus on is how to get the right balance , while adhering to our international obligations , that allows people to invest here and obtain more jobs.

Q76 We recently received evidence from some of the industry that suggested that perhaps the priorities of t he Crown Estate leasing rounds are not always aligned with some of the pressures of the C f D bid process. How do you intend to ensure that the priorities for both processes are more closely aligned? Industr y stakeholders particularly will struggle with regard to that tension between ensuring local procurement and many local contracts versus the inevitable pressures of price that come into the C f Ds.

They have moved, as shown by the introduction of the supply chain plans into their processes, and their membership of the offshore wind acceleration taskforce , among others, which has helped them to have a better understanding of broader Government and industry aspirations. We can see evidence of this starting to impact their decision making, while recognising their statutory independence. That work is going to continue.

I was given two graphs when I first arrived in the D epartment. One showed offshore wind in the UK— fantastic, leading the world. Then another graph show ed how long it takes from the start of a project to getting the turbines actually spinning. M ost of the processes taken in isolation looked perfectly reasonable, but taken together, instead of three years from start to spinning it was taking 10. We want to ensure that we avoid duplication, that we are proportionate, and part and parcel of that is ensuring we have co-ordination with t he Crown Estate as an important player and their auction process.

There are interesting questions as to the auction and monies generated from that as to the impact on the long -term pricing of energy and where t hat place s us as a country competitively . Of course , that is T reasury management and I would not de ign to go near it, but it is important to understand all these pieces together, not only in terms of deployment but also ultimately of the outcome.

I would personally not only like to have an enormous industrial sector generated from us leading the rest of the world but also, if possible, looking to be the most competitive electricity and indeed energy market in Europe. That would mean not only that we have the industry directly from delivery, but that we could be in a position where we attract other industry because we are one of the most competitive, as well as the first net zero compliant industrial base in Europe. That is where we want to be, and we have to pull these pieces together and ensure that we are not looking at them in isolation. We have to look at t he Crown Estate, the money to the Treasury and the subsequent stages as a whole.

It might be worth emphasising that t he Crown Estate, as the Minister has said, are evolving their process , a s are we — we evolved the C f D. This is the first time we are bringing supply chain plans for floating offshore wind projects , so we are both somewhat evolving in the same way. The Minister talked about speeding up the consenting processes and the Celtic Sea leasing round. The Crown Estate are looking at doing the environmental assessments at an earlier stage , which will save delays later down the line.

At the same time, we are working very closely with DEFRA to put in place an offshore wind environmental improvement package — legislative —that will enable strategic issues around the environment to be looked at from an earlier stage so that they do not act as blockers right at the end. Both t he Crown Estate and ourselves are working closely as we look to improve on what we already have.
Q77 In endeavouring to speed up the consenting process, does it really entail greater co - ordination?

One of the main things we are doing through the offshore w ind environmental improvement package is called strategic compensation. At the moment, through an HRA — the habitats regulation assessment process — you have to do no harm. If you cannot avoid doing harm, then you need some compensatory measures to improve the environment. This has to be done on a project-by-project basis , so e ach individual project ha s to resolve this for themselves , and it can become a blocker towards the end of the DCO process. So what we are trying to do is to put in place structure s so that those conversations happen at a much earlier stage of the DCO process and so that something called strategic compensation can be put in place so that projects can work together on environmental protections.

We are also setting up a m arine recovery fund. The idea is that once some of these measures have been worked out for various areas of the sea, industry can pay into that fund and that counts as the discharge of their environmental measures. T hose will be implemented by another organisation. That is an example of the work that we are doing — not reducing the environmental protections, but looking at them in a more strategic way so that they happen earlier in the process and projects can work together with the support of G overnment to deliver them more effectively among multiple projects.

Q78 That is very interesting — thank you. It is very useful information. W here potential sites might be located within areas of Welsh Government competence in terms of NRW — Natural Resources Wales— and the habitats regulation assessment , i s there early consultation and co - operation with them to ensure that there are no miscommunications or further delays down the line?
Yes, we are working very closely with our Welsh and Scottish counterparts to pull together the legislation.

Q79 Is there a resource issue here when it comes to the consenting bodies having to make decisions? Presumably if this industry takes off in the way that we have been talking about, and in the way that we hope, that will place an enormous pressure on consenting bodies to take timely decisions. Are you satisfied that they are adequately resourced and staffed to be able to do this in a timely way?
It is a discussion that we are having both with industry and with our counterparts in DLUHC and DEFRA, that own those arm’s length bodies , so it is an ongoing conversation.

Q80 There is a discussion there around N atural R esources Wales as well. W e have already picked up some concerns from within the industry in Wales that N atural R esources Wales may not have the capacity to take timely decisions. Is that a conversation you are having with them? Is there a way for some sharing of resource, making sure you have the right teams available to provide the specialist support to take good decisions?

I cannot sit here and say we have the solution at the moment, but it is an ongoing conversation. A s you say, certain elements are devolved in Wales. It is quite a complex picture in terms of planning and environmental legislation— what is devolved and what is not—but we work very closely with D EFRA who obviously have links to N atural R esources Wales as well. That is probably the best answer at the moment.
Thank you, that is helpful. We are going to move on to grid capacity now. I invite Ben Lake to begin this section again.

Q81 Thank you. Another concern we have had quite a bit from industry is good connection , which is probably a general issue in Wales , but specifically when it comes to offshore wind. W hat engagement are you having with the Welsh G overnment and o ther stakeholders on preparing the grid for a further 20 GW of floating offshore wind post 20 35?

I men tioned earlier that we need practically everything from floating wind to fixed-bed wind , w e need SMR, w e need gigawatt-scale nuclear , w e need hydrogen carbon capture —w e need all of those deployments. U nder all that is the grid, and N ational G rid say that, on a UK basis, they are going to need to invest six times more in the next seven years than they have in the last 30. I t is an enormous financial, logistical, supply chain and deployment challenge, and it is an enormous political challenge because this is going to require change. It is going to require a large amount of infrastructure, not all of which is going to be popular. We have to manage that, and if you do not have the grid then all the other stuff is not going to function and we are not going to be on target. For me, in my recent arrival in this role, g rid is right up to the top of a list of priorities .

I n terms of what is being done to ensure the grid in Wales has the capacity for future floating offshore wind projects , m easures include moving to a more strategic approach and planning the network for efficient identification of infrastructure needs, including through the recently published h olistic n etwork d esign . T hat should have been No. 4 , but we did the HND 1 , and we have HND 2 , which is going to be looking very much at the Welsh and the FLOW elements of that in the first quarter next year.

Because of this transformation we need to make, perhaps historically, if I have understood this correctly — Nicola will correct me if I have not — projects have effectively just been linked in a sort of linear fashion to shore. T hat is why we are looking for the h olistic n etwork d esign so we can minimise negative impacts on land. More can b e done off offshore. There are legislative changes : the e nergy s ecurity B ill , which has been proceeding through the Lords, has elements around these multi-connectors, offshore connectors . S o there is a lot of work going on there.

T he aim is that Ofgem e xpedite approvals for new network build, including exempting certain projects from competition. Sometimes everything is stopped by the competition system . We need to revise national policy statements to ensure joined-up approaches and the speeding up of planning and consenting processes. Through the British e nergy security s trategy — the BESS — the Government have committed to accelerating electricity network delivery, including speeding up regulatory and planning processes. W e will speed up regulatory and consenting processes for network projects, reducing timelines by three years and aspiring to halve the end-to-end process by 2025.

A s I say, the HND— the h olistic network d esign— published in July provides a first and significant step towards a more centralised and strategic approach to network planning. For the first time, offshore and onshore networks are being designed together and holistically to support the UK ambition of 50 GW of offshore wind capacity and, of course, up to 5 GW of floating. W e are going to have the HND follow-up exercise reporting, which will be shared with developers in March covering the Celtic Sea. T he new strategic approach to network planning includes upfront consideration of community and environmental impacts , which should provide more certainty in the planning and consenting process and reduce consenting times and project development risk. That is where we are at.

Q82 Does the D epartment have a view as yet on whether the good connection for the projects in the Celtic S ea should come on to land, as it were, in Wales, as opposed to say , n orth , Devon ? Has your thinking developed into that area yet?

T hat thinking is done as part of the h olistic n etwork d esign . As the M inister said, the first one of those has been published, and that has 1 GW of Celtic Sea in it, because that was what the C rown Es tate were planning on leasing at the time. An update to that has been done to take account of the further 4 GW th at the Crown Es tate are now leasing as well as some of the ScotWind projects, which were also not in the first one. T hrough that process there will be an assessment of where projects should come online. I t is literally a map of how to join things up. That is the process through which the optimal location in terms of environment, cost and communities will be looked at as to where to place those onshore landing points.

J ust to add on that, g iven the importance of the grid, it is important that we carry communities with us so they understand what we are trying to do, and that we also listen to communities and hear their messages. It is not just an engineering and financial challenge ; i t is also a challenge to en sure what we do goes with the grain of local communities.

There will be a consultation on that early in the new year on community consulting , which wa s committed to in the BESS , and options for how a community benefits from onshore networks. That is coming in the new year.

We can go with the grain and provide benefits where, in essence, necessarily there will be some disruption and we should show —at least where we cannot find a way of eliminating that—that we are listening and providing compensation and working with them rather than just riding roughshod over them. We are not going to be able to do something of this scale without that. S ometimes G overnments give the impression that it is so important we just make it a central priority and we will just r am it through. Anyone who thinks that we could r am this through against the grain of communities does not understand how a democratic country works. Working with this C ommittee, i t would be really useful to ens ure we do it in Wales in a way that people are proud of what has happened, feel compensated for where they are disrupted, but generally buy into it.
The idea of the HND process i s to reduce the number of landing points, which obviously helps community engagement.

Q83 One of the things the C ommittee has heard recently— it is quite an exciting suggestion—has been that of making the most of this opportunity in the Celtic S ea, and especially the landing points in s outh Wales, to work with industry to produce green hydrogen, and then to almost create a sort of closed - loop system. I t is quite appealing to us as Welsh MPs because, historically, we had such a closed loop between fuel source and industry back in the coal days and it strikes us that, potentially, there is an opportunity here now with offshore floating wind to produce green hydrogen, which could then, potentially in future, be an alternative to industry in s outh Wales and further a field. I am interested to know whether that is part of the Department ’ s planning, and whether you have had any representations or discussions with industry about such a proposal.

The first thing to say is , as we set out in the h ydrogen s trategy update to the market in July, we recognise that electrolytic hydrogen projects can bring significant system-wide benefits by locating them in an optimal position to help manage network constraints, or by using excess electricity that would otherwise have been curtailed or constrained because, of course, we pay for generators not to generate at certain times. If, as we massively increase our capacity, we have issues around storage to do with the intermittency and fluctuations in demand then to be able to channel that into something like green hydrogen is, obviously, a very positive outcome for us.

In that update, we committed to assess the expected impact on the electricity system of electrolytic hydrogen deployment and build evidence to ensure our position remains appropriate and facilitates economy-wide decarbonisation. My understanding is that, if you look at industry, there are certain parts where there is pretty well no route that anyone has to decarbonise it other than hydrogen and in partnership for other parts of it with carbon capture.

W hat we need is hydrogen and carbon capture in tandem, potentially coupled with negative emissions. If we can have sustainable biomass, then that could, as part of a network, provide negative emissions and, overall, give us the potential to create genuinely net zero industrial clusters, which would secure those jobs that we have in the long term. If we are a world leader and can create Europe’s leading centres where some of these major players with their commitments know they will be part of a net zero industrial cluster, then certain companies would feel this was the place to come and establish their manufacturing and other facilities. T hat is an enormous benefit in itself, especially if we develop it first and then build capacity here and then export it, but the bigger benefit might be that if we lead on creating competitive and affordable net zero industrial clusters, we can help re-industrialise areas that have lost their industry and that could be an exciting prospect.
T he C rown Estate have noted that they are happy to look at hydrogen projects as part of the Celtic Sea leasing round offshore wind projects that want to link up with hydrogen production.
Thank you. That is very useful to know.

Q84 Minister, j ust on that point, will c ontracts for d ifference need to be tweaked or amended to take account of projects that are linked together—floating offshore wind and hydrogen—so they are not being assessed purely against a floating offshore wind project ? Perhaps Dr Higgins can help .
I think i t is a very good idea to give it to Dr Higgins.
We are always looking at how the CfD needs to evolve to support—
Innovation, right?

Innovation in new technologies. As we say, the first floating wind farm came through in the last auction round, so that is pretty novel to start with. I do not have a direct answer to that but yes, we always keep the CfD under review to look at what it needs to do to support the technologies as they move forward.
Q85 O n grid capacity, we, as a Committee, recently p roduced a report on grid capacity in Wales, and we look forward to the reply from your D epartment.
Next month, I believe.

We look forward to it, but I guess one of the punchlines from that report was really recognising that what is needed is not just an incremental improvement in the timeframes for delivering new grid connections and capacity, but a massive step change and really calling for the G overnment to be very energetic and ambitious on improving the grid.

I cannot anticipate our response to the C ommittee, but you can tell from everything I have said that that is exactly what I think we need. Essentially, we have had a reactive system which has served us pretty well , looking to do the minimum necessary at lowest cost over time and respond. W e now need—I think the term is—anticipatory investment, but in order to do that and not end up creating orphan assets, you need to have a joined-up spatial strategy.

A s I say, we have the h olistic n etwork d esign process starting with that. We might, arguably, need something above that because we are going to have m arine protected areas in the N orth S ea . We are going to have hydrogen; we are going to have carbon capture. We are going to have floating offshore and fixed offshore wind. Who knows what else? The N orth Sea is this tremendous asset , along with the Celtic S ea, of course, all around the country and we need to plan it. If we are going to put the grid infrastructure in place , we need to have a strategic plan rather than just leaving it to the market and leaving it to developers to do it . I t will need more co-ordination because it is going to be such a crowded landscape.

Q86 That is an important point that came up both in relation to the grid inquiry that we undertook and also this current one into floating offshore wind : the extent to which things cannot just be left to the market , industry and the private sector to do, and the extent to which a Government plan is needed with somebody at the very top of the tree, if you like, lacing together the strategy. Minister, is that you, in relation to floating offshore wind? Are you th at person? Earlier in the session you talked about a complicated institutional landscape, I think, in relation to floating offshore wind. Are you the person that is ultimately bringing this all together?

As the M inister for E nergy, I think my title is morphing. I am appointed formally, but I think it is now the M inister for E nergy and C limate, obviously under my S ecretary of State who is the boss of the D epartment, but yes, through me, that is where we need to look to help come up with an overall approach which fulfils those strategic needs.

I should not morph off too much, but if you look at nuclear, interestingly, in a sense we had a kind of development-led approach and decided that did not work and that is why we are setting up G reat British N uclear—again, it will be a s tate-led organisation—to help recognise how hard it is for the private sector at their own financial risk to battle t hrough all this complexity when what they really want to do and what they are good at, hopefully, is building a nuclear power station and running it.

Great British N uclear is there to try and de-risk that as much as possible, which ultimately should mean that there is lower risk, lower financing cost, a better focus on what the operators are best at, and lower costs for the consumer in the end. You could make the parallel — I cannot leap to say we are going to do th is as we have no such plans at the moment — that this needs holistic joined-up leadership, which can probably only come from G overnment and, therefore, currently that is me.

Q87 I was aim ing to bring this session to a close by 11 am and we are on track to do that. Y ou mentioned the timeframe for a f reeport decision. Did you mention what the timescale is for deciding on allocation of FLOWMIS ? O r has that not been decided within G overnment yet?

We have not. We are still processing the request for information ; hopefully it will be sooner rather than later. I think we originally indicated that we would hope to do something by the end of the year. T he end of the year in G overnment terms often means March in my experience but, hopefully, we might stick to the calendar as conventionally used by others.
Thank you very much. Any final questions or remarks from colleagues? No . Minister, thank you. Dr Higgins, thank you very much for giving us your time and expertise.

sessions.iT: The effect of paramilitary activity and organised crime on society in Northern Ireland
sessions.w: Daniel Holder (Committee on the Administration of Justice (CAJ)); Úna Boyd (Committee on the Administration of Justice (CAJ))

segs.tx: Northern Ireland Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: The effect of paramilitary activity and organised crime on society in Northern Ireland , HC 24
Wednesday 23 No vember 2022
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 23 November 2022 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Simon Hoare (Chair); Sir Robert Buckland; Ste phen Farry; Mary Kelly Foy; Sir Robert Goodwill; Claire Hanna; Carla Lockhart; Ian Paisley; Bob Stewart; Mr Robin Walker.
Questions 231 - 254
Witnesses
II : Daniel Holder, Deputy Director, Committee on the Administration of Justic e (CAJ) ; Úna Boyd, Immigration Project Solicitor and Coordinator, Committee on the Administration of Justice (CAJ) .
Written evidence from witnesses:
– Committee on the Administrati on of Justice (CAJ)
Examination of Witnesses
Witnesses: Daniel Holder and Úna Boyd.

Q231 It is my pleasure to now welcome Daniel Holder—it is very nice to see you back in front of the Committee—deputy director of the Committee on the Administration of Justice, and Úna Boyd, the immigration projects solicitor and co-ordinator for the Committee on the Administration of Justice. You are both very welcome and thank you for joining us this morning.

Let me kick off panel two with the same question that I s eem to be asking everybody, which means that I can try to remember my question and, one day, I might get it right. It is on the terminology of paramilitaries and paramilitarism. It adds a certain, I am sure, lustre or status in the minds of some people, or a sense of self-applied importance for people who might otherwise feel that they do not have a role, who feel rather insignificant in society, et cetera. What is your thinking on that issue?

You will have heard in question one that we have been taking evi dence where people have pointed to the child grooming and child abuse element of this, and to people trafficking, modern slavery, indentured labour, gangmasters, and so forth. Your views on that issue would be welcome.

The term “paramilitary ” has been around for quite a while. We have tended to increasingly use, I have to say, the term “armed groups”. I do think, though, that there is merit in characterising some of the actions that are undertaken by armed groups. Using some of the terminolog y that you suggest, to throw a few more in, paramilitary-style attacks are a form of torture. We would not shy away from that word being used.

In addition, in terms of our area of focus and our research, which you will have seen from the written evidence, we have focused a lot on housing intimidation and some of the accompanying expression. Calling out paramilitary expression or paramilitary protected expression that is designed for the purposes of racist and sectarian intimidation as such is also helpful. Calling stuff out that is racist and that is sectarian delegitimises that type of activity.

That said, I do not think that it would be comprehensive enough just to deal with the issue of paramilitarism as some sort of extended crime wave. I am sure that that is not what is being suggested. The harms of paramilitarism and the nature of the groups are much broader, and will need a tailored and very different process.
That was very much the professor’s view of that sort of granular approach.

Conflating the whole thing just as an organised crime issue would not be effective. A broader strategy is needed in terms of getting these groups out of business, wh ich is what we all want, that goes beyond criminal law.

Q232 You are the first witness in this inquiry to use the word “torture”, which is a very powerful word. For the record, which would be helpful to this Committee and to the wider audience who may re ad or listen to our evidence, could you give us one or two examples of cases that you have looked at, heard about, read about or been briefed on that legitimise the use of that word “torture” and how it has been deployed?

The word “torture” has a very specific legal meaning. As you know, it is protected under article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, is part of the Good Friday Agreement, is incorporated into Northern Ireland law and is a key part of the peace process.
Q233 I was not questioning the legitimacy of the use of the word. I was merely asking you just to evidence it for the record.

In terms of that threshold and that legal standard, de facto—and I am not talking now about individual cases—all punishment s hootings and punishment beatings meet that threshold and should be rightly considered as acts of torture. We are on a different path at the moment , but, if we end up with a proper ECHR-compliant process for dealing with the past, it would have to be able t o deal with and investigate issues of torture, which would include punishment-style attacks, as they have been called, or paramilitary-style attacks, which is the phrase that this Committee has been using.

Q234 There is going to be a differential, is the re not, in community response and possibly authorities’ response? If somebody is trying to muscle into somebody else’s turf, they get beaten up or shot in the leg, or whatever it may happen to be, which will engender a set of responses. If somebody is pedd ling drugs in an area where the police are not a viable presence, they get taken off and sorted out. A lot of people would see the people who do the sorting out or who do the torture as local heroes, would they not? How do we address that? How do we take a way this caped crusader, community champion approach?

Essentially, you are asking, “How do we end paramilitary-style attacks?” That is a very difficult question. You would have to have the will of the groups themselves to go out of business, which requires some sort of process with those in existence. Thankfully, within the mainstream IRA, that process of punishment violence has ended in that sense, where there was the political will more broadly to go out of business. With other groups, you would need to work with the elements who were willing to transition. You would have to have some sort of process. They would have to have the authority within those groups to carry that through.

When you are dealing with groups that are very factionalised and disparate, that is going to be an awful lot more difficult. You would also have to have some sort of alternative in place, and that is where the successes of the various restorative justice schemes at community level come in. You do need some sort of transitional process, which is not really in place at the moment , in order to move that issue forward.

Q235 In her evidence in the first session, Professor Breen- Smyth talked about people living in pockets. If you are talking about the Fall s Road, the Shankill or the Bogside, you know exactly which communities you are talking about. People living in segregated housing send their children to schools that are, in effect, segregated. What evidence is there that paramilitary intimidation is a ma jor driving factor behind housing segregation?
Housing intimidation is pretty rife . We know that from the statistics, and they are in the written evidence, but there are hundreds of cases every year.
Q236 Does it have to be o vert or do people just understand that it is not a good idea to go and live in that area?

It is the latter. The recorded cases really are the tip of the iceberg. People will generally know where it is not safe to live, because of their backg round, and where they are likely to face sectarian or racist intimidation if they move into a particular area.

One of the issues, however, which we raise in our written evidence, is that there are significant data gaps here. You can map where some of the p ockets are by where the attacks are taking place, but sometimes journalists have had to try to work out, from what limited information they have been able to get under freedom of information, in which areas housing intimidation and people being made homele ss through paramilitary intimidation is occurring. The disaggregated data that you would need is not being produced, in terms of setting out which groups are responsible for this in which area.

The PSNI and the Northern Ireland Housing Executive are making assessments on individuals that “must be rehoused”, because they would be at risk of serious injury or death if they were not moved out of that situation. We would like to see a situation whereby the state response to that moves beyond simply verifying th at the threat is credible and moving the victim. At the moment , it is not even being properly documented what patterns there are in particular areas or which group is felt to be responsible. It is known, if you are making that assessment, but information o n patterns is not being made available. If you produced the pocket-type map that you are suggesting, the policing services and other public authorities would have something to go on in terms of a strategy for dealing with this.

What is remarkable is that t his is rife and is known in the areas in which it occurs. It is known that it is unsafe and that you cannot live there. It is part of a much broader pattern of paramilitary coercion, but it is not mentioned anywhere in the Executive’s action plan to tackle paramilitarism. Nor was it mentioned in the 2015 assessment of paramilitary groups, commissioned by the Secretary of State, which had a long list of areas of criminality that named paramilitary groups were involved in, from drugs to counterfeit goods and things like that, but made no reference to housing intimidation, despite how prevalent it is.

It made no reference to racism or to sectarianism, despite the well-documented and connected links between some elements of loyalist paramilitarism and racist vio lence. It was not mentioned at all, so there are clear omissions in the strategy and in the practice of public authorities in dealing with this very serious issue.

We also find that a related issue to this is the use of paramilitary expression. I am not ta lking about legitimate political expression but about the use of flags or other items to mark an area of territory as a form of racist and sectarian intimidation. It could be in the form of, say, a black family moving into a street and paramilitary or unio n flags being put up to try to intimidate them out of the property or, indeed, having a new shared housing development and paramilitary flags being put up to deter people from other communities.

At the moment , there is a policy not only of non-intervention by the PSNI with such displays, but, in some circumstances, of protecting that paramilitary expression, because it is all done through the lens of public order. “Will the people who put this up riot if it is taken down? Therefore, we will prevent it from being taken down”. In that sense, you lead, paradoxically, to a situation where you incentivise and institutionalise paramilitary control of public space. There are a lot more state interventions and different approaches that could be but are not taken to deal with this particular issue . It is a source of huge concern.

Q237 Would that extend to businesses—either the ownership or maybe people employed in a business? If you are in a particular area, would you be very much discouraged from taki ng on staff who maybe came from a different area?

I am sure that the answer to that question is yes. A specific focus of our research has been on housing intimidation, but workplace intimidation has been a problem for many years. It is one o f the areas where there has been at least a degree of success through quite vociferous equality law and intervening in changing the composition of workforces, as well as being able to deal with harassment in the workplace.

Q238 You referenced in your wri tten evidence the issue of housing intimidation. What has been the effect of not including housing intimidation in the overall assessments and what is the route to getting it being so?

One issue that was raised by your previous witness is vi ewing everything through the national security lens. I know that another member had asked for a definition of that. From our perspective, strategies to tackle paramilitarism need to deal with all the harms created by armed groups, whether they are targeted at the state or at individual citizens. If you take the annual threat assessment that is conducted by the security service and published by the Northern Ireland Office—the Northern Ireland-related terrorism threat, separate to the UK threat—it focuses on national security threats. This is teased out in the reviewer’s reports.

Things like housing intimidation are not included at all in that threat assessment. Threat assessment ultimately focuses mainly on threats to the state, the majority of which have bee n to police officers and are from dissident republicans. The majority, but not all, of housing intimidation comes from loyalist groups, so it is not factored into that threat assessment.

But then the resource issue kicks into this. We have issues with the arrangement of the national security resource through MI5 in terms of an accountability gap that it creates. The problem is that you end up with very significant resources going into tackling a particular element of the paramilitary threat, which is import ant, but the same resources not going into tackling this particular phenomenon of housing intimidation, which is not even considered as part of the official assessment of paramilitary threat. That may be one of the reasons why it was missed out of the 2015 assessment, and its omission from the 2015 assessment has had a knock-on effect, in that it is not in the action plans then picked up by Stormont.
Q239 Are there alternative approaches that could be used to verify?

Yes. There are alternative approaches that can be used to deal with the issue far more broadly. We need to move away from simply verifying that a threat is credible and moving the victim. It is almost as if this area has become normalised. As in the previous answer, it i s not even properly documented. The patterns are not put out there.

The policing board has raised questions about this. At times, the police have even said, “We do not know what policing purpose it would serve”. It was pretty clear . If you identify the pat terns of paramilitary intimidation on housing and which groups are responsible, then you can develop a strategy to deal with that, to intervene and to begin to convict people of these offences.

Intimidation is a criminal offence. When The Detail, the inve stigative website, looked at this a number of years ago, they identified a couple of thousand cases of paramilitary intimidation and only 32 convictions, so clearly the rule of law needs to be applied to this area. We should cease approaches that are simpl y trying to manage this type of paramilitary activity and are effectively normalising it rather than dealing with it.

Q240 You will be aware, Mr Holder, that this Committee held an inquiry relatively recently on the impact and experience of migrant and i mmigrant communities coming to Northern Ireland. Would you say a word or two about housing intimidation that you might be aware of with regard to those communities?
Yes, I will do. I will maybe pass to my colleague Úna as well.
Ms Boyd, let us hear from you.
Úna Boyd: Daniel can start. I will come in. He was on a roll.

There have been clear links identified for a long time between elements of loyalist paramilitaries and racist violence. That was brought up by the previous Independent Reporting Commission. A German magazine dubbed Belfast the race hate capital of Europe at one point, and that experience is pretty rife . We have heard the theory that there are more attacks against ethnic minorities in mostly unionist areas because that is where most ethnic minorities live. We think that is a flawed assessment.
Q241 Why?

Black people do not bring racism to an area by living there. That is the simplest way of putting it. Racism is an ideology. It is supr emacism and contempt for people of other ethnic groups. There are racist attacks in particular areas because there are armed groups who practise racism, and they target people in particular areas. There are racist attitudes across the community in differen t places. Unless there is an armed group there prepared to practise racism, that does not turn it into a racist attack.

There are plenty of nationalist areas where there are no racist attacks. There are plenty of mostly unionist areas where there are no r acist attacks, but areas where there are loyalist paramilitaries involved in racist violence tend to be areas where there are racist attacks. The thematic review of the Policing Board into race hate crimes looked into this, and there is not necessarily a c orrelation between where people live and where there are attacks.
