In other registers, is there a benefit of registering because you are getting easier access and physical access into buildings? Is there an incentive to register because it will help some of that? Is there a carrot and stick?

I am not aware of any incentives that are offered. The intention is that a good lobbying register is comprehensive . It is not just that the easier your access , the more transparent you need to be . T he intention of these rules is that, if you have access, you need to be transparent.

Q35 The Act covers direct communication. Does this adequately capture the range of means through which lobbying takes place? If not, what is being missed and how could the Act be changed to rectify this omission?

Fundamentally, the Act does not give us a lobbying register; it gives us a register of consultant lobbyists. Whatever your means of communication, we are not really finding out about the lobbying; we are just finding out about some of the people who do it. This is a very pertinent question for designing a good lobbying register. The legislation does not give us a lobbying register. Given the scope of the register that we have, if all you want is a list of people who engage in consultant lobbying, it is not a very relevant question. If, as I hope you do, you want to shine a democratic light on lobbying, it is a very relevant question. I am sure almost everyone sat round this table knows what it means to be lobbied, whether in the way their constituents do it through their democratic freedoms or the way other interest groups do it because they are interested in the influence that you have over outcomes. It is not just done through meetings.
Q36 How do you go about capturing that?

One way you would do it would be by recognising that there is a lot of activity that is not done by consultant lobbyists. I started this conversation by explaining that I lobby. I am lobbying for a lobbying register this morning, right? I am not a consultant lobbyist. I would argue that think-tank s lobby. They have quite a strong argument that it is right that they are not required to be registered because they are not lobbying on behalf of other persons, which is the term in the Act. What happens is that they independently , in the course of their mission to educate and inform, do research and develop policy ideas . They ask people to fund that endeavour and to fund them to promote the outcomes of that work. In traditional lobbying, the client has something that they want to lobby for and the lobbying outfit is engaged to promote the client’s interests. But, if the client’s interests happen to coincide with the kind of findings that the think-tank is going to produce, you do not need to hire a lobbyist; you just hire the think-tank that is going to come up with a view that is aligned to what you want. By funding the think-tank , you get the same result—perhaps even more effectively—as you would hiring the lobbyist.
Yes, you are absolutely right that we ought to think more broadly about how our democratic process is influenced and where people should be able to see who is paying for that influence.
Q37 Is that easy to capture?

I said earlier—it was good questioning that I had from Mr Cowan—that you can see who funds all of our work, and it is freely published on our website. That is not the case for all think-tank s. It could be but some resist that very heavily.
Q38 Ronnie Cowan: The registrar has the power to issue fines up to £7,500 or to refer for prosecution. Is that a sufficient deterrent?

I am trying to think of a case where those fines have been issued. There might be one pending that is expected to result in a fine but, that being the case, it would probably be inappropriate for me to outline it now. If you do not issue fines, the size of fine that you can issue is not very relevant, is it? This is largely administrative and, therefore, we need to find ways to make the whole thing more inclusive.
Q39 Ronnie Cowan: How many cases have been referred for prosecution?

I do not know of any. I would argue that what we are trying to do here is to shine a light on the democratic process. This is something that we ought to be able to achieve by having the right culture in our democracy. To overly criminalise the matter is probably not the best way to get this to work. Rather than having something that is stigmatised —“ You are on this register so does that mean I should not really be talking to you?”—do the opposite and make transparency about these kinds of conversations the norm, so it becomes counterintuitive not to be open.

That is one of my concerns about this foreign influence registration scheme . We would be much more likely to capture the foreign influence activities in our democracy if we had a comprehensive lobbying register. M oving, as Parliament seems set to, to have this secondary register of people who are basically acting as foreign agents, does not strike me as the best way to actually get people to volunteer this information. I can understand the intentions behind the measure but I am rather sceptical as to whether it is actually going to result either in prosecutions or in people volunteering information . Take the National Security Bill, for example. I very much doubt that the kind of people you want to be brought into the net by that measure will comply.

Q40 Ronnie Cowan: Given that, is it up to the people who are being lobbied to report this ? Let us presume that there is some unscrupulous lobbyist out there or maybe foreign agents who want to influence what is happening in this place. You say they are not going to register themselves or declare that. How do we make it that this place is better at governing itself to declare the approaches in the first place?

There are two parties here: the lobbyist and the lobbied. Therefore, we have an opportunity, wherever the two are not conspiring, to bring transparency to the situation if we have both openness about the lobbying received and an obligation to be open about the lobbying conducted.

Q41 Ronnie Cowan: Going back t o my original question , if there is maybe one fine , and no conviction s or prosecutions, does the registrar have the sufficient resource to monitor compliance effectively in the first place?

I doubt that. I am sure you will ask him, but t he principal deficiency is the information available to him, not his appetite to check that information or his capacity to do so. A broader, more comprehensive set of ministerial or departmental meetings declaration s would be a very valuable asset to the registrar or anyone with a job to enforce the provisions of lobbying transparency in Parliament and Government , if that was a better information set for them to work from.

One area where this would be useful is AC O BA’S recommendations. AC O BA often tells former Ministers, when they seek advice on private sector business appointments, having left Government, that it would be acceptable for them to take on this role as long as they do not meet with former Government colleagues on matters relevant to their past ministerial experience. AC O BA has no means of monitoring whether former Ministers comply with the requirements set out in those letters. One of the reasons it does not is that , if they are working in - house, they are not required to register as consultant lobbyists, and they are unlikely to be named in the Government ’s ministerial meetings declarations. Even if they were, the subject of those meetings would be so narrow as to not provide much of an evidence trail as to whether they were in breach of those restrictions that they have been encouraged to adopt in going through the revolving door.

Q42 Mr Jones: You made the point that we are considering two parties—the lobbyists and the lobbied. The lobbying Act was designed to work in conjunction with Government Department s ’ quarterly transparency returns. As a matter of fact, how well do those two processes complement each other?

You very accurately describe the intention as to how this system was meant to work. I hope I have described some of the inadequacies in Government meetings declarations, which make it hard to work as intended. There is certainly a lot of confusion. There were a series of meetings that were first declared by Liz Truss before she was Prime Minister , which were then removed from her Department ’s meetings declarations and then reinstated. That does not suggest that anything wrong was happening but it does demonstrate that there was a degree of uncertainty about what meetings should be declared and what should not.

An investigation was published in T he Guardian about hospitality received by Matt Hancock from Randox. He had ministerial meetings during the day and was at a political setting in the evening where he had other meetings, and neither the hospitality nor the meetings that he had in the evening were declared. I hope that points to how the content of the ministerial meetings declarations gives us only a select view of the external engagement that is happening . That is quite a hole to depend on if, as you say, the legislation intends for the substance of lobbying to be revealed through those declarations and the identity of the lobbyists, where that is not intuitive, to be revealed by the register.
Q43 Mr Jones: In the example you have just given of the Hancock meetings, were consultant lobbyists involved?
Not to my knowledge, no.

Q44 Mr Jones: So, in that particular case , you are entirely dependent upon the departmental returns. There are no means of counter - checking , through any other procedures, which of course would apply if there had been a consultant lobbyist involved.

You are entirely dependent on ministerial returns. The register of consultant lobbyists does not help you very much even if there was a consultant lobbyist involved because it does not require the consultant to say who they were lobbying or what they were lobbying about. It just requires them to register the fact that this is the business that they practi s e.
Q45 Mr Jones: Meetings can be held at which important matters can be discussed, and it is quite possible that there would never be any record anywhere.
Yes, I am absolutely certain of it. That is the way the boundaries have been drawn both in the ministerial code and in the legislation that you are looking at.

Q46 John McDonnell : I think you have just rendered the next question superfluous but I will ask it anyway. How confident can we be that all lobbying of Ministers and Permanent Secretaries has been disclosed?
Certainly not all lobbying of Ministers.
Q47 What about permanent secretaries ?

I would have more confidence that there is no ambiguity as to whether lobbying of a permanent secretary needs to be declared. But there is this approach taken where Ministers wear multiple hats. In certain contexts, the Minister is an MP. In other contexts, the Minister is a Minister of the Crown . In other contexts , the Minister is a leading figure in a political party . Their activities in each of those settings have different reporting responsibilities. As a result, you do not end up with a comprehensive picture at all.

Q48 You keep answering the question I am about to ask. Let us go on to it , because you have raised it with regards to Matt Hancock’s meetings. It is this issue about the classification of meetings as political rather than Government business. How easily are they distinguishable? Are the rules surrounding how the meetings are classified sufficiently robust and satisfactorily adhered to?
I am not sure they should be distinguished. If you are a Government Minister , people do not think you are not a Government Minister because of where they meet you.

When David Cameron was Prime Minister, he published the attendees of what was called the leader’s group , which was a group of party funders who he would meet regularly. They published attendance and he was clearly meeting them in his capacity as leader of his party. It was a party-organised thing, not a Government -organised thing , but he considered, given the ambitions his Government had at the time on transparency, that the existence of these meetings and the attendance at them ought to be put into the public domain.

This is not a practice that has been sustained by his successors. I appreciate that the names of the groups change over time. We do not have anything like the same transparency over the access to Ministers that members of the Government party’s policy advisory board have , or over who attends and gets the benefit of that access. They know they are offered access to senior Government Ministers . The fact that they are doing that in support of their party, as part of how a political party works — you have conversations in your political party — is by the by e . From the point of view of lobbying, they are still Government Ministers who are being given the benefit of the wisdom of these individuals in terms of what Government policy should be.

Q49 You have mentioned a few international examples. In other spheres , do they have these distinctions about the nature of meetings and, as David pointed out, who i s attending the m ? Are they classified in that way or is there a broad definition that all meetings are covered?

If you have a lobbying register, rather than a list of meetings and a register of lobbyists, you are much more likely to have a comprehensive view. I would be very happy for us to take a look at the examples we have put in our submission to the Committee and perhaps provide that additional insight into which address that issue successfully and which do not.
That would be helpful. Thanks.

Q50 Mr Jones: Clearly , these meetings are all intended to exert influence of some sort over the lobbied. Should, therefore, the register extend not only to those who are lobbying Ministers , but to those who are lobbying others in positions of influence, which could potentially be any Member of Parliament —certainly , for example, shadow Cabinet members ?

Yes, indeed. At the moment , with this two-part system we have, one is the register of the lobbyists , governed by legislation ; the other is ministerial meetings declaration s, governed by the ministerial code . The Government themselves choose to do it. When you design a system like that , you will inevitably not shine a light on lobbying of people outside of Government . Governments change. People enter Government having not been in Government and having been very extensively lobbied.

I went to the Labour p arty conference this year and lobbied Labour politicians. I have told you, but it is not on a register anywhere. Some people spent an awful lot of money on a big bus to promote hydrogen at that conference. I think they were actually gas producers. Lobbying of politicians happens in all political parties. Lobbying happens through the work of all ‑ party parliamentary groups. I know the Standards Committee has done a review into those and has recommendations. You are absolutely right to say that , if we are interested in making our democratic process more transparent , we should look not only at the lobbying of Government Ministers .

Q51 You have made a distinction between a ministerial hat and a political hat that they might have. Do you also include a hat for them as a constituency MP? How do you regulate that? I know when I was shadow Environment Minister , when Keir first became leader of our party, suddenly people in my constituency came out of the woodwork who were in charge of air quality and water protection and who wanted to have conversations with me. They were genuine constituents, but they were only really talking to me because I had been appointed shadow Minister . If I had been Minister , I am sure even more would have come out of the woodwork. Do you recognise that that is also an area that might need some sort of consideration? Have you thought about it?

Yes, this c a me up in the debates around this legislation when it was first introduced. I would not consider it a priority ; I would consider it relatively low risk. It is part of how people understand that you do your jobs and it is part of the job you do in a representative democracy.

If we were able to address all the other things we have discussed this morning, I would not lose too much sleep about that being a back door. I suspect some constituencies would be more populated with people in a position to do significant lobbying than others.
They might happen to be a constituent of Jenrick, in that example . Suddenly you are representing an area where lots of those people live .

When I was a Member of Parliament I was once lobbied by senior people in a business in my constituency , which was concerned that it was not going to be awarded a defence export licence for a product. I did not anticipate that was the lobbying I was going to receive, but I received that lobbying. I was lobbied. There was a clear constituency interest. There was an obvious reason why I opened my door to be lobbied by this company, and there were constituents who would be affected potentially by the outcome. I felt uncomfortable that there was nothing in the public domain about this. There was no normal practice to put that kind of conversation in the public domain. I declined, for the record, to involve myself in any advocacy in relation to that particular decision , but I still recall it to this day as one of the reasons why I tended to have external meetings in the atrium of Portcullis House where people would know that anyone walking by could overhear what was happening in the conversation, rather than having meetings in a private room. I took the view at the time—I appreciate it might not be practical for everyone in the House of Commons to take the same view—that it helped foster an environment in which the kind of conversations people had when they had access to me were ones that they were happy to have in the open.

Q52 F O Is have been very successful in obtaining information regarding lobbying activities. Do you think they are sufficient or that they should compensate for the inadequacies of the Government’s current transparency data? Should they be used?

In theory , they would be very helpful. In fact, on the platform I described, Open Access, there is a link to where you can submit a freedom of information request to try and find out more information about a meeting that has appeared in the Government declarations. We encourage people to use F O I to supplement and to improve the information that is released.

In practice, however, F O I requests are not being granted as commonly as they used to be . I think it was an Institute for Government report that recently found that , in 2020 , 42% of resolvable requests were withheld in full, which compares to only 21% that were withheld back in 2005. Over the course of time , Government have become rather less forthcoming in response to freedom of information requests. Unless that were to change, there are limitation s to the contribution that that can make.

Q53 If Ministers and senior officials were required to release details of all their meetings with external bodies , regardless of what particular hats they were wearing at any one time, would the register be required at all?

As Mr Jones pointed out, that would tell you only about what was happening in Government . Our democracy is more than the function of the Executive . I appreciate the reservations that, as policymakers, you might have about the idea of having parallel systems. That does not feel very efficient. We are very supportive of maintaining a system of the lobbied and the lobbyists both making declarations. One of the reasons for this is that it can help fill the gaps. If you want to have, as I said at the beginning, exemptions because this kind of disclosure is disproportionate for people who very rarely engage in lobbying, you might feel more confident about having those exemptions if , where the person who is lobbied is significant , some information will still enter the public domain.

Q54 I should emphasise that was a question posed as a devil’s advocate, really. As a final reflection before this meeting closes, you have mentioned culture in one answer . When we embark on an inquiry like this , there is sometimes an interest because lobbying is seen as a dirty word by some , but it is arguably integral to the democratic process. I wanted perhaps a final reflection on the role of transparency and lobbying in creating a culture that perhaps empowers people to do these things appropriately and more openly.

One of the Nolan principles , which I am sure everyone here aspires to, is openness. I totally accept that lobbying is part of the democratic process. The exchange of information to reach decision makers is an important part of a healthy democracy. Rather than stigmatise it, having a culture of it being out in the open and conducted in a manner in which people are happy to be held to account for it , and where it is not secretive , is an important part of achieving that cultural objective. At the end of the day, this is about people’s confidence in democracy — confidence that decisions are being made in the public interest and not according to other interests, and that their democratic process serves them well. All of us—certainly all of you—have a stake in bolstering that confidence.

I n 2009 David Cameron said that lobbying was the next big scandal waiting to happen. In recent years, there have been stories about lobbying every few months, which may not individually constitute a big scandal, but it erode s public trust in the democratic process. As I hope we have demonstrated this morning , there is a lot further to go in addressing that than relying on the existing ministerial code and legislation we have on the books.

Thank you very much indeed, Mr Hames, for your evidence this morning. We are very grateful for it, and if there is anything you wish to say to us additionally , do feel free to write. For the moment, thank you very much again.

sessions.iT: Responsibilities of the Secretary of State for Wales
sessions.w: The Rt Hon David TC Davies MP (Office of the Secretary of State for Wales); Dr James Davies MP (Office of the Secretary of State for Wales)

segs.tx: Welsh Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Responsibilities of the Secretary of State for Wales , HC 219
Wednesday 2 November 2022
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 2 November 2022 .
Watch t he mee t ing
Members present: Stephen Crabb (Chair); Simon Baynes; Virginia Crosbie; Wayne David; Geraint Davies; Ben Lake; Rob Roberts; Beth Winter.
Questions 490-5 59
Witnesses
I : David T. C. Davies MP, Secretary of State for Wales, and Dr James Davies MP, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Wales.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: David T. C. Davies MP and Dr James Davies MP.

Q490 Good morning. Welcome to this session of the Welsh Affairs Committee in Committee Room 16. I am delighted to welcome this morning a former Chairman of this Committee and now the new Secretary of State for Wales, the right hon. David T. C. Davies. Welcome to you, and to your colleague Dr James Davies, the Under-Secretary of State—very recently appointed to the Wales Office. Congratulations to you both. We are delighted that you have given us your time this morning, so soon into your time in office.

Because we have a lot of ground to cover this morning, I implore you both, and my colleagues asking questions, to keep our remarks succinct and to the point. Could I ask you to briefly outline your priorities as the new Secretary of State? What do you want to achieve in your time at Gwydyr House?

Bore da, Cadeirydd, a diolch yn fawr iawn am y gwahoddiad i ddod yma heddiw. [Translation: Good morning, Chairman, and thank you very much indeed for the invitation to come here today.] Thank you very much. It was very important to us that we took up the invitation, even though it was rather soon after we were both appointed. In very simple and brief terms, in my role as Secretary of State for Wales I hope to ensure that Wales has a very strong voice around the Cabinet table and that the rest of Government are fully aware of the needs of Wales. I want to make sure that we get as much investment and create as many jobs as possible. I am very enthusiastic about a couple of big potential projects that could come to Wales, about which I am sure we are going to be asked later, but essentially it is to make sure that Wales has a strong voice in Government, and that Wales is aware of the enormous commitment that the UK Government have towards Wales, and its importance within the Union.
Q491 Did the Prime Minister give you a particular mission? Did he say, “David, I want you to go out and do x, y or z?”

The Prime Minister emphasised to all of us how important it was to display professionalism at all times. He certainly said to me that it was important that we develop a good and positive relationship with the Welsh Government. I was very pleased that, I think the day after I was appointed, I was able to talk briefly to Mark Drakeford online in respect of another meeting, and I am looking forward to having a proper one-to-one conversation with him today.

Q492 Do you think that the essential role of the Wales Office will continue as it has been? Is there any reason for us to suspect that there might be a difference in direction, in terms of the role that you want to play as the Secretary of State, with a seat at the Cabinet table, and as a bit of a bridge into the Welsh Government? You have previously done the Under-Secretary job, and you have sat in this chair as Chairman of the Welsh Affairs Committee. Do you think that the role of the Wales Office is recognised, established and therefore permanent?

I think there are two ways to answer that, Chairman. You and I have both been in Parliament for 17 years, so we will have seen changes taking place, and you do not always notice them day to day. Obviously, those changes will continue, but I get the feeling that your question might be hinting at whether there is some suggestion that all the territorial offices be rolled into one, which is an idea that seems to raise its head every couple of years. If that was the question, I do not see that happening. I think that it is vital that the territorial offices remain in place, and that Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have their guaranteed place around the Cabinet table. Obviously, there will be minor changes as there always are, but I do not foresee a substantial change.

Q493 Okay, that is helpful. Dr Davies, I do not know whether you have had time between the two of you, and with your officials, to work out different portfolios within the Wales Office. Dr Davies, are you able to give the Committee a sense of what your priorities will be?

Diolch yn fawr, Cadeiryd d. It is good to be back at the Welsh Affairs Committee, having been a member between 2015 and 2017, and it is a huge honour to have been made the Under-Secretary of State. I have a steep learning curve, clearly. We have had preliminary discussions about how various topics might be divided up, which will need to be approved at high levels, but I see myself very much as supporting the Secretary of State and trying to be proactive in flying the flag for Wales at the UK Government level.

Q494 Fabulous, thank you. Perhaps we can get into some specific issues now. Can I ask about freeports and investment zones? When Liz Truss was Prime Minister, one of the new ideas that emerged was investment zones. It was not entirely clear to me, and I think perhaps to other colleagues in the House, whether investment zones were to replace, displace or be welded on to freeports. Secretary of State, can you give us a sense of whether this idea has now been dropped? Are we back to the pure freeport idea that was in the manifesto in 2019? How should we see this area of policy and what implications does it have for Wales specifically?

As you will be aware, the UK Government have provided up to £26 million to get a freeport up and running in Wales. Bids are in at the moment. The bidding process is open until 24 November, and we all look forward with great interest to see what will happen there. That is going ahead. It seemed that there was a bit of a delay in terms of discussions with the Welsh Government, but that has all been resolved now and it is moving ahead very well. The Welsh Government recognise the potential for jobs and investment from having a freeport—an area where a slightly different tax regime will apply. The general idea is that things can be imported and tax is not paid until they are taken out of the freeport zone, so manufacturing can take place. If things are going back out again, it creates jobs and investment for the area. That is the principle of a freeport.

An investment zone works in a similar way, but with further freedoms perhaps in terms of taxes and planning. The question you really ask is whether that is still going ahead. As far as I am aware, the answer is yes. I have heard reports that it might be being reviewed at the moment, but I have not been given any official reason to think that they are not going ahead.
Q495 Okay. But from what you are saying, even if it is going ahead, in terms of what is being delivered in Wales, it very much is the standard freeport concept that we had been looking at previously.

The bids are going in at the moment. The Government are taking a flexible approach, and they have even said that there might be room for more than one freeport if there is a high number of excellent bids. Flexibility is the key. I am just setting out the general principle, and something similar could apply to investment zones, but to be fair, there is a new Government in place, and I am sure that the relevant Cabinet Minister will want to look at all sorts of things before moving ahead with them.

My focus is very much on bringing a freeport, and perhaps even more than one freeport, to fruition as soon as possible. Once I have more information about how the Government want to take forward investment zones, I certainly hope we could work with Welsh Government to develop that in Wales. We have already seen the success of the Deeside industrial area. I have visited it on a number of occasions as the Wales Office Minister, and we have seen what a huge success that has been for the north Wales economy. If we could replicate that, I would be very positive about it.

Q496 Brilliant; thank you very much. Last week we had a session on the economic potential of floating offshore wind in the Celtic sea and how that relates to the Welsh economy. We had a number of industry leaders in front of us—all of them, really—including the Crown Estate and the UK Government’s own offshore wind champion, Tim Pick , and they all seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet, talking up the economic opportunity for Wales. Indeed, Henrik Pedersen , the chief executive of Associated British Ports , which owns Port Talbot, talked about this being a “once-in-a-generation” economic opportunity for Wales. Is that view shared by you, Secretary of State? Do you recognise this as a big prize to go out and seize for Wales?

Absolutely, Mr Chairman. You will be aware that I have visited the Pembroke Dock area to look at similar infrastructure; I believe you were present on one of those visits. I think it is an enormous and very exciting opportunity for us. I could probably eat up 10 or 15 minutes talking about my enthusiasm for that.

We need every single gigawatt-hour of electricity we can get that is produced within this country. There are five potential zones out there in the Celtic sea. One of the first things I have done already as Secretary of State is meet the Crown Estate to see how much more quickly we can get a bidding process up and running for those five areas, and they are also enthused about it. The simple answer to your question is: yes, I am enthusiastic. I have already undertaken some work on that, and I look forward to visiting again in the near future.

Q497 Fabulous; that is really encouraging to hear. Your officials hopefully followed last week’s session, where numerous witnesses talked up the importance of the freeport concept to help deliver some of these economic opportunities and ensure that there is real economic value held in Wales from doing floating offshore wind at an industrial scale.

I have one more specific question before I bring in my colleagues, and it relates to the Newport Wafer Fab business. You will be aware that the UK Government previously announced a review, given national security concerns around the purchase of Newport Wafer Fab . The decision following the review has been delayed about three times. Are you able to give the Committee an idea of why a decision keeps being delayed?

What I can say to you is that I am well aware of the issues around this, and I have had a number of briefings on it, but obviously there is a national security issue here, and the advice I have had is not to comment further on it but to say that it is being very carefully looked at at the moment by Government.

Q498 Thank you. In terms of the representations we have received, there is a strong concern about the workforce and the uncertainty that is hanging over the workforce in that facility in Newport . It would be remiss of me not to ask you whether you are aware of the feelings of the workforce at the moment and their desire to get some certainty and clarity on the future of the facility.

I am fully aware of that. I know that there are 200 jobs at risk. [1] Some of the people working there are my constituents, so as a constituency MP, I have been contacted by some of them and also by the union. I am absolutely aware of it. Nobody wants to see any jobs being lost anywhere, but the process that has taken place has arisen because of national security concerns, and I can confirm that I have had briefings about that and have been advised not to say anything further.

Q499 I understand that. As a Committee, we are not in a position to make judgments about the information that will be feeding into the national security side of it, but we would probably want to see the issue resolved as efficiently and as quickly as possible.
I share your concern about the jobs, and I have made that known.
Thank you very much. Geraint, on this issue.

Q500 Would you accept, other than the security issue, that this is a strategic global economic asset that the Government should be investing in to grow our economy, as opposed to people feeling, “Oh, my job might be at risk.”? We should be going in there and investing, and securing it for Britain. Isn’t that your position?

I can confirm that, obviously, compound semi-conductors are a very strategic asset, and the Government are very well aware of that. I would agree completely. The ability to produce compound semi-conductors is vital from a strategic perspective, yes. [2]

Q501 Thank you, Secretary of State, and thank you, Minister, for giving us your time this morning. I am particularly pleased to see that we now have what I think is the correct balance in the ministerial team, which is representation from north Wales and south Wales. Sorry to put it in that order, but as a north Wales MP I feel strongly about this. I feel that north Wales is perpetually under-represented and under-appreciated in the overall system of Wales, so would you both, as a general point on which to start, comment on ways in which you would want to ensure that north Wales gets its fair share of attention and benefits within Wales overall?
I feel I should hand over to my colleague.

Thank you, Simon, for your welcome. Clearly, I am a Minister for the whole of Wales, and that must not be forgotten, but equally, as a north Wales MP, as you are, I have my own thoughts about opportunities and risks for the region. For instance, when it comes to transport infrastructure, you and I know how important that is to north Wales, and we know the importance of plugging into Warrington and Crewe in terms of rail.

We also know about opportunities for energy, such as the nuclear industry and Ynys Môn and Trawsfynydd , as well as possibilities for additional wind power. Clearly, the Celtic sea has the floating wind opportunity in south-west Wales, but in north Wales we have a 20-year history of wind power, with more, as you know, being put out at sea. I want to make the most of that and to look at tidal opportunities as well, which are very interesting to me. There is also the general levelling-up agenda and ensuring that our communities and seaside towns see the benefit of the Government’s agenda.

Q502 Thank you for that. It leads neatly into my second question, which is about transport. My understanding is that the Avanti West Coast franchise has been extended by the UK Government until April 2023, unless I am much mistaken. Clearly, there are many problems with the performance of Avanti West Coast within Wales. Would you comment on how you see that situation and the degree to which you, as the Wales Office, are putting pressure on the Department for Transport to take a long, hard look at the underperformance of the franchise?

If I may, Mr Baynes, the issue was raised in questions to the Wales Office approximately a week ago. We had already been in touch with the Department for Transport. My understanding is that it acknowledges that there have been a number of complaints—I certainly am well aware of them—and that, although the franchise has been extended, it is looking very carefully at the levels of service being offered. If you would like, Mr Baynes, I am happy to get confirmation of that from officials, but the complaints—the many complaints—have certainly been noted by DfT.

Q503 Okay, thank you. Transport for Wales made two bids to the Union connectivity fund, which sought to improve journey times on the south Wales main line and enhance infrastructure in the Chester/Cheshire area. What discussions has the Wales Office had with the Treasury about the decision to decline both these bids?

In actual fact, I am not certain that they have been declined. This is an ongoing process and, as I understand it, those bids are very complementary to other work that has been ongoing. Certainly, the Secretary of State and I have work to do to speak to DfT and ensure that, wherever possible, work is progressed on plans such as those that you highlight.
Just to confirm, I do not think those bids have been refused at all. There is an ongoing discussion about them, and an announcement will be made in due course.

Q504 Excellent. Rail infrastructure, or part of it, is a reserved competence. I speak parochially as somebody seeking step-free access at Ruabon station in my constituency, but there is a broader point. From the Committee’s point of view, it is important that the Wales Office applies pressure, wherever possible, on the Department for Transport to come through with the funding and support. I used an example from my constituency, but I know of many other such projects across Wales. Could you comment on that in general, and on how you interact with other Government Departments to ensure that we get the best deal possible for Wales?

I feel that there might be a number of slightly different questions there. In respect of step-free access, my understanding—I do not have this in front of me—is that that is coming out of a separate fund, and that Wales has been given various awards. I believe Abergavenny had one recently. While there was input from me as the local MP, each of those bids has to be assessed on transparent criteria.

On the overall point about spending on rail infrastructure, the UK Government will spend £340 million on it during this control period. Obviously, the improvements taking place that are not part of that £340 million will still improve services for Welsh passengers, such as the work taking place in Gloucester, which will have a hugely beneficial impact for travellers from south Wales to the midlands.

The third part of your question is about our interaction. When I was the Minister in the Wales Office, I had regular meetings with D f T Ministers—the former Rail Minister and others—and I would certainly expect that to continue.

Q505 Two final questions. In north Wales, the cross-border aspect of our lives, economically and otherwise, is vital. There is the Mersey Dee Alliance and so on. To what extent can more work be done to build links across the border? I think I am right in saying that about 25% of people in Wales go across the border each day to a job in England.

Perhaps I will bring in my colleague in a minute. First of all, I have had a number of meetings with the Mersey Dee Alliance, and I am happy to continue that relationship. Obviously, I met the North Wales Growth Board and Ambition North Wales on a number of occasions, and I hope that that will also continue.

As you will know, Mr Baynes, there is a potential project in the RNEP to make improvements on the north Wales coastline. Although I do not want to presume what questions may be asked, I suspect that HS2 may come up at some point this session. Of course, HS2 will improve journey times to London from Crewe, which will also be beneficial to passengers in north Wales. Perhaps I can bring in my colleague.

This matter is critical, as you know, to the region as a whole. I will now have to relinquish my chairmanship of the APPG that oversees this; perhaps you could take it over, Simon—that would be a positive for the region.

The rail agenda is so important, as you know. I mentioned Warrington and Crewe. Warrington is where north Wales would link up with Northern Powerhouse Rail and northbound HS2; it is Crewe for southbound HS2. Beyond that, there is the issue of regional services. The fact that, effectively, you cannot use the train to get to Manchester and Liverpool from north Wales—it takes much longer than driving—is a real problem. That is holding back opportunities for my constituents and yours. That is absolutely critical.

Much of the infrastructure work that needs to take place is not necessarily in Wales. There are bottlenecks at Chester station, for instance. Electrification clearly needs to come through from Crewe and Warrington as well; it is absolutely critical. Merely understanding that is a good start, in terms of liaising with Government and other bodies.

Q506 Thank you. My time is almost up but, I have one quick last question that you can give a quick answer to. Obviously, we have a new Administration under the Prime Minister. Could you please confirm unequivocally the commitment of the UK Government to levelling up? That is vital. I think only one substantial bid for money from the levelling-up fund has been granted in north Wales; it happens to be from my constituency. Many people across Wales are badly in need of such funds. Could you please confirm that the Government remain as committed as they were a few months ago to the levelling-up agenda?
David T. C. Davies : Yes.
Thank you.
Beautifully succinct.

Q507 Thank you, Chair. Diolch yn fawr iawn i’r Ysgrifennydd Gwladol a’r Gweindiog. [Translation: Thank you very much indeed to the Secretary of State and the Minister.] Secretary of State, you mentioned to the Chair that the Prime Minister expressed the desire to create a positive relationship with the Welsh Government. Quite simply, how do you envision going about fostering such a relationship?

Mr. Lake, as you know , for the last three years I have served as a Minister in the Wales Office. During that time, I have had numerous meetings with Welsh Government Ministers, many to do with covid. As the Minister responsible for growth deals, I also had a lot of personal meetings with Ministers—mainly Vaughan Gethin; sometimes others; and, when we were on growth deal visits, Mark Drakeford.

At a personal level, there has never been any difficulty in our relationships at all. When it comes to growth deals, we are all on the same side. We all want that investment, and we want them to succeed. I do not see anything changing. I spoke to Mark Drakeford a couple of days ago, and will be talking to him later. One of the first things that we did was try to set that call up. Obviously, he has a very busy diary, so I think this was the first time that he was available.

Q508 The Welsh Government have, however, complained recently about lack of engagement on a number of UK Bills. How can those sorts of concerns be addressed? Do you envision any circumstances in which certain UK Ministers in other Departments will need to foster a direct relationship with their counterparts in the Welsh Government?

I think there have always been direct relationships between the Welsh Government and other UK Secretaries of State. I know that at official level, a great deal of work goes on. Clearly, there have been a number of Bills—I think eight or 10—in which LCMs were involved. The co-operation continues reasonably well, I think.

There will always be tensions; I picked that up. I read things in the press. It is to be expected that a left-wing Government in coalition with those in favour of independence might occasionally have a slightly different view from a moderate centre-right Government in Westminster. At the personal level, we are all professionals and we all have a shared interest. I very much hope that will continue. All the conversations that I have had with Mark Drakeford over three years have been perfectly warm and professional. I do not think I have ever fallen out with any Welsh Government Minister directly. I look forward to that continuing.
Q509 What sort of role do you envision the Inter-ministerial Standing Committee and the Finance Inter-ministerial Standing Committee serving in future?

Those committees are already in place , and I do not know of any plans to change them . Over the last few years, I took part in a lot of those committee meetings. Basically, they were all online because of covid, and I often sat in for the Secretary of State when he was doing other things. We have a new Government who may make a few changes here and there, although I am not aware of any. I think you can tell a lot from the fact that one of the first things that the new Prime Minister did was telephone Mark Drakeford and Nicola Sturgeon . As I say, it is no secret. He said to me, “I want a good, professional and positive relationship with the devolved Administrations.” I very much doubt that any of these committees will be torn up or rejigged in a way that will not be appreciated by the Welsh Government. That is very much not the way the Prime Minister wants to go about things.
Q510 In the past, have these committee meetings been an opportunity to discuss legislation at UK level that perhaps the Welsh Government—

Yes, absolutely. I have taken part in a number of the agricultural ones. In some of the discussions, some comments made by Welsh Government Ministers were not entirely supportive of what the UK Government were doing, but that’s politics. At least there is the opportunity on those committees to express disagreement. I am sure that it will not surprise you, Mr Lake, to hear that disagreement has occasionally—or perhaps regularly—been expressed, but it can be discussed in an open way on those committees.

Q511 So if the Welsh Government refused to give consent to certain parts of a piece of legislation, you would not necessarily consider that a failure of relationship, but perhaps more a function of politics.

Not necessarily. If you take something like the UKIM Bill, I think the UK Government felt that one could argue that if the legislation had not been carried forward, the Welsh Government would have effectively been able to block important trade Bills, which are very much a reserved matter. At all times, the UK Government will look to work with the Welsh Government in order to reach agreement without needing to legislate and without LCMs, and will show proper respect to the democratically elected body.

Q512 I was heartened to hear in your opening remarks that you want to be Wales’s voice in the Cabinet, and to ensure that Wales’s needs and interests are understood across Government. Have there been any difficulties in the past with other Departments not necessarily appreciating some of the specific circumstances that Wales finds itself in? There have, of course, been many concerns expressed in the past, but sometimes the devolution settlement is not well understood, and that can have an impact on decisions made in Whitehall. Do you consider your role to be partly educating other Departments about the intricacies of the devolution settlement, as well as championing Wales’s interests?

I can’t think of a specific instance off the top of my head but, to be honest with you, I think that probably would have happened. It is bound to happen that people will not always be aware of the specific cultural differences that arise in Wales over things such as language. I suppose that I concur with you that part of the role of the Wales Office will be educating. I have always sought to meet Ministers from DCMS quickly to explain the importance of S4C and its role in fostering the Welsh language. While I haven’t done that in the last week, I can assure you that it will be a priority, as well as an example.
Q513 You touched on growth deals. What is your understanding of the situation regarding the mid-Wales growth deal? Could you say whether progress is satisfactory or otherwise?

That is a very good question because, obviously, in the other three growth deal areas, projects are up and running and are being developed. We are not quite there yet with the mid and west Wales growth deal, and I think that getting there needs to be a priority for me and my colleague here. It is fair to say that perhaps we are not quite where we want to be yet in mid and west Wales on growth deals.
Q514 Has progress changed at all since the local elections this year? Have you found any changes in the dynamics? Obviously, there is regime change in Powys .

I suppose it is fair to say that any new set of councillors coming in will have their own priorities , and a lot of work. I have not seen a change. My colleague will want to talk to both the local authority leaders about how we can support them in bringing projects forward quickly. Perhaps, Mr Lake, you will have a role in this as well. The last time I came down to visit your local authority leader, you very kindly took me to one or two places, so I would highly recommend a visit for my colleague, if he gets the opportunity.
Very well.

I am advised that the Growing Mid Wales board recommended in September that six projects should proceed to an outline business case stage. The projects include a green innovation park in Aberystwyth and a bespoke tourist facility in the Elan Valley, and at least two projects should be delivered by summer 2023. That is the ambition.
Thank you. That is good to hear—and the invitation stands.

Q515 Welcome, Secretary of State. I was very pleased that you said you would be a strong voice for Wales in Government and that you aim to get as much investment in jobs as you can. With that in mind, you might be aware of the alerts from the vice-chancellor at Swansea University, Paul Boyle, about the loss of 50 projects and 270 jobs because of the cliff-edge loss of European structural funding. Those jobs are very important for green growth and local business. Will you speak up on that, perhaps meet me and Swansea University, and basically champion green jobs and growth, in order to stop the cuts in Wales? This happens further afield than Swansea as well.

I do not recognise that will be cuts in Wales because, obviously, all the money coming from Europe will be replaced by the shared prosperity fund. I have visited Swansea University on a number of occasions as a Minister, and I am happy to do so again. To the best of my knowledge, the last time I visited Swansea, I do not recall that particular issue being raised.

Q516 It is being flagged up as an emergency now. Those projects are on hold. The specifically point is that the shared prosperity fund is not in place to sort this out. People urgently need bridging funding until the new systems are put in place, so that jobs can continue. You might be aware that a lot of them are at the cutting edge of green growth.

The shared prosperity fund is a matter for DLUHC, but as I have said, we have a role in making sure that Wales’s voice is heard at the Cabinet table. I have written to DLUHC already to ask that progress be made quickly on the shared prosperity fund.
Q517 Perhaps you can have a word with Grant Shapps as well, to whom I have already spoken. There is interest in this, but if you could fly the flag for Wales, it would help.

I am sure my officials have taken note of your comments, Mr Davies. I sense that we might be doing another letter on that specific point about Swansea University when we have a bit more information about it. I am very happy to write on that issue.

Q518 Moving on, in a similar vein, the Welsh Government decided to give local authorities 3.5% of extra funding, but inflation is running at 10%. Given that the profile in Wales is older, poorer and sicker than the UK average, and the average wage is something like 70% of the UK average, will you press the Government to ensure that we get our fair share for local authorities—something closer to the level of inflation—so that we can hold up public services?

You will be aware, Mr Davies, that we gave a record-breaking increase of £2.5 billion to the Welsh Government. What they do with it is a matter for them. I am aware of the concern about inflation, which is running at those sorts of levels across much of western Europe and the United States. Although I do not sit in the Treasury, I am aware that the Chancellor is going through the figures at the moment. He will do everything possible on the 17 th to ensure that the areas that have the most need will get what we can provide.

Q519 In Swansea, for example, the energy cost to the local authority will go up by £15 million—from £5 million to £20 million—next year. For the health service across Wales, energy costs will go up by £200 million. I appreciate that you have not got a money bag sitting beside you, but the issue here , again, is that Wales has special needs , and our profile is more vulnerable. Will you work hard to ensure that we get our fair share in difficult times?

Yes, I will certainly be doing that. Obviously, the NHS and many other public sector organisations have been hit by increases in energy costs. That is why we brought in the guarantee until April, which will mean that most organisations will only be paying half of what they would if the guarantee was not there. Clearly, that will be reviewed before April to see what we can do to continue it.

The problem that we faced—it was well publicised a month or so ago—was that trying to keep that going for up to two years could have cost up to £130 billion. It would have been very difficult to do that without borrowing at much higher rates of interest. As you rightly say, there is no sort of cupboard anywhere in Whitehall marked “Money” with a load of cash in it. The sums of money that we would need to keep energy at the cost it was at 18 months or two years ago are absolutely immense.

However, having said all that, as we all know, of course, I will be doing everything possible to ensure that Wales continues to get as much money as possible out of the Treasury. Under the system in place Wales gets about £1.20 for every £1 spent in devolved areas in England.

Q520 You will be aware that there are problems with children and other people in hunger across Wales and the UK. The latest figures are that one in four people—and one in five children—are in hunger. Through the Welsh Government, in Wales we have free school breakfasts and are rolling out free school lunches. However, I am told they have not got the money for free school lunches in the holiday period. You will remember the campaign by Marcus Rashford and others. Will you be prepared to press the Government to help Wales to get that extra money for the holiday period, because it is a desperate situation?

Mr Davies, you will be aware that all I can do is try to get money from the UK Government to the Wales Government. The last time around there was an increase by £2.5 billion. What the Wales Government do with that money is entirely a matter for them. Were I to start suggesting that they spend it on this, that or the other in devolved areas, obviously I would create exactly the sort of row that I have said we are hoping to avoid. I am not here to tell the Welsh Government how to spend their money. They have a large sum of money. They also have tax-raising powers, and the ability, if they want—
I guess what I am saying is that they do provide this food for children who are otherwise hungry at school—
And that is a wonderful thing to do—

I am glad you said that, because they do not provide that in England—that is the point. I want you to encourage England to provide English children with some food at the start of school, and to provide the money for everyone to have that food, rather than it coming out of other pots.

This is a much wider discussion, but clearly one would have to decide whether it is a good idea to provide one, two or three meals a day every single day of the year to every child in the country, or whether, perhaps—
It is not three; it is two.

Well, I don’t know; if two were provided, I can guarantee that some people would say, “What about dinner?” It is a difficult issue. The UK Government are trying to target help at those who need it the most, and are supplying money to the Welsh Government.

The Welsh Government have the freedom to do what they want to do. They could raise taxes if they wanted to, and provide as many meals to people as they wanted as often as they wanted if they thought that was a good use of—

Q521 There is a poorer tax base, of course, in Wales. One of the reasons for that is that we have not got the investment in railways to raise productivity and wages. You will know that over the years Wales has had 1.5% of announced rail investment for 5% of the people, and we have not had our 5% of HS2, which would give us about £5 billion. If you remember, I met you and Professor Mark Barry to discuss that. Will you urge, as Tories in Wales are urging, that Wales gets our fair share—mainly our 5% of HS2—so we can provide more productivity and wealth creation in Wales to pay the taxes that you want to raise?
First of all, Mr Davies, I am not sure that I recognise the £5 billion figure. I mean, 5% is normally what Barnett consequentials mean, is it not? I think that phase 1 of HS2 is £40 billion.
I think it is projected as over £100 billion for the total project.

I think that is the estimate for the whole thing when it is finally finished. A s I understand it —my officials may correct me if I am wrong; it is not a Wales Office matter —between now and 2029-30, the cost of phase 1 of HS2 is about £40 billion. I do not know exactly when work starts—
Q522 Will you fight for the £2 billion for the first phase ?

That is over 10 years or so, so that is about £200 million a year. Over this control period, £340 million has been spent on rail improvements in Wales. We have had the Core Valley Lines—£125 million; £76 million for the electrification of the tunnel; £58 million for Cardiff Central station.
There has been some money, but less than our proportionate share.

Well, actually, if we just leave aside that straightforward spending on rail, we also have to remember that the Cardiff metro is a light rail system, and that is a match-funded UK Government growth deal. That is worth well over £500 million.

With the greatest respect to Mark Barry, who is no doubt an expert in his field, he keeps bandying around this £5 billion figure, which I just don’t recognise. It doesn’t bear any relation to the figures that the Government have published on HS2.
It is our share of the total projected cost.

But if one takes 5% of £40 billion over 10 years, one has a figure of £200 million. I can already point to £340 million of spending over a control period in Wales, plus the Cardiff metro, plus the spending that is going on outside of Wales that benefits Welsh passengers. I politely suggest to you—a keen environmentalist—that HS2 is there to get people out—

Order. Sorry to cut across you, Secretary of State. In terms of time keeping, we need to move on to my next colleague. I’m not sure we’ll get to the bottom of the funding figures, but maybe we could come back to that on another occasion. Beth Winter, please.

Q523 Llongyfarchaiadau are eich apwyntiad a diolch yn fawr am ddod heddiw. [Translation: Congratulations on your appointment and thank you very much for coming today.] I really appreciate it. I don’t know if you are aware that the chair of the Welsh Local Government Association over the past week has been highlighting the decimation of public services that is likely to happen—a black hole of over £800 million. Andrew Morgan has said, “We are clinging to the cliff edge by our fingernails. This won’t simply be about cutting services. If there is not UK Government intervention, there will be wholesale closing down of services.”

Like my colleague in Swansea, my local authority is facing a shortfall of between £45 million and £47 million next year. Mr Morgan has said that even if we totally cut library, leisure and bin services, there will still be millions of pounds in shortfall. What do you say to the council leaders in Wales?

First and foremost, we are facing very difficult economic times. As you will recognise, Ms Winter, we tried to borrow our way out of an energy crisis that has been caused by a war in Ukraine, and followed a global pandemic, and we found we were not able to do that. We simply couldn’t borrow that money.

That leaves us having to make a decision about taxes and spending, and those decisions are going to be difficult. I have not heard Andrew Morgan, or anyone else who has made those perfectly valid points, suggest where extra money could come from to deal with the problems that have arisen.

With the greatest of respect to Mr Morgan, with whom I had a very positive informal discussion at the weekend when we appeared on a TV programme, some of the local authorities—Rhondda Cynon Taf might be among them—do have large amounts of reserves. Some seem to have a lot more than others. Monmouthshire does not have much at all, but some have quite significant reserves. This may be the moment to look at that.

The other point I would make is that it is not down to the UK Government to tell the Welsh Government exactly how much money to give to each of the 22 local authorities in Wales. That is a matter for the Welsh Government to decide. They did receive an increase of £2.5 billion and they do have tax-raising powers. If they think there is a simple way to fund local authorities better, they have the ability to do that themselves, and probably would not welcome me telling them exactly what to do.

Q524 You will be unsurprised that I am going to challenge you on some of the figures. As a result of inflation, the Welsh Government’s budget in the three-year spending round of 2022-25 is now worth up to £4 billion less in real terms. The budget for 2024-25 would have been £3.5 billion higher if it had increased in line with the economy since 2010. Obviously, there is £1.1 billion in unreplaced funding as a result of us leaving the EU. Those are Welsh Government figures, not my figures plucked out of the air, and the purse strings lie squarely with the UK Government.

Jeremy Miles recently said that it is a disgrace that the UK Government has left us in an impossible situation. He has assured education workers that he will continue to work with colleagues to push the UK Government to provide Wales with a fair funding settlement. The figures I gave you clearly contradict the position that you are relaying to me. What do you say to the Welsh Government?

First of all, I have not seen those figures, so I am not able to give a full analysis of them. I hear you say that the Welsh Government are saying that they will lose out as a result of leaving the European Union. I certainly don’t recognise that figure. I know that they have tried to count the tail on funding that went on beyond the EU structural fund period. They are trying to suggest that, had we stayed in the EU, they would have got the tail and a whole load of extra money on top, and that is not the case. The EU money does not usually start flowing in straightaway, whereas the shared prosperity fund money will, so I completely reject the argument about losing out as a result of leaving the European Union.
Can I—

I will concede one thing, which is that like all other countries in western Europe and the United States, we are facing high levels of inflation at the moment, which clearly has an impact. To gently throw it back to you, the Labour party expressed concerns about the Government borrowing money, which we tried to do in order to get us through an energy crisis caused by international circumstances. We know that we cannot do that—certainly not paying the levels of interest that we want. We are then left with difficult decisions over spending or taxes. With the greatest of respect, I haven’t heard anyone from the Labour party who has criticised the Government over these issues actually saying where they would get the money from. If you are able to tell me, I will go back to the Treasury with some ideas.

Q525 Well, I led a Westminster Hall debate yesterday, and I quoted Tax Justice UK, which said only last week that the Government could raise up to £37 billion a year by taxing wealth. Most people would agree that it was absolutely astonishing that BP recorded profits of £7.1 billion in the last three months.
Can I move on to two other questions? Today, all parliamentarians are being lobbied by trade unions, which are coming to Westminster. Will you meet the trade unions that are coming up from Wales?
I am meeting one of my constituents, who represents a trade union, at 11.30 am. I will then be going off to call the First Minister and then to attend an event in Cardiff. It is already happening.
Q526 Do you agree that public sector workers deserve an inflation-proof pay rise?

I would love to see everyone getting inflation-proof pay rises in an ideal world. Again, if we could find the money, we would all want to see that happen. It is not the case that anyone in Government wants people not to have inflation-proof pay rises; it is a matter of making very difficult decisions in times of economic crisis. I am confident that the Chancellor and the Prime Minister will be looking at making sure the most vulnerable have help targeted at them.
Q527 And people on benefits?

Again, I know the Chancellor is a very compassionate man and will want to support those who are least well off. We will target what help we can at the most vulnerable. That is quite right; that is what we should be doing.

Q528 Finally, you have been recorded in previous years as being a bit of a climate sceptic in quotes that I have seen—but that is going back a few years. It is an issue that is very close to my heart. We have had climate assemblies in my constituency, and we now have a climate ministry in Wales. Can you give me some assurances that you accept we are facing an existential crisis, in terms of the climate, and that you will champion the issue of climate change?

I have spoken on this issue on a number of occasions over probably 10 or 12 years. On virtually every occasion, I have made the point that CO 2 is a global warming gas. We have been emitting a lot of it ever since the industrial revolution, and therefore it has had an effect on climate. I have looked back at various speeches that I have made, and that has always been very clear.

I have not changed my view that carbon dioxide is definitely a global warming gas, and it is having an impact on the climate, as I have said many times over the last 10 years. I know that at least one journalist in Wales, who seems to have a personal animus towards me for some reason, has spent an unhealthy amount of his time trawling through every single speech I have ever made on anything to see if he can pluck things out to have a go at. He celebrated the fact that he managed to find one speech or article somewhere online where this was not clear; it came back to me, and I took it down—when I eventually found it.

I have already said that I am hugely in favour of things such as floating offshore wind. I am hugely in favour of nuclear energy, which we have not talked about; that also creates large amounts of baseload electricity without creating carbon dioxide emissions. Ms Winter, you have just made a very strong point about the cost of living crisis and the cost of energy, which we are all facing, and the impact that is having on the public sector among other things. I hope you would also agree that we need to do everything we can to ensure that energy is as cheap as possible for people.

Q529 C roeso . Thank you both for coming to my Anglesey skills day in Westminster on Monday. My first question relates to St David’s Day. What assessments have you made of the potential effect on the Welsh economy and tourism industry of denoting St David’s Day as a bank holiday?
First of all, thank you very much for the event you organised; it was wonderful.

As far as the argument about St David’s Day is concerned, clearly bank holidays do have a cost. I think there has been a suggestion that one might want to move one bank holiday to another; possibly, May Day—the festival to celebrate international socialism—might be moved to 1 March to celebrate St David’s Day. That is not Government policy at the moment.

There are some issues where I feel very strongly and there are others where I feel rather more relaxed. This is not something I would ever storm out of Cabinet over, whatever happened. I accept the Government position as it is, and on balance I support it because I think there are some advantages in not having a bank holiday.

I have three children who all went to a state school in south Wales, and they always used to celebrate St David’s Day in school. I have been there a few times to watch them dancing and singing. I suspect that had they not been in school, rather than celebrating this wonderful part of Welsh culture and enjoying a bit of the language and the dancing, there might have been a tendency to flop down on a sofa and mess around with the PlayStation. I would rather them be celebrating Welsh culture. On balance I am happy with things as they are and our children celebrating St David’s Day in school. If that policy changes at some time in the future, I would look for other ways to ensure that our culture is celebrated.

Q530 The number of MSs in Wales is due to go from 60 to 96. One MS will be responsible for about 53,000 constituents. MPs represent about 103,000 constituents. There is an estimated cost of £100 million for the increase. Have you had any discussions with the Welsh Government about this? Where will the £100 million actually come from?

That is a very interesting question. I am tempted to ask it of the First Minister, but perhaps that would not kick off the relationship that we are looking for. It is not really a matter for me if the Welsh Government decide they want to spend £100 million during a cost of living crisis on creating extra Members of the Senedd. However, I must observe one thing: when I was first elected to the Senedd in 1999, one of the advantages that even I acknowledged—as someone who had recently been in a campaign against having a Welsh Assembly—was that it was sometimes easier to get hold of a Senedd Member who was in Cardiff and near to a constituency than it was a Member of Parliament. One of the issues here is that the direct link with constituencies is going to be completely broken as a result of the plans that are being brought forward. Clearly, it is a matter for the Welsh Government; I am just surprised that they do not want to put it to a referendum and see if the public support it or not.

Q531 It is great to hear that you are a supporter and fan of nuclear. My question relates to the fact that the Welsh Labour Government have a co-operation agreement with Plaid. Adam Price has said that “We are a party that doesn’t believe in nuclear. We do not support nuclear power. It’s the wrong answer.” How practically can we therefore get nuclear investment into Wales, given the co-operation agreement with Plaid, who do not support nuclear?

Obviously Mr Lake is not here now to speak for Plaid Cymru on that issue. I can only say that we are 100% in favour of nuclear, and I, as Welsh Secretary, am hugely enthusiastic about nuclear coming to Wylfa on Ynys Môn and SMRs coming to Trawsfynydd . Within those areas, as far as I can see, there is cross-party support. It is interesting that, while some parties nationally may take a view that they are against nuclear power, where a nuclear power station is being proposed those very same political parties are all in favour of it. That goes to show why nuclear power is one of the answers to the energy crisis that we are facing at the moment, and I hope that all members of the Welsh Affairs Committee might agree.

Q532 You mentioned the record £18 billion funding to Welsh Government in 2021, which was the equivalent of £120 per person in Wales for every £100 per person in England from the UK Government. You also mentioned that the distribution of that funding is a matter for the Welsh Government. My concern relates to healthcare, in terms of A&E targets and the fact that our waiting times for treatment and for ambulances are significantly worse in England and Wales compared with the rest of the UK. Where is the accountability for this £18 billion?

Again, that is a very good question. When Wales is getting more money per head—£1.20 per head is being given to Wales in devolved areas for every £1 being spent in England—it is quite hard to understand why we have longer waiting lists and less access to ambulances than patients in England, and why so many patients in Wales actually want to be treated in England. These are all very interesting questions, and it is difficult for me to understand the answers to them, but unfortunately, they are not questions that I am in a position to answer; they should be directed towards Welsh Government Ministers. My colleague could probably add to that.

One of the benefits of devolution was to be that we could compare different policies across the United Kingdom, to see which are most effective. I am very much of the opinion that openness, transparency and comparison of performance and outcomes is really important, because it helps the democratic choice of our voters and drives up standards. That is what I would be looking to push.

Q533 I have two quick questions. One is on freeports. There is going to be at least one freeport in Wales. I understand that four freeports have expressed interest, and the deadline is 24 November. You talked about the £26 million funding for the first one. How will it work practically for the second one? Does that mean liaising with Treasury? What will be your involvement, and what will be Welsh Government’s involvement?

The only information I can give you about that is that the Government would take a flexible approach if there were a number of good bids towards a second freeport, but I am not in a position to say what, if any, extra funding might be available to get that up and running.

Q534 Thank you. You talked about targeted help. We have the Budget on 17 November. We have talked about the cost of living in Wales and the very rural communities, where many businesses and homes rely on off-grid energy for heating. While the £100 is welcome, we are going into a cold winter. What conversations have you had with Treasury to make sure you fight on behalf of our communities?

I have not directly had any meetings with Treasury since being appointed, but obviously I have attended Cabinet. I do not want to give away any details of what was being discussed, but I think it is fair to say that the Prime Minister has made very clear that we should be targeting all help at the least well-off. If we look at the Prime Minister’s record as Chancellor, that was always the case. That is why we had the £650 payment to people on benefits, £300 to pensioners and £150 to those who are disabled. He was the Chancellor who brought in the furlough scheme, which supported millions of jobs and millions of people who are self-employed all the way through the covid crisis. He has a very strong record of targeting help at those who need it and targeting it at the least well-off, and I am sure that that approach will continue and will be seen when the statement comes out.

I could also come in on that. I have had similar concerns about rural constituents. It is important to remember that virtually everyone has an electricity contract, and they therefore benefit from the energy bill support scheme—the £400—in addition to the energy price guarantee on electricity.

When it comes to alternative fuels, I believe that, once the energy price guarantee has been factored in , the increase in the cost of natural gas over the last year for those on the grid is 130%. The equivalent figure for oil is 147%. The £100 makes the difference between 130% and 147%: it brings the 147% down to 130%. But it is important that the costs of oil and other alternative fuels are monitored closely. Clearly, if they go up more than natural gas, that figure may need to be re-examined.

Q535 Before I bring in Wayne David, can I press you on that issue, Dr Davies? Some 57% of homes in Pembrokeshire do not have access to mains gas, so it is a live issue for them. W ith th e explanation that you have just given to the Committee, are you saying that the £100 is an adequate and appropriate amount?

The point is that those who are off grid have always paid more, haven’t they? BEIS has not tried to bring the cost down to match that of natural gas. Its argument is that it is fair, and the statistics that I have claim to prove that. I would be happy to share those, if it helps.

Obviously, we accept that there are many people in rural areas, off grid, who are suffering at the moment. I am sure that the Treasury will want to look at that. We are not in a position to say what help may or may not be given, but one immediate thing that could be done to support those in rural areas would be for the Welsh Government to re-evaluate the local government funding formula, which seems to count local authorities with urban areas and not rural areas. That is an example of something that could be done to support those in rural areas.

I just make the point that I have a lot of constituents who are trying to get ready for winter and are being told that they have to pay for a minimum amount of 500 litres of heating oil. These people do not have £500 in cash to hand to buy heating oil. I will leave that thought with you.

Q536 Congratulations, Secretary of State, on your appointment. Could I begin by making a comment regarding HS2? The Committee prepared a report last year.
