The leader of the Welsh Conservatives commented that, if there was a realisation that HS2 is an English-only project, which it is in reality—you know that—there would be a Barnett consequential to Wales of £5 billion, or perhaps slightly less. You cannot get away from that fact, can you?
I cannot get away from the fact that, if it was classified as an English-only project, there would be a Barnett consequential, which would be about 5%. That is correct.
Q537 In other words, the Government are short-changing Wales by not accepting that obvious categorisation—that objective reality.

Well, not necessarily. First, I do not recognise the £5 billion figure. That would suggest £100 billion, which would be over a period of many years. Phase 1 is due to run up until about 2029 or 2030. Dare I say it, the way things are with construction projects like that, I would not be confident that it will necessarily finish exactly on the day planned.
Q538 Okay, then we will say slightly less, but nevertheless the point is still there.

Well, quite significantly less. If we took £40 billion, which is the presumed figure for phase 1, over a 10-year period, that would be £200 million a year. That would be the sort of figure we are talking about. The uplift for the Welsh Government last year was £2.5 billion , which is obviously more than 10 times £200 million. The other issue is that the UK Government are spending a lot of money on the rail network in Wales. It was £340 million over that control period. There are projects in RNEP that may come forward. It is basically—

Q539 I am sorry to interrupt you, but you have said all this before. You are basically arguing about angels on the head of a pin. What I am saying is that Wales would have had more money if the Government accepted the reality that HS2 is an English-only project. That is true, isn’t it?

Well, it is a fact—you are correct, Mr David. It is obviously a fact that, if any project is accepted as English-only and is devolved, there is a Barnett consequential. You are factually correct in that sense.
Q540 We’re correct and you’re wrong; thank you very much indeed.

Let me turn to the cost of living. I am sure you have seen it, but t he Bevan Foundation prepared an excellent report in July this year. I will quote exactly one of the things they said: “More than half of people in households with an income of less than £70,000 report that they had to cut back on their heating, electricity and or water.” The likelihood is that things will get a lot, lot worse during the next few months. You have already said that you are keen for resources to be targeted at less well-off people, and that is absolutely necessary. What representations are you therefore making to the Chancellor on what the specific policies should be?

I have not spoken to the Chancellor yet in this current role, but there have been discussions in Cabinet. All I will say is that there was a clear feeling that targeted help needs to go to the most vulnerable. That is a Government view. I believe that the current Prime Minister’s previous role as Chancellor underlined his own commitment to targeting help at the most vulnerable. I cannot go through those books myself; the Chancellor of the Exchequer will come out with a statement on 17 November, but I am confident that he will target all the help that we can at the least well-off, and rightly so.
Q541 Thank you for that; I hope you are correct. A number of your colleagues have said that increases in benefits should be keeping up with inflation rather than earnings. Is that your view?

In an ideal world, of course that is what I would like to see happen. We are not living in an ideal world at the moment, and I do not know what we will be able to afford to do. I think you have been in Government, Mr David; you will be well aware of the difficulties that any Government faces at a time like this. There is a limit to the amount of money that we can spend. We have already discovered that we cannot borrow money, or we cannot borrow in the amounts that we would like at the levels of interest that we want. That leaves only two alternatives: either putting up taxes—but I do not believe it is your policy, sir, to support tax increases—or cuts to spending. The Chancellor will have to look very carefully and be very clever in how we spend the limited amount of money that we have.

I think you will find that we are probably on the same side in wanting that help targeted at the most vulnerable. But is it necessarily responsible, sir—not that you are doing this—to call for more money for this, for everyone to have inflation-busting pay rises, for more money for every public service, but to say, “No, we don’t want extra taxes and no, we don’t want to borrow the money”?

Q542 Okay, you have answered the question. What you say is true, of course—we have to make sure that everything is properly costed—but nevertheless there is a contradiction between what you say there and what you said earlier about the principle that help must be targeted at those who need it most. That is what I am asking you about specifically. One of the best ways to do that is to make sure that benefits are increased with inflation. That is a sure way to do it.
That would be a sure way to help people, but I don’t know what is affordable and what is not at the moment. I know that is what the Government would want to do, if they possibly can.
Q543 Would you be in favour, then, to ensure that that happens, of the introduction of a special tax on non-dom status? It is a clear choice.

I cannot start giving you answers on what specific taxes the Government may need to bring in in order to fund help for the most vulnerable. With the greatest respect, sir, I have heard members of your party already today saying that every person who works in the public sector, which I presume includes even MPs, should have an inflation-busting pay rise. I can understand the argument for those on lower wages to have pay rises, but there are a lot of people in the public sector who are earning as much as the Prime Minister or more. Are we saying we should all have inflation-busting pay rises, because we are in the public sector? What about those in the private sector on low wages?
I would love to answer your question, but we are not in government yet.
It is a hypothetical one, sir, but you see the problem.

Q544 If I may go on, the shared prosperity fund is an important initiative that the Government have taken to largely replace, you would argue, Wales’s European funding, but we have heard from local authorities, and they are very critical of a number of aspects of the shared prosperity fund. One of the biggest concerns is that the timescale is such that local government has been given impossible deadlines to meet to come forward with projects that would qualify for support. Why have you determined those tight timescales? If local authorities are in a position where, according to your timescale, they are not able to use all the money that has been allocated to them, will that money stay with them and there will be a carry-over, or will it go back to the Treasury?

First of all, my understanding is that the four lead local authorities for Wales have already submitted their regional investment plans, which are being looked at by DLUHC. Anecdotally, I have spoken to various local authority leaders over the last 12 months, at different times, and they have all told me informally that they are very happy to be having a direct relationship with the UK Government and feel very positive about that. As to whether, if there is an underspend, any of that money will go back to the Treasury, I am looking—I don’t actually have that information in front of me. My thinking is it probably would, but I don’t see any reason—that is because I think I have read that elsewhere. I will check that.
That is an extremely important point. You really want to have been briefed on that.
I will see whether I can get any confirmation from officials on that, and I will absolutely write to you. I believe it probably will, but—
Yes, exactly—it will.

But if there are projects that are ready to go, I cannot understand why local authorities, which, as you have just said, are all saying, rightly, how difficult things are economically at the moment, would underspend that money.

Q545 But there is a suspicion—I put it no more strongly than that—that the Government have deliberately concocted this process to ensure that local authorities, although it looks good on paper if they have been allocated large sums of money, in practice are not able to spend them, and the Government are using this as a smokescreen basically to retain funds that should be going to local authorities.
Mr David, I have an answer for you, as it happens.
Oh good.

The three-year funding period for the UK shared prosperity fund ends in 2025. No funding will be provided for activity after 31 March 2025, and the expectation is that any further underspends in the final year of the programme will be paid to DLUHC. I think the answer to your question is that if the underspend goes as far as the year 2024-25, it will be paid back. I would hope, now that we know that, that all local authorities putting in bids will want to ensure that there are no underspends, because it is not my role to get money from Wales into the Treasury—
Absolutely not.
It is my role to get money from the Treasury into Wales; I am very clear about that.
Q546 That’s right, so I would very much hope that the gun that is being placed to the head of local authorities will be put back in its—

I am sure local authorities will now have heard this, if they didn’t know it already, and they will all be making absolutely certain there are no underspends. I will cheer them on as they put that money to good use. I look forward to visiting—
And I will hope that the Government are more flexible in ensuring that the principle of spending money is upheld.
Thank you very much, Wayne David. On that note of clarity, Rob Roberts, please.

Q547 Welcome, gentlemen. I have the dubious honour of going last and mopping up with questions that follow on from things that you have already answered. I also went on my social media a couple of days ago and said that you were coming and asked constituents what they might ask you if they were sitting here, so I have a couple of those—just to channel my inner Corbyn.

We will start with devolution and intergovernmental relations generally. When Ms Crosbie asked about going from 60 to 96 Members of the Senedd, you said, “It’s not a matter for me.” I am going to say that it is, because we are not talking about what happens in devolution; we are talking about the nature of devolution itself. The Senedd was established with 60 Members and a hybrid voting system. Do you believe that a change to the structure and the voting system should go back to the people for approval over whether they want to spend that extra £100 million?

If you are asking me personally, Mr Roberts, I think that would be a fair thing to do, but it is not my role as Secretary of State to advise the Welsh Government on how they should reconfigure devolution. But given that there was a second referendum over tax-raising powers, in which people voted, by the way, for tax-raising powers—as a democrat who always believes in supporting the result of referendums, no matter what they are on, I absolutely support the fact that the Welsh Government have got tax-raising powers—I am surprised that such a big change is taking place without further consultation with the public.

Q548 Thank you for that; I appreciate the sentiment. Last week, I attended the Interparliamentary Forum in Cardiff, with Members of the Senedd, Holyrood and the House of Lords. The overwhelming concern from the other legislatures in terms of intergovernmental relations is around the Sewel convention and legislative consent motions. With regard to Sewel first, do you agree that wording like, “The UK Government will not normally” is a little bit too woolly? Does that perhaps need to be codified in order to provide a bit more certainty and a little bit less animosity between the Governments?

We do not want to see animosity, but I think the wording is okay, isn’t it? I mean, the UK Government would not normally want to legislate without the full support of the Welsh Government. That is a reasonable position to take.
Q549 It is, but isn’t it too easy for the UK Government to then say, “Yes, but these aren’t normal times”? That is a subjective thing, right?

If we take something like UKIM, the point the UK Government were making was that had they not legislated, we would have effectively been handing the Welsh Government control over a major aspect of foreign affairs, which is the ability to strike trade deals. That would have given the Welsh Government powers that went far beyond what anyone had agreed in any referendum. I believe there were either eight or 10 Bills that went through with LCM, so the vast majority of them were all sorted out perfectly constructively. There are conversations going on all the time between officials in both the Welsh Government and the UK Government to make sure that things can get sorted out.

Q550 With regard to the LCM process, there seems to be a general consensus among the other legislatures that, quite often, the engagement on those comes reasonably late in the day. It means that they then have to scramble to pull things together quickly, which leads to a bit of wasted resources. Do you agree that there should be a standard time limit allowed?

That is a good idea; I had not heard that put before, but it does not entirely surprise me. I do not think one should read too much in the way of conspiracy into any of that. There have been many occasions, dare I say it, when, as a Minister, I have been handed papers rather later than I would perhaps have liked, and I believe that is a problem that many people have raised over the years. I am sure that officials work very hard to try to make sure that consultation takes place in good time, and I am sure they will have heard your comments, Mr Roberts, and taken note.
Q551 I appreciate that.

I come to the first of my guest questions now. I have a question from Andrew, who is an assistant headteacher in my constituency. He asks: “Given the differences with the demographics in Wales, do you believe that the Barnett formula—which was a temporary measure many years ago—remains the best funding formula for Wales to reach its potential?”

Currently, as Ms Crosbie has said, Wales is getting £1.20 for every pound that is spent in devolved areas, so we are doing quite well out of things at the moment. My worry is that if we went back to the drawing board and came up with a completely different formula, there is, of course, the possibility that Wales could end up getting significantly less than it does at the moment.
Q552 I completely appreciate that. It is something that has been looked at over decades.

I want to turn to cost of living and economy-type questions. Another Andrew—a different Andrew—who runs a local caravan park wants to know whether you think the tourism tax is a regressive step for Wales, or whether it will be useful.

I think the tourism tax is an incredibly bad idea for the tourism industry, even more so in border areas. Where, for example, people have a choice of going to either Monmouth or the Forest of Dean in my own part of the world, there is going to be a financial incentive to go to the Forest of Dean rather than coming and staying in Monmouthshire. I think we will see that all the way up the Welsh border, and perhaps beyond. It is a great shame.
It is indeed.
It is a matter for the Welsh Government, of course, not for me.
Of course.

Dr James Davies : There is another issue on tourism, actually. I have many constituents with holiday lets who are extremely concerned that because they have not been able to let out their property for a sufficient number of days, due to the Welsh Government’s own lockdown rules, they are now being penalised in retrospect by having to pay council tax at an inflated rate. That is another aspect whereby tourism needs a voice.

Q553 Indeed. On the cost of living more generally, you answered questions from my colleague Mr David earlier regarding uprating of benefits by inflation, but you did not mention pensions and the triple lock. Do you agree that pensions should be increased in line with inflation?

In an ideal world, I would agree. I would want to see pensions, benefits, public sector pay, and the pay of anyone—particularly those on lower wages—increasing in line with inflation, or even beyond. That is what I would like in an ideal world, yes, but we are not in an ideal world.

Q554 Indeed we are not, but we are not sure whether there will be uprating of benefits, and you talked about people on low incomes. There is also talk of freezing the income tax thresholds for longer, so people will end up paying more tax by stealth almost. Do you agree that that is an appropriate policy in such difficult times?

You will be aware, Mr Roberts, and I am sure everyone in the room is aware, that I do not know the specifics of what is going to come out in the financial statement. I doubt whether I will be told in advance—maybe, but if so, it will probably only be a few hours in advance, if at all. I am sure I will learn about it at the same time as everyone else.

I can only say to you that I know the Chancellor and the Prime Minister to be compassionate men who are acutely aware of the need to target all possible help at the least well-off. By that I mean those on benefits, pensioners, those who are disabled. I just don’t know what they are going to do. Even if I did know, I would not be able to say so at this meeting, but I genuinely do not know. I think you will appreciate that I do not know. The Secretary of State for Wales is not going to be given advance notice of what is going to go into the Budget.

I do know there are going to be some difficult decisions, because we all accept the financial problem that we face. It is not one that the UK Government have brought about, but it is going to mean some difficult decisions. I don’t know exactly where those decisions are going to affect people.
Q555 I would just like to pick up on something the Chair mentioned about lower income households and off-grid households. Do you think the support for off-grid households is enough?

I think £100 was certainly not generous, given the circumstances. I accept the argument that in general those who are on network gas will have seen much steeper rises in percentage terms than those are who off grid. None the less, everyone has seen huge rises in costs. I don’t feel that £100 was overly generous and I am sure that is another item that the Government will be looking at.
Q556 Given that that is a relatively larger demographic in Wales, compared with the rest of the country, what kind of representations are you making to get that changed?

I will make a representation about that, given the percentage of people in Wales who are off grid. I believe the Government are already well aware of it. It doesn’t just affect Wales; it affects people in rural areas across the whole of the United Kingdom.
May I have one more quick question, Chair?
If you are super quick.

Q557 I will be. Following on from the shared prosperity fund question earlier, local authorities expected to receive answers in October about whether their plans were acceptable. Have they received those responses? If not, when can they expect to receive them, and when will the funds be released?

We have already been in touch with DLUHC to express our view that it is important that that question be answered as quickly as possible. It is not actually a matter for me; it is for my colleague in DLUHC. As soon as I have an answer, I will be happy to share it with the Committee.
I think the end of this calendar year has been given as a cut-off date.
There’s a slippage.
Thank you, Rob. Geraint, you had a quick supplementary as well.

Q558 Yes. Throughout this hearing, you have mentioned that Wales gets £1.20 per head compared with £1 for England. Would you accept that that is because the demography of Wales is poorer, sicker and older, and therefore we need more money, and that relative to Scotland it is not generous at all? Or are you saying that we should have some sort of poll tax where everyone gets paid the same, irrespective of need? Is that what you are saying?

I wouldn’t read too much into the comment, Mr Davies. I was just making the point that Wales actually receives more money per head for public spending than England, which is why, as I said, I am sometimes surprised that public services do not seem to be offered at the same level.
We need it more, because we’re sicker.

The Welsh Government are getting more but not delivering as much. We have lower ed ucational standards according to the independent PISA report , lower health standards—I would love to answer your question, but I have to go and meet my union representative in three minutes, and I am sure Ms Winter would not me to be late. She is very welcome to come and say hello as well, if she wishes.
I have many constituents coming up myself, but thank you very much.
Can I ask one other question?

Q559 Sorry, Geraint, we are running out of time. Secretary of State and Under-Secretary of State, thank you for your time. I will finish with one quick question. When Virginia Crosbie asked you about the issue of a St David’s Day bank holiday, you said that it is an issue that you probably wouldn’t stamp out of Cabinet over.
Correct.
What is an issue that you would leave Cabinet over? [ Laughter. ]

Mr Chairman, I have only been a Cabinet Minister for a week or so; given the superb Prime Minister we have got, I cannot imagine that there will be any issue at all that will lead me to want to walk away from such a fantastic Prime Minister.

Thank you very much. That is very helpful. We look forward to welcoming you back very soon, Secretary of State. There are lots of issues that are of direct relevance to us and our constituents, and we value the opportunity to discuss them further with you.
[1] The Secretary of State stated in correspondence after the evidence session that there are 550 jobs at risk, not 200.
[2] The Secretary of State stated in correspondence after the evidence session that the semi-conductors manufactured at the Newport site are “simple” semi-conductors, not “compound” semi-conductors.
