You have rightly identified that a lot of the global motivators have come from the big tech companies, the big five in Silicon Valley, in terms of hardware and investment. The cultures we are now hearing about in these sorts of committees and trying to get ahead of, which are around the commodification of data and the exploitation of user behaviours, are in danger of just travelling into this next paradigm by default, because the business model of these companies is about data extraction and data commodification. If this sector is led only by the Metas and Googles of the world, that will happen by default.

It is not inevitable at this point. With conversations around regulation that are happening around the world, and with the question of decentralisation and how that is going to play in, there is an opportunity to create a 21st century culture around these new technologies that does not just have to inherit the toxicity from Web 2.0. A lot of that will come down to what we do with things such as the Online Safety Bill, how we hold companies accountable and, to an extent, not accepting the fact that immersive technology is a goldmine for data enthusiasts, which it is.

Just to backpedal a little, the reason this is a really appealing proposition for Meta and others is that the data available about users suddenly shifts from, “What do I click on? How long do I spend here? What do I swipe? What do I share?”, which is useful, to, “What am I looking at and for how long? What does that mean about what I care about? Do my pupils dilate when I look at that? What do I say to you? What do you say to me? What do you then say to someone else?” The behavioural data available, particularly through these social virtual reality encounters, and the absolute richness of that data as we move into a world of augmented reality —excuse me for jargoning— is spectacular for a data capitalist.

It is not reasonable to assume that data belongs to those companies just because they are doing the early investment in the hardware. The decisions that are made in rooms such as this in the next two years are going to make a big difference to whether that business model proliferates or whether there is an ability for others within the marketplace to come in and offer alternatives. If we do not want innovation to come only from Silicon Valley and for users to be commoditised by default, there have to be some decisions made about how we understand privacy and data rights, and how we create a more accessible, inclusive marketplace that can be moved into by companies from around the world, empowering users to operate within those spaces, without the presumption that to do so is a parasitic endeavour.

Q34 Is one of you able to offer a view on how well the UK digital businesses in this area are taking advantage of or indeed have new commercial investment available to them? We know the potential value, and indeed the current value, of all of this globally and in the UK. I just wondered about the UK’s ability to take advantage of that potential. We will come back to data later on, because that is really important. Is there anything on the investment and the funding stream that is either available and not being taken advantage of or is just not there?

I can give our view. We have 2,500 games companies in interactive entertainment that are doing VR and AR in the UK, but 95% of them are SMEs; they are very small. One of the biggest barriers at the moment is talent. We are all in competition with fintech for the same kind of talent. We are in competition now with other sectors that are adjacent to us because of virtual production techniques. We are not seeing the flow of diverse talent —people who are going to create these incredible experiences that appeal to different audiences. We are not seeing that come through. This a global issue; it is not just a UK issue, but that has been exacerbated, unfortunately, by Brexit, which has prevented the free movement of people across Europe.

We are well placed. We have seen a record amount of investment in video games companies, in the kind s of companies that are creating these kinds of experiences, over the last two years. Over the last five years, it is over £7 billion in investment and acquisitions. That has been a real shift over recent times, which we did not see previously.

However, there is not really access to funding for risky content. It might be stories and experiences being created by underrepresented groups who are diverse and who want to tell different stor ies and bring those experiences to new audiences. There is no BBC equivalent for games companies or companies that want to make that kind of content. There is an opportunity there.

We are grateful for the video games tax relief, which, as it does across the other screen sectors, incentivises the production of cultural content. It is utterly critical to our future and current growth. We are also very grateful for the extension and investment of the UK games fund for prototype funding, but that is about it. When it comes to that kind of funding, if we want that diversity of content and experiences to appeal to different audiences, we need better routes to funding to really take advantage of this opportunity.
Aside from any public subsidy or tax relief, is the City willing to invest in your businesses?

The City has become extremely interested because a bunch of tech bros are talking about the metaverse. That is great. Everyone is very excited about crypto and NFTs and where this leads. I get concerned that is not a sustainable route. There is more confidence now in video games companies, for instance, from investors, which is very welcome, because games now are more of an ongoing service and creative product. So w e have seen a shift but we are in for some potentially interesting times.

I note , on investment from outside of London , that s ome research was done in the south-west on barriers to immersive companies getting investment. It was done by SETsquared as part of round table sessions . They found that a lot of the barriers to investment are around the angel investors at the smaller scale of seed funding tending to invest in areas that they know. When you have this really new space, how can they feel comfortable investing? There can just be that knowledge gap. Running virtual reality event s and showing virtual reality to them , improving immersive literacy among those smaller-scale investors, could actually be a really great way forward.

Just to add a little bit of data, the Immerse UK report on Monday has been looking at private investment in immersive companies. We have seen 83% growth in immersive tech companies in the UK in the last five years. Private investment in those UK companies is also growing. The latest figures that they had were that there w as £224 million invested in 2021. That wa s specifically private investment in immersive companies, and that is looking like it is going to double this year. So i t is still quite a small amount, but it is on a significant growth curve.

One of the things that does not get discussed in the report, which is perhaps anecdotal from the companies I am working with, is that a lot of that private investment is having to be found overseas. The companies are still staunchly basing themselves in the UK and trying to capitalise on the opportunity to have that convergence between the arts and the tech sector that we are very good at in this country, but often they are finding a massive issue with talent drain.

The two biggest barriers identified in this report are access to finance and access to talent. Sometimes the companies that are hanging on in there in the UK are still going largely to the US, Canada and China. We are seeing a difficulty in the volume of investment available, the understanding of investors in this immersive space and the access to talent within the UK ecosystem, which is creating a bit of hesitancy in that investor landscape.

Q35 You have already covered some of the aspects of what I was planning to ask, which was around the challenges and risks involved with the expansion of these technologies. You can think about that in two ways. You have talked a lot about the risks that might prevent expansion, such as skills and investment. I am really glad you brought up talent pipelines, because that is key and might be good to touch on again.

Let us assume expansion. Let us assume these things do take off. What are the risks involved? I am thinking about who gets excluded. Of course, you are all talking positively, and we share your positivity about the impact of these technologies, but let us put the negative hat on. What are the risks of seeing this expand? Who misses out?

I would refer you as well to the Safeguarding the M etaverse report that the IET commissioned, which Verity and I co-authored, and the importance of asking that question and asking it now. I was quite surprised, at the end of last year and the beginning of this year, when pitching this report to the IET, that when we were starting to have conversations with policymakers, politicians and government departments, even though there had been tens of millions of pounds of funding going into the immersive sector through Audience of the Future and creative clusters, there was so little conversation about the risks, which seemed really strange. It is not for lack of funding that this sector has not appeared to be thinking about it. That is one thing. There was an issue.

However, having had it confirmed, as has been said quite a few times now in the Lords and in the Commons, that AR and VR are included in the Online Safety Bill, that puts us in a really good position in comparison with the rest of the world in thinking about regulation. I am now part of various working groups of different law enforcement organisations and government departments, where they are really waking up, having seen this report and some great work that others have done as well, to looking at this right now.

We have this golden window of time and this opportunity. It is important enough that we need to be thinking really seriously about regulation. As Mark Zuckerberg said in a recent podcast, the level of adoption of the Meta Quest 2 is similar to Xbox or a PlayStation. You have this level of adoption that is high enough that it is important, but at the same time you also have a malleability that still exists, because it is still emerging. The scale is not at all anything like the level of social media yet, so it is a golden window of opportunity to ask that question: what are the key risks? Maybe I will hand over to Verity now.

Let me do some naysaying. We have talked a bit about data, and there is a big conversation there that we can return to. One of the really concerning areas that we have seen through our research—you may have seen various investigative journalism pieces through Channel 4’s “Dispatches”, the BBC’s inquiry and others—is that, particularly as we move from these experiences being one at a time, personal experiences, to more what you might call “ metavers y” spaces, where there are people co-located in a digital space together, we are seeing an almost endemic proliferation of harassing behaviours.

When there are these multiperson, unregulated, unmoderated spaces, that is what we are seeing. The Centre for Countering Digital Hate did some research and decided that you can expect to be harassed in one form or another every seven minutes, and that goes up exponentially if you are presenting as female, as a child or as a person of colour. The proliferation of hateful and harassing behaviours in these open, unmoderated spaces is becoming almost the culture of these metaverse spaces.

From a purely economic point of view, that will absolutely create market flight. Nobody wants to go and be harassed on a regular basis, but it is not being particularly well addressed by the providers and platforms. There is a worry coming up in our research that, if they overly police these behaviours, they will lose the audience that they have, so there is a reluctance to create any form of feedback loop or accountability for these negative behaviours. These are very different to experiencing trolling and griefing behaviours online and in the square format games, because of the things we were talking about before: this enhanced sense of presence and feeling that you are physically with someone because of the spatial dimensions of these technologies.

We have seen this time and again in psychology research from the 1960s, 1970s, 1980s and particularly the 1990s, when we really understood the psychological impact of being in these simulation environments. You quite quickly forget that you are not physically there with someone, so when they invade your personal space, shout at you or simulate behaviours that you might not appreciate and that, in physical space, would be unquestionably harassing behaviours, this can be highly traumatising when experienced in virtual reality. It can be deeply upsetting and, in many cases, qualify as illegal behaviour. We are increasingly working with law enforcement, Ofcom, the Information Commissioner’s Office and so on to understand where criminality exists within these harassing behaviours.

That is so important, and that is where we can become leaders, because the games industry does have techniques around best practice on how to have friend spaces. As a team, we never go into the public spaces in virtual reality. We go as a team with our friends, and you create your friend lists and so on. It is about sharing that best practice and that experience. I am sure that is covered in the report, because those are the techniques that we have learned over the past 35 or 40 years of being in MMOs—massively multiplayer online games.

There are techniques but , crucially , it is also about education right down at school level. Through research we have done in our education projects, we know that children who play online games are much more adept at understanding how to protect their privacy, and how to protect themselves in other digital arenas. Again, it is harnessing the experience and the reality that young people, children and adults are already in these spaces, but understanding how we make sure of that best practice on how to inform and empower people so that they can take control themselves and have a good time in these places.

That is really helpful. I am glad that you took that angle about risk and safeguarding. In terms of other challenges, have we touched on all the groups that might be excluded from playing? Are there other exclusions that we should be aware of?

If you look at who experiences digital exclusion anyway, there is still quite a proportion of the UK population who are not on the internet, so of course we have these groups. From the research that Limina has done, when we used to run virtual reality events, we had this VR theatre experience where people could come and collectively experience an immersive night out with their friends and family. We learned a lot about who feels excluded and why, because often they would tell us afterwards, “This was great. I did n’t think it was for me beforehand but now I know it is ”. Overwhelmingly, women would say, “I thought this was something for teenage boys. I thought this was a boys’ toy”. It was really rewarding to see how easily you could change that with a different marketing style, and not a stereotypically ‘ girly ’ marketing style at all. Just the way you market and the language you use can make a huge difference.

Age is also a factor, with people tending to feel that this is something for teenagers and young people, meaning that they can self-exclude. They sometimes think, “I do not have the digital skills”, when in fact, if you have experienced VR, you will know that it can be a lot easier and more intuitive than using a standard computer. It is often more about perception of digital skills than the actuality.

You asked a brilliant question about who is being excluded. There is a really practical exclusion that happens with the way that the hardware is currently designed. We have even seen silly things like how having an unremovable strap across the top of your head will often exclude people with afro hair. For people who use wheelchairs, often the musculoskeletal assumptions about your spine and neck strength are really precluding participation. It is largely being solved, but there were early problems with the presumed line of sight being a six-foot-tall person, so if you are in a chair, you are o n the floor.
That excludes me then.

There are some really obvious blind spots that the designers of these technologies are just not acknowledging, or not acknowledging the need for. That makes it feel like it is for a protected group of 22 year-old white men.
Tall white men.

Very tall white men, yes. The optical illusion that virtual reality gives you is based on where two lenses are in front of your eyes. If you, usually for reasons of ethnicity, have eyes that are slightly wider or narrower than these headsets are presuming, you are fresh out of luck. There is a personalisation to it that involves the bridge of your nose, the width of your eyes, the style of your hair or whether you use a headscarf. At the moment, all of these things are making it more and more difficult to participate, and making it feel like it is not for you.

If people are being left out on that scale in these early stages, they will not be influencing the design of the future technologies, so we do have an issue around diversity and inclusion in terms of the basic things such as how the kit is made.

You have opened a Pandora’s box. O ne reason why people will not put the headset on is sometimes because they do not trust it. They just say, “I do n’t trust this. I will not put it on”. Coming back to the Online Safety Bill, trust can equal adoption of technology.

I do not know whether you are going to come on to this, but there is also an issue here about the way in which some of this is designed to incorporate the disability access issues in technology as well.
I do not know whether you wanted to follow on.

It was just to get on the record that there is an issue here about the alignment, at the point of design, with the special needs for disabled access in terms of the technology, which is slightly different from what you have just been saying. That was all.

On a positive note, t here is some fantastic research within UK higher education authorities , and lots of PhD students are looking into things such as audio description for virtual reality and various sensorial ways of experiencing immersive content. We are well positioned to be advocating for difference and leading on some of these more inclusive practices for the way that the design operates. We just need to empower those experts to be able to do something about it.

Thank you for clarifying that. The second half of the question, although it feels like a slightly different question, is around the difference between large and small organisations , and between privately funded and publicly funded organisations. In evidence from Martin Smith, we heard that bigger institutions such as the V&A and the Royal Opera House are better placed financially to pick up on the spillover from the games industry and to do this stuff.

We would all find that in the history of art innovation has very often been difficult in those big organisations because of the weight of history, stakeholders and expectations. Innovation happens at the outside and then comes in once it has proved to be successful. Jo, you are nodding your head. Is that the way you are seeing it: that we should be careful in assuming that the big organisations are going to take on the innovation, because actually we need to empower the little ones to do it?

Yes, absolutely. My observation is that, particularly during the pandemic, you were seeing a lot of cultural institutions trying to pivot digitally, which is probably what they should have been doing 10 or 15 years ago or more. It was actually the skill set that was really lacking. We need to empower the skill sets within those organisations. They do not necessarily have the skill sets. They might have the funding, but then it is a one-off project that lives for a bit around that exhibition or that moment and then disappears.

That is important. I keep asking where our metaverse strategy for the cultural industries is. Where is our cultural and digital asset bank? You are going to hear from witnesses. I wish I could hang around for that bit. I will watch; I will do a catch-up. Where is our digital infrastructure that includes skill sets, being able to bring in the R&D, but with a more sustainable approach to how we create these experiences? That is so that it is not just big institutions that might have the funding to do that, but small companies that are innovating, which might not be on anyone’s radar, that can be brought in and innovate.

To build on that quickly, this is an art form and communications medium in its own right ; it is just so different. Often people who have a bit of experience in gaming, immersive theatre or film making can come to it with skills that really help. When a large institution that has already built up its heritage in a certain art form then says, “Okay, we ’re doing immersive”, it can set it up as if immersive is an extension rather than its own thing. When I have seen the really successful examples, it is often when the creators have come to it fresh. The same applies to regulation and law. It is about seeing this as its own thing.

I have a quick data point just to help frame where we are currently. The Immerse UK report identifies that, in the UK, 80% of companies specifically working on immersive are micro-SMEs, w ith between one and nine employees. We are seeing the dedicated and focused work on immersive being done by small, agile companies that can exploit R&D quicker.
There is a real question about how that becomes integrated into the organisations in a way that bridges the points that Jo and Catherine made there. Thank you.

Q36 On th e point about 80% being SMEs, if you actually look at the total value of the industry, how much are the SMEs as a value? In most things you get lots of very small organisations and a few big ones that are dominant. Is th at true in this case?

It is a good question. It is quite a difficult one to get data on. The UK has certain larger companies at scale such as Framestore, which has been operating in this space and has come from more of a film and television background; it has moved into this very quickly and is proliferating. So y es, to an extent.

One of the things that we noticed was that there was a massive hype cycle around 2016, and a lot of companies set up and grew very quickly and took on lots of employees. As that hype cycle settled, a lot of companies strategically started to work with their freelancer networks more than having this bloated staffing pool, because they could not necessarily rely on consistently available investment and commissioning, but also because there is this incredibly prolific network of micro-SMEs within the UK that are highly specialised. It seems like even the big companies, because they work in these emerging territories, are choosing to hold a certain amount of expertise at core and then look for those micro-specialisms in the freelancer network and in small company networks.

Q37 I will start by declaring an interest in that my daughter is a gamer and has been for 20 years, and now is writing the narrative for a big new game. Her partner composes music for the games industry. When you talk about talent, there is infinite opportunity amongst the creative, but I do not see the pipeline myself. That is just a point I wanted to land.

This really goes into how others are doing around the world. There is significant projected growth in this industry. Countries elsewhere seem to be making dynamic and large investments to facilitate that growth. My understanding is that here we are not properly capitalising on the opportunities, and that there are difficulties in scaling and with skills shortages. I would like you to talk about how internationally competitive the UK’s current position in this area is, and what the risks are to our future success.

Speaking to people working in the sector, such as creatives and founders of start-ups in the space, one strength that we have is that there have been quite a lot of small pots of R&D money around that have had quite an impact on the sector and its growth. As you say, the next step is that scal e ability. You have something. You have made some content that you are really proud of. You want to get it to the audience beyond a bit of user testing with your friends. That is where it is really hard to get that funding for that next step. There has been lots of this push to get things going, but then what do you do next? When you go to private investors, if it is a t seed level, and they say, “I do n’t really have the experience in that. I don’t feel confident investing”, it can feel like a serious barrier to that next step.

We saw a real opportunity in our own venue, and then seeing other organisations as well where there is a significant demand. People really want to experience this content. Ideally, a queue is not the best form of ticket management, but people will go through long queues to experience some immersive content. However, it is strange that, when looking at the funding opportunities available in 2018 or 2019, there were predominantly these small R&D pots.

If we are not careful , looking from a funding policy perspective, public money could keep going into “ another cool R&D project ” , and these really talented people may actually leave the immersive sector due to a lack of career development, taking those skills elsewhere. That is ultimately a waste of that great content and expertise, so supporting and stimulating the next stage would be fantastic.

I completely agree with that. It is the scale-up. It is either go big or go home, and that is the funding gap. For the games industry, where a lot of this innovation is, and which of course combines the excellence that we have in the UK in creative industry storytelling, as well as audio design and so on, with technology industries, a lot of companies are struggling to get to that next level. A huge breakout hit can be exported globally by a team of 10 people but that is quite rare, so it is really difficult.

Incentives such as the creative enterprise funding for the scale-up programme, which we partner with Creative UK on, are fantastic, because they are giving those businesses that leg-up for free. It is accessible. We really focus on getting diverse leaders of those businesses to hon e their teeth and tak e the opportunity, but we are facing stiff competition. Countries such as Germany, Australia and Ireland have consulted with us and looked at the games industry’s success over the last 10 years and how that has affected immersive industries generally. They have looked at our video games tax relief, they have looked at the R&D tax relief and they want the same, and they have created the same but with better rates.

We still have the talent, but we are in that competition with fintech, which is offering insane salaries for graduates out of particular courses, which is just impossible for a lot of SMEs, in particular, to keep up with. We are in a really favourable position. We are concerned that we will not remain in that favourable position, so we would like to be able to protect that position and make sure that we remain more competitive and the envy of the world, because that is what we are.
What would be the thing you want done?

Speaking from our perspective, the tax relief for all the screen industries is incredibly valuable. For the games industry, it has been essential for that growth over the last 10 years, and it has been essential to then leverage that investment that has happened into the games industry. The growth of those companies then means that they have been acquired.

We want to see more companies coming through the ecosystem that are retaining their British-owned IP in this country and collaborating with others. We want to see that protected, but we also need a serious injection of skills investment and support. We do not have the right combination of people who have arts and humanities expertise combined with computer science and computational thinking. Those are the critical skill sets of the fourth industrial revolution if we want to maintain our globally competitive position.

I agree 100%. In terms of what we need, this has been discussed in previous sessions and so I know we are aware, but there has been such a damaging attitude to the value of arts subjects at higher education at all levels, and mass disinvestment in arts and humanities learning at university level. That is the bit that I am involved in most, so I see it very profoundly, but it has a massive knock-on effect for things such as parent confidence for where they are going to allow their children to study.

There have been so many toxic narratives in recent years about not studying something that will not have this certainty about becoming a doctor or lawyer. If there is one thing that we can do to counter that, it is illustrating that my graduates, who are absolutely in that middle space between arts and creativity and technology, are so employable; they are ridiculously employable. They cannot fend off offers quick enough. It is a massive opportunity for our graduates, particularly when they have the opportunity to do that STEAM thing, where they can meld science and technology with artistry. It makes them absolute unicorns in their field. If we continue to presume that encouraging our young people into the arts is somehow discouraging them from productive careers, we are kidding ourselves. We need a reversal of that narrative.

There are plenty of academic marketplaces that are providing STEM graduates. There are some fantastic examples of how Asian markets in particular are really investing in their science and technology graduates, and they are proliferating in all markets. Historically, the difference from the UK sector has been that we have been able to give these really well-rounded polymath people the opportunity to develop their skills, not just in one sector but in these convergent spaces. Arts and technology are so well matched in the UK right now, but increasingly I am finding people come in quite nervous about whether they are taking a risk by investing in their own creativity. We have to tell them that it is worth it and we have to mean it.
That would be the key message.
It is the one from me, yes.
Polymaths are the future.
Yes, we heard.

Q38 In terms of the jobs that are available to people who have the level of skills, training and qualifications that you have described that are now becoming so short, because the education opportunities are not there for them, can you bring this to life? We hear this message, but what sort of jobs could graduates who qualify in the way that you would like them to be walking into that they are missing out on?

We have a huge shortage of technical artists. There is a huge need in our immersive industries, our video games industry and our virtual production industry, which is nascent but growing in the UK. Technical artists are on the shortage occupation list, as well as AI programmers, level designers and analysts, who are taking in, understanding and feeding data back into how an immersive creative product is experienced. It is not the same product design as these things.

Those are the skill sets, but the challenge that we all face is that these jobs do not exist yet. If we are looking at what we need to grow the sector, these are jobs that simply do not have names yet, but those are some of the typical kinds of jobs that we are really struggling with filling.

Am I right in understanding what you are saying when we look at the competition, particularly from the Far East but also, as you have already said, Germany and closer to home in Ireland? I am generalising here, but in the Far East their focus on the technical aspect of training is what is, at the moment, putting them out in front of us, because we do not have enough of that, but what they are not doing is the art, and we could steal back an advance if we were able to combine these two things.

From my experience, that tends to be the story that we hear, as well as from territories like the Indian continent, where computer science skills might be really strong, but that curiosity, that storytelling, the humanities, and the arts and cultural skill set that you combine with computer science are not quite there yet. That is our opportunity. In Australia, Germany and Ireland, they are really focusing on the financial incentives and tax reliefs.

Q39 I just want to check what Verity said and match it with something that Jo said. You talked about people fending off job offers, and you talked about jobs that do not exist yet. I suspect that both are true, but what you might have been saying, Verity—correct me if I am wrong—is that the overlapping technical, creative and problem-solving skills that your students are getting have an application both within but also beyond the creative industries, the creative economy and, indeed, the broader economy. Is that what you were saying?

It is a little bit of both. We are seeing a lot of our graduates going into the creative industries and making really significant waves internationally in terms of the media and entertainment space and the arts and cultural space. You are quite right that one of the things about immersive technologies is that they are permeating almost all verticals. A lot of our students are going into training and simulation, virtual education, architecture and various industrial contexts that are picking up these tools and technologies. A number are going into gaming. There has been a massive explosion in haptics and gesture-based interfaces that, again, they are incredibly well suited to work within, because they understand interaction design as well as the technologies that underpin them.

We are seeing a proliferation across different market sectors, but I would say that a significant number of them are moving directly into the arts and cultural sector and trying to make change in that space.

Thank you very much. It has been a fascinating session. We are very grateful to you for your time and for your clear evidence. I do not normally comment on things like this, but it is quite interesting that, on a topic such as this one, we have three women in front of us. I did not want that to go by without acknowledging it; we did not deliberately do that, but it is impressive. All of three of you have been very impressive witnesses and I am very grateful to you. Thank you very much.

sessions.iT: Work of the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland
sessions.w: Chris Heaton-Harris (Northern Ireland Office); Madeleine Alessandri CMG (Northern Ireland Office); Chris Flatt (Northern Ireland Office)

segs.tx: Northern Ireland Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Work of the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland , HC 86
Tuesday 18 October 202 2
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 18 October 202 2 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Simon Hoare (Chair); Mr Gregory Campbell ; Stephen Farry ; Sir Robert Goodwill ; Claire Hanna ; Fay Jones; Ian Paisley ; Bob Stewart .
Questions 326 - 418
Witnesses

I: Rt Hon. Chris Heaton-Harris MP , Secretary of State for Northern Ireland ; Madeleine Alessandri CMG , Permanent Secretary , Northern Ireland Office ; Chris Flatt, Director, Strategy , Northern Ireland Office .
Examination of Witnesses
Witnesses: Rt Hon. Chris Heaton-Harris, Madeleine Alessandri and Chris Flatt .

Q326 Good afternoon, colleagues. Welcome to this one-off show — this spectacular — with our new Secretary of State, Chris Heaton-Harris. Chris, you are very welcome, and your team as well. Could I ask you to introduce your team for the record?
I have Madeleine Alessandri, the Permanent Secretary, who m I believe you all know , and Chris Flatt, who is a strategy director in the Department.

Q327 You are all very welcome. Secretary of State, you have recently started in what many would argue is often the most challenging, certainly the most fascinating and one of probably the best jobs in G overnment. By way of opener, could you flesh out for the Committee, say over a year timeframe, what a successful Heaton-Harris Secretary of Stateship looks like? What does an unsuccessful Heaton-Harris Secretary of Stateship look like?

I am sure the Committee will tell me what an unsuccessful one will look like. As for a successful one, in my ideal world, in my dream of dreams—and thank you very much indeed for the welcome and the invitation to the Committee—it would be very quickly to have a re - formed Executive , so decisions for the people of Northern Ireland are taken by the people elected in Northern Ireland. That would be obviously a signal that things are moving on a subject I am sure we might just touch on briefly : the Northern Ireland protocol and our relationship with the European Union.
Q328 The odds on that happening were not particularly good, were they?
I have some form in these areas and I am a glass ‑ half ‑ full man, as you know. Let us see how that works through the system and maybe we will talk about it a bit later.

You have got to have an Executive com ing back, so that decisions are taken. Then there is a build-up to the 25th anniversary of the Belfast / Good Friday agreement, which a whole host of people in Northern Ireland, the south, Great Britain and America will be wanting to celebrate in a big way. I hope it will demonstrate lots of chances of prosperity, with huge amounts of inward investment flowing into Northern Ireland, a celebration of peace and prosperity for 25 years , and a look forward from there. Then, hopefully , the role of the Secretary of State will not diminish, because it is fairly well determined, but will go back to what would be a relatively old-fashioned version of what a Secretary of State does , where most things would be conducted by the Executive.

Q329 You have answered the question of what an unsuccessful Secretary of State should be: none of those things occurring. On your point about the Good Friday agreement and its 2 5th anniversary, do you see that as a moment for marking and celebration, or do you see it as an opportunity for both assessment and potential collaborative review?

I see it as a bit more than that even. There are three members of your Committee who are members of my political party , and I used the slot at my party’s conference just recently to talk about the Belfast / Good Friday agreement with my other two Ministers. The reason I did that is that I have become very aware, in the short time I have held this role, that there is actually a bit of education to be done in England, Scotland and Wales as to why the Belfast / Good Friday agreement is so important and what it has done.

It is not just the things that you talked about — a general build-up. I also want to do a bit of a reminder to people. At the weekend I was looking at the build - up to that agreement and all the political capital that was staked by so many people at that period of time. I remind people all the time that, in my lifetime — in my political lifetime, in 1997, in the general election — motorways were closed because of bomb threats across the country.

There have been plenty of unbelievable tragedies , which I do not particularly want to linger on here , that have really hit the people of the four nations massively hard, and yet somehow, because of maybe 25 years of growing peace and prosperity and it being less in the news, there is a lack of understanding in England, Scotland and Wales — maybe more England and Wales. I would not say I worry about it, but I do not think people quite understand the importance of the Belfast / Good Friday agreement.
Q330 Do you have a concern that the sort of dividend that flows from it is hard-baked and taken for granted as always being there?
Yes, and the peace that has flowed from it equally so. It has been hard won over a long period of time.
Q331 Maybe enforced viewing of the final episode of “ Derry Girls ” in every school actually would not be a bad thing. There may have to be a few bleeps.

There is an opportunity , though. I hope that it is going to be a time for reflection on what was good in the past and how it can be built on for the future. We can use the moments that we will have in time, with maybe some big visits, big moments and speeches from fantastic orators, such as you, Chair, so people will be reminded of the importance of the Belfast / Good Friday agreement and what it has done for peace and prosperity in Northern Ireland as we move forward.

Q332 On a general political thing, you are a former Minister in the Brexit Department, a committed Brexiter and a former chair of the ERG. Northern Ireland voted a different way in the referendum. What are you doing, as Secretary of State—I am not talking about a distillation of your views—to build bridges with the other political parties? There was not an assumption, but always an anxiety , that the Conservative Party is closer to one party than another. What is your strategy for making sure that all the political parties in Northern Ireland have equal access to your phone, your ear, your desk, your time , and so on ?

It is not a strategy. Cla i re Hanna asked me a question in my first OPQs about my political views, as it were. It is easy to say anything, so you will have to judge me on what I actually do. I have five or six weeks now of demonstrating that I am happily talking to all sides. I do not necessarily have an open-door policy, but I have pretty much an open-door policy. Too many people have my mobile number, but fortunately not the Daily Mail for that leak thing they did. I believe in talking to people.

Q333 In any of those initial conversations, has anything pleasantly surprised or disappointed you? You do not have to attribute the surprise or the disappointment to an individual. You are engaging, but whether people are engaging with you is, I suppose, the question .

I think people are genuinely engaging with me. I certainly feel that way and I am sure others will tell me if that is not the case. I really think I am getting the fullness of everybody’s views. No one is holding back but, in all my dealings with anybody from Northern Ireland, they are yet to hold back. I like that, because I am a great believer that politics is about doing what you say and saying what you do. I think that I am getting real answers to my real questions , and I am being asked proper questions about what I intend to do and how I intend to conduct myself. I am happy to give fairly short and straightforward answers to that.

Q334 Thank you to the Secretary of State for joining us. You will know that there was an election in May. Despite the people having spoken, they have not had the opportunities to discharge their mandates. I hope the Secretary of State understands the frustration and cynicism i t breeds in Northern Ireland when we have the election part all the time, but much less of the governance, achieving outcomes , and scrutiny parts that are supposed to come in between. It reduces the democratic process to just sending messages and not actually delivering on the promise of the agreement or creating opportunities. I will ask what steps he has taken to ensure that the institutions can be restored, including decoupling the issues of restoration and achieving a protocol deal, because they are different things and on different tracks. What steps has he taken to avoid an election having to be called next week, which would ultimately face the same challenges and the same cast of characters on the other side of it?

I think I have been fairly straightforward in everything I have said and done in this job that I would like to see the Executive re - form. I understand that there is a reason why it has not and so there has been another twin track to try to make sure that we can demonstrate that there is going to be some movement on the issues around the protocol that stop people coming into the Executive. That is a job of work in itself.

I do not know how popular this is in my party anymore, but I am still a localist. I still strongly believe in devolution and I think it is the right thing as a practice. I know maybe some of the models around the country might not have worked as everybody would have wanted, but it is an evolution as well. I believe that the best decisions about people’s lives are taken by people elected by them and close to them.

I have been fairly straightforward. Every time I have been asked that question, I have been urging everybody to go back into the Executive, because there are some decisions that need to be taken by that Executive, when it comes to—I am sure we will talk about it—the Budget and a whole host of other really important areas where decisions are best taken by MLAs in this particular case.

What have I done? I have met all the party leaders. I have met pretty much every MLA who has asked to meet me. I am happily meeting all the MPs from all political parties. As I say, most people seem to have my mobile number , and they are actually very generous to me and not using it too much, but I am in constant contact. We had the press conference after the British-Irish Intergovernmental Conference a couple of weeks ago, which I used to say this again. If we do not get a re - formed Executive by one minute past midnight on 28 October, I will be calling an election. That is what the law requires me to do and that is what I will be doing.

I know that lots of people do not want that to happen, but it is a legislative requirement. In this place, I cannot see the space for any emergency legislation, let alone a general will for it. I discussed it with my Cabinet colleagues this morning. I cannot be clearer: that is what will happen on 28 October.

Q335 Colleagues will come on to the Budget and other legislative necessities that would happen in that event. Do you feel that an election campaign and people painting themselves into even tighter corners would be conducive to some of the outcomes that you have discussed, in terms of restoring governance and addressing the issues you have raised ?

The best solution would be having an Executive up and running, without a shadow of a doubt. In no uncertain terms, that is the best course of action. Every other course of action is suboptimal . The Executive going ahead, just bumbling along as it is at this point in time, with Ministers appointed but not taking decisions, obviously is not working. Having an election is a legal requirement — fine.

If we come back and people choose not to go into positions, almost immediately the Ministers fall away and it gives me a few tough decisions to make, which I would much rather not be taking. I am fully cognisant of the issues that I have been reading about in the newspapers and being told about by real folk I know — in real streets, on real doorsteps, as it were — that they are facing with the health service .

I have a particular issue, which I will doubtless come on to, about how we get the non-domestic fuel subsidy paid for those who use heating oil. Lots of things would be a lot easier if the Executive were running that have real ‑ world outcomes for people in Northern Ireland. My focus is trying to charm , be guile and coax everybody in to that place that they come back into the Executive . I would like to think that I will be successful, but, if I am not, I am afraid it is that election.

Q336 Secretary of State, do you think, in terms of the constitutional settlement and the power sharing agreement, that we are maybe going through a bit of a generational change? Most of us could not believe that Ian’s dad, Ian Paisley, and Martin McGuinness could even be in the same room, never mind work together. They became known as the Chuckle Brothers . I do not know if you agree, but maybe that long shadow of the t roubles is darkening the political situation less so , which may be changing that incentive and the importance of making that work . I do not know.

I just want to make sure I have understood your question correctly. Essentially, the institutions, as set out in the Belfast / Good Friday agreement, are fairly straightforward. Are you asking whether I think there should be an evolution of those institutions , based on what is going on ?

I think Sir Robert’s question was more whether you think people are taking it for granted and are therefore not as focused on seeing it as one of the main institutions. Is that right? That was my understanding.

Q337 It has often been described to me as like hav ing a system that means that Jeremy Corby n and Iain Duncan Smith must always work together and form a Government. If we suggest that here, people say, “That will never work . ” It did work a generation ago, but is that something that is less likely to work now , because the scars of the t roubles are maybe slightly more healed as time goes on?

I do not for one second think that any singular MLA or any political party does not want to do the best for the people who elect them. I truly believe that , and I have seen individual examples of MLAs from different political parties that demonstrate to me that they are just the same as every Member of Parliament and doing the best for their constituents in every way they can. There is a political problem that we have, which is one between the UK Government and the European Union , so not necessarily one that could have been foreseen in the Belfast / Good Friday agreement .

Do I think the institutions are working? They are not at the moment. You look at strand 1 of the Good Friday agreement and think, “That is not in a good place. The E xecutive have not been working, on and off, for a decent period of time , ” but b y God is it better than what went before it. I would never be so presumptuous to think that a Secretary of State with an English constituency would have the solutions to these problems . I know that a lot of thought has been going on among the Northern Ireland parties, and within the Northern Ireland parties , about what that might look like. There could well be a time coming when those conversations break out into the public domain and there is a proper debate. If I am Secretary of State at that time, I will fundamentally engage at the appropriate time. The institutions can work and , when they do work , they have tended to work very well.

Q338 Welcome to the Secretary of State. As we transition from the election question, would one of the unintended consequences of an election be that the momentum that has now built up between you and the European Union around the protocol negotiations would come to a halt? Previously , whenever we had an Assembly election , the European Union decided that it would be prejudicial for it to be involved in negotiations that may be seen as having an impact on the election. Could that be an unintended consequence?
No. I think talks will continue .

Q339 Moving on to the budget issue , as you are well aware, Secretary of State, there are a lot of challenges at present in Northern Ireland with how to budget , and Government Departments cannot effectively plan ahead. We are losing the impact of a multiyear B udget. Some Ministers, without a proper framework, are currently overspending. I think it is over £660 million at this stage. Authorisation to Departments at the moment is only about 65% of last year’s allocations.

It is probably realistic to think that we are not going to have an Executive in the next few weeks , I am afraid. What are your plans in terms of any intervention from Westminster to set a B udget? What discussions have you had with the Northern Ireland Departments in that regard? I noted that, in one of your previous answers, you said that there are no plans or no space for any emergency Northern Ireland legislation, which would perhaps concern us as it pertains to the B udget issue.
I want to get the Executive running. Let us start with that .
I take it as read, absolutely.

Please take it as read, because it is really important that I get that message across. Realistically, it falls to me and the M inisters . We will be bringing forward a B udget Bill, a small technical piece of legislation, which would authorise the Departments to draw down sums out of the C onsolidated F und and to use those resources . It would give the D epartments in Northern Ireland the legal power to spend and allow them to access all the funding available to them, but it would set departmental budget limits, which gives the Departments certainty against which to plan their spending .

This is not my preferred option by a long , long way, but it does not preclude a new Executive springing into life. Should it form within the financial year, it could make its own budgetary decisions again. As I say, as someone who believes in devolution , and the settlement that Northern Ireland has and how it could work, those decisions are much better taken in that format than having a technical piece of legislation basically carve up the money.

Q340 I have two follow-ups. First, in the event that a B udget Bill was taken forward through Parliament, what opportunity would there be for potentially this Committee, or indeed other structures, to have some detailed scrutiny of decisions in that respect? That probably leans into the second point. How far can you go , in terms of ta king almost strategic decisions around allocations, rather than simply going forward with pre ‑ existing budgets? Can you make differential allocations in line with the emerging pressures in Northern Ireland? I am particularly mindful that there is money sitting at the centre , which is unallocated from Barnet t consequentials that have arisen over the past six or seven months, some of which are cost - of - living - related.

On the first point, I would be very keen and do what I can so that this Committee, or indeed others, can scrutinise this technical Bill before and throughout the process . I am quite sure there would be a decent amount of scrutiny of it. I do not know what format that could take, Chair , but I am sure there is some way that it can be done. I am completely up for that , but I do not think it would be that sophisticated , or as sophisticated as you would hope.
Q341 What about in terms of those central allocations?

That is where I do not think it could be that sophisticated. It would be more as in making sure that the Departments could pay the b ills, as it were. It would also be ensuring that they ran within their annual budget.

Q342 That runs the risk that mone y s in the centre that are unallocated fall and are returned to Treasury at the end of the financial year, which could be a loss to spending power in Northern Ireland . If you do not allocate the money that currently sits in the centre, that £250 million or so, that money could be lost.
We will work with Treasury very closely on that . There is a budget exchange mechanism as well.
I do not think you have to worry about that particular issue.
Q343 To be clear, a budget underspend would not automatically be transferred to HMT ; i t would be held and rolled over .

A technical negotiation would need to go on between the Treasury and our Department to wor k through that. In the past , at end of financial year, the Executive have made use of a budgetary exchange mechanism. When they have not drawn down money, it has been able to be taken into the following year.
Q344 I appreciate we are now getting quite late into the financial year. I think the preference would be for that to be spent in year, given the current pressures.

Based on what we know from the Finance Minister, for example, there is quite a big overspend at this point in time. I am not convinced there would be much money in pots that would be underspent at this point.
Q345 How flexible or kind are you going to be to the Executive, if they are re - formed, around their current overspend? Can you have a word with the Treasury?

You should get a Treasury M inister in here to talk to that. I will always do my bit for Northern Ireland, but we all might be waking up to the fact that finances are a bit tight, in a sense. Everybody will have to cut their cloth accordingly .

Q346 It is very much, as you said yourself, better than what went before, but I think everybody acknowledges that governance can run a little better in Northern Ireland, even whenever it is up and running. What assessment have you made of the effectiveness of the strand 1 institutions and how they are being operated? In particular, what assessment have you made of the risk of them disincentivising compromise—if the bigger parties get their vote out, they can block the formation of a Government—and the risk of locking in, I suppose, green and orange thinking through designation?

In strand 1, the Executive have not been running while I have been Secretary of State , so it is very difficult to make an assessment from my experience as Secretary of State as to how it is running . Historically, from all the background reading and briefing I have had, while obviously there is always going to be political debate around things, it has worked. Decisions have been made ; things have happened ; policies have been changed ; the powers devolved to the Assembly have been used . I could probably make the odd political point, but that would be political point scoring.

I tend to think that there are a decent range of powers available to the Executive. Based on my briefing, when they have been operated by the Executive they have worked quite well. I am with you that everything can evolve and get better, but I would like to take that first step fi r st and see w hat the current Executive c ould do .

Q347 I feel your pain. I joined the Assembly in 2015, and the F inance C ommittee , and I was trying to get my head around the budgetary process. I had to go back to, I think, 2003 before I found a year where the process had run in a normal way, because it is full of interruptions. Is exploring those mechanisms, including those veto mechanisms, something that is on your radar if you end up having to run an election and be presented with the same problems in spring next year?
Currently, no, that is not on my radar.

Q348 Secretary of State, good to see you. Thank you for your visit to North Antrim earlier in the month, to Wright b us. I look forward to a visit to another industry later this month as well, here o n the Terrace , which affects my constituency quite considerably. It is good to see and I thank you f o r your engagement . I think you said you are very accessible , and s o far that has been the case.

Could I come back on one of the questions Stephen asked? Stephen asked a point about negotiations on the protocol with the EU. You answered about talks. Of course, there is a very important difference, in that there has not actually been a minute of negotiations since the protocol Bill. I want that to be confirmed — that there have been zero negotiations with Europe — because the mandate has not been changed , which means there is no intention, until that mandate is changed, to actually negotiate. That mandate change lies in the hands of Europe, not in the hands of the UK.
First, I know that Mr Paisley became a grandfather for the first time on Saturday, so I congratulate him on that.

The thing that everybody needs to understand is that these are quite complicated on all sides . They are talks at this point in time. There are conversations about what a landing zone could look like for those talks. The Foreign Secretary, who leads from our side, is having regular conversations with Maroš Šefčovič , who is the lead negotiator from the European Union. I think the latest conversation was yesterday.

Everybody is approaching this in a positive and grown-up fashion , but just because the mood music has changed it does not mean that the talks are not quite tough . They are on different areas where there has not been agreement in the past. It is very important that we work on the basis that everybody is in a much better place, but these are talks.

The importance of the Belfast / Good Friday agreement was recognised by the European Union in its negotiating directives back in May 2017. Basically, nothing in that agreement between the UK and the EU should undermine the objectives and commitments set out in the Belfast / Good Friday agreement , and all its parts and its related implementing agreements. T here is a recognition of the importance of the Belfast / Good Friday a greement on both sides. There is a positive atmosphere, but these are talks at the moment to make sure we get to the right place.

Q349 I want ed clarity and it is important to have that clarity , because in your opening comments to our Chair you have put hand in hand the issue of re - forming the Executive and I think what you called movement on the Northern Ireland protocol . Until there are actually negotiations, there is going to be no change on t hat second side of the coin .

I understand that. I will very gently push back , because I have had different positions articulated to me as to how far we need to go with the Bill that we are putting through the Houses of Parliament and what a landing zone might look like. I want to emphasise that the talks are taking place in very good faith and good humour, with a positive agenda . The European part in those talks completely recognises how important it is to have an Executive up and running in Northern Ireland as well.

Q350 I have taken you down that road probably far enough , because I know others will want to ask a question later on. I wanted to come back on this issue about the institutions and the assessment of getting institutions to work . You have used the term “ mood music ” , so having things right and the right atmospherics .

Do you appreciate how difficult it is when , in the last days and hours, we have had a situation where a Sinn Féin councillor, now a former Sinn Féin councillor, Jonathan Dowdall , has been convicted for facilitating murder in a gangland murder? We have numerous examples now of inexplicable chants , with the Republic of Ireland ladies football team chanting pro-IRA slogans , and then other pro-IRA chants going on now in airports in the Republic of Ireland. We also have a political leader in Northern Ireland saying that there has been really no alternative to IRA murder and violence. Are you able to push back on the Irish Government , the Dublin Government, on the Sinn Féin leader and on others to indicate to them just how difficult these actual examples of people’s conduct are going to make negotiations to fix the Northern Ireland peace ?

I thank you for raising the point you do in the manner that you did. I have not had the opportunity to raise those personally, but I am the sort of person who absolutely would , and so I would happily . I put it, again, into that historical context. I completely understand how significant and important these things are. Twenty-five years ago, when the Belfast / Good Friday agreement was being formed, there were at least equal, if not much worse , things going on in the background, and yet people still chose to come together for peace and prosperity for Northern Ireland.

I know that it is a big ask , because trust between all sorts of sides has broken down over a period of time. I completely understand the different views within the communities of Northern Ireland and the different views between the communities of Northern Ireland . I am with you.

Q351 Twenty-five years ago, I was 25 years younger , but I also had an expectation that my children , and indeed my grandchildren, would grow up in a world where the IRA was ancient history and where comments about supporting violence were in our past, but i t is the politics still of today. While at some points it seems we have travelled a long way, in some instances we have travelled in a circle for some parties and we are back there, 180 degrees . I am wondering how you actually break that cycle.

You know yourself, tak ing it away from Northern Ireland, if there was a pro ‑ Nazi song raised at a football match in Germany, or anywhere in Europe, the authorities would clamp down so hard on that, because of the intolerance towards that intolerance. What c ould the Secretary of State do to really emphasise that that is intolerable behaviour and is stopping a n d impeding progress?

You are talking to a football referee, so the football analogy is well made. I really understand the point , and the hurt and the memories that get re-invoked by people who might not even understand the chant or whatever they are saying, what it means and why, in this particular case, a community can be so offended by these things. It is down to the different authorities to sort it out, but it is all about respect, is it not?

To me, this is about trust and respect. That is how the Belfast / Good Friday agreement came about in the first place. I remember it, but I do not remember it as vividly as you do, Mr Paisley, in the slightest. It was, at that time, also a leap of faith. I am someone who always tries to look forward. It is great to look back. I am an amazing Eurosceptic. I can blame all sorts of things on our relationship with the European Union. I can do all that, but you also have to look forward.

The first question the Chair asked me was where I see Northern Ireland in my tenure . I would like to see it as the most prosperous place in the United Kingdom to live and work, where peace is absolutely the norm. There will always be, because of the tragic circumstances of the t roubles, people who—we will maybe talk about it—quite legitimately want to have either justice or closure, or both, of things that happened in the past. The prospects for the future, for people’s kids and grandkids, c ould be absolutely amazing if we get this right.

It is a big “ if ” and I know there are lots of moving parts, including a European piece that the UK Government do not have complete control of . What you have given me examples of are remnants of the past we want to get rid of , because the more people look to the future, the better the outcomes for the people of Northern Ireland will be.

Q352 I wanted to come back to your answers to Claire Hanna around the issues of institutional reform. Particularly from my party perspective, we find it untenable that there are now 18 MLAs in the assembly who are officially down as “ other ” , but, if and when the Assembly is restored, their vote does not quite count for the same value as others . Do you agree that that is not something that is sustainable?

The second point is probably even more immediate. Genuinely, if we a re facing a situation where there is prolonged deadlock , in terms of the current structures being restored , and, on the other hand, we are seeing a vacuum, with you intervening on a very light-touch basis , basically civil servants keeping the lights on, is the consideration of reform really that unpal at able an option?

T here is a place for a conversation about this in the future , but I do not think it is for the Secretary of State to engender that debate. It has to come from the people of Northern Ireland who it directly affects.
Q353 The Government obviously have a role, as a co ‑ guarantor of the agreement .

Absolutely, and when that time comes I will use my convening power , my good auspices and whatever knowledge I might have garnered by that time to help . I am strongly of the belief that any evolution of the institutions has to come from the grassroots.

Q354 On that point, as a point of philosophical principle, if you will, do you see any merit, in terms of trying to guarantee greater stability to the Executive and other political and civic institutions across Northern Ireland, in exploring a moving away from—and I put this in inverted commas—“them, us and other”?
I see your point. Theoretically, I completely understand , yes , but practically —
Q355 I get the practicalities of where it comes from , but, philosophically, do you see some merit?
I am a great believer that things can be improved and institutions can evolve, without a shadow of a doubt.

Q356 Can we have a brief word on the British - Irish Intergovernmental Conference ? The most recent one mentioned ongoing work to enhance relations between the British and Irish Governments . You would have to be pretty tin-eared not to realise that those relationships have been pretty poor and, since you have arrived, they have got a whole lot better. That allows you, Secretary of State, to claim credit for that improvement. You will have a conference, but we need processes, not events. What is the ongoing work?

There is quite a lot of ongoing work . I wanted to have a reset of the relationship. I thought it was very important that we did . No one benefits from there not being a really positive relationship between the UK Government and the Irish Government, so I was keen to do that. I happen to know my key interlocutor well from my days in the European Parliament. I trust him and I would like to think that he can trust me. It is Simon Coven e y, the Irish Foreign Minister. He knows I have very strong views on all sorts of things that he has different view s on . In fact, we have probably, over a pint or two in the past, discussed these in boring, tedious detail.
You have history .

Yes , we have a bit of history. There is all sorts of ongoing work. The cross-border issues of security are quite important. The Irish G overnment also ha ve a view on legacy that is important to recognise. As I have said, I am keen to improve the legacy Bil l.

There are the relationships that develop between the NIO and the Irish Government. They are already good and strong, but I want them to function and it needs to be something where the issues that the BIIGC was set up to talk about can be talked about in a full and frank way, where we do not have to agree all the time, but we can have the frank discussions and understand each other’s positions. I picked two off the top of my head, but I am sure there are plenty of others we could delve into.

Q357 Your Minister of State gave a rather emotional set of words, but very powerful . Certainly from the feedback I have had, they were viewed by many as being very important. There was that language of building up relations and talking about closest friendship , et c. He was mentioning this at the party conference just this month. There are the formal staging posts of relationship , meetings and so on and so forth . It is your vision — your plan — to have more day-to-day conversations and engagement? You have mentioned things like security, where clearly there is a common interest in that, i.e. to develop as a more organic thing, rather than just compartmentalised.
Yes.

Q358 Mr Campbell : O n the issue of the BIIGC and your Minister of State’s comments, there did appear to be an improvement, in terms of mood music. As you said, your previous form and involvement may have helped with regard to that . All of that is quite good in terms of helping to go forward for meetings and C ommittee sessions , et c . In the cold, hard realities of Northern Ireland, where people need to start to see tangible process that they can see, feel and touch, how has the mood music translated into potentially getting that tangible progress, particularly as it affects the protocol that is poisoning the atmosphere at the moment?

Friendships are one thing. Friendships allow us to talk much more in a blunt way without people taking offence. Maybe it is a weakness of mine, but 10 years in the European Parliament means I have a fairly good understanding of the European institutions and how they worked at that point in time, and I have paid fairly close attention to how they have evolved in their time. It is also important to have a knowledge and understanding of the institutions you are dealing with.

As Mr Paisley was talking about, Commissioner Šefčovič ’s mandate is given to him by the C ouncil and impressed upon him by the Commission President. If you want to expand the mandate, there obviously has to be some leeway given, informally or formally, at those levels. Understanding that is quite important. Friendships go a decent way, but , at the end of the day , we need to have a negotiated settlement . That is the best way forward and everybody is committed to it.

Q359 Mr Campbell : If people back home hear about better mood music, potential movements of some kind and potentially people shifting slightly, they want to know what that means. That all sounds very nice and it show s that people are working better together, but they need to see the evidence of what that is likely to translate into in those cold, hard terms I alluded to at the start of the first question .

Equally, I have been around enough, in both European and British political terms , to know that it is quite foolish to comment on any current state of talks, negotiations or whatever because things move. Things change. I also am not someone who will draw timelines as to when things need to be done by , because you get to that point where everyone is concentrating on the date , rather than the issues.
Q360 Mr Campbell : Are things moving now ? You said things changed and things move.
Talks are going on in good faith, with both sides trying to find a solution and negotiating.
Q361 Mr Campbell : That is not the same as saying things are moving.
No, it is not exactly the same as saying things are moving , but I am not going to comment on the talks or the negotiations . It is not my job. I am not in charge of them ; I do not run them .
Q362 Mr Campbell : If things were moving, I am sure you would be made aware of that.
I think I would have a clue.

Q363 Can we try to establish something ? There are a lot of people who go, “Why is the FCDO doing this?” It is effectively a trade matter, so why is it not with the Department for International Trade? It is an issue that affects Northern Ireland. Why is the S ecretary of State not doing it? What is the formal reporting mechanism? Is th ere a Cabinet s ub- c ommittee? How does the Foreign Office liaise with DIT and NIO in seeking advice, a steer and up-to-date information?
There is a Cabinet sub-committee : the F oreign P olicy and S ecurity c ommittee , which the Foreign Secretary reports to , and I sit on when matters pertaining to Northern Ireland are talked about.
Q364 When was the last time that met?
It was l ast week. Is that right? I think so.
Yes , last week.

Q365 Before the Foreign Secretary or whoever agreed to something, would it be your expectation that the phone would be picked up to you to say, “You are talking to all these people ; how do you think it will play” ?
Yes.
Q366 You do not have a right of veto, though.
No , it would be a Government decision. I guess it will be a Cabinet decision.
Q367 This would not be done by Foreign Secretary fiat. It would be a decision of Cabinet.
Yes, and the Prime Minister of course.
Thank you ; t hat is helpful.
Q368 We have touched on the protocol quite a lot. I am not sure quite what more you can say. What is the situation on current negotiations? What is your feel for how it is going?
As you know better than anybody—I said this earlier—I am a glass-half-full person, so I think the talks are going as well as you could expect and I am hopeful for the future.
Q369 You a r e hopeful. Are you increasingly hopeful?
I am always increasingly hopeful. I do not want to comment on the status or any of the usual things.
Yes, sure, you cannot. I get that.

Knowing how these things have worked in the past, you can get to a really good place and then they can all topple over. There were some fundamental differences between the two sides when we set off, but the talks at least now are really being done in good faith and good humour.
Q370 I am not sure how far we can push this. Has an implementation meeting taken place since February? Are you able to make a comment on that?
Talks between officials have been ongoing for two or three weeks now.
Q371 There is no such thing as an implementation meeting.
No. The European Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and James Cleverly have regular catch-ups to make sure that things are going in the right direction.
Q372 Are we in the tunnel, Secretary of State? Are we approaching the tunnel?
This is a metaphor I do not quite get.
Have we bought a ticket to get into the tunnel? Is there a tunnel? Is there light at the end of the tunnel?
There is always light at the end of the tunnel.
There is more tunnel.
Has the driver arrived yet?

In negotiations, I am very aware, especially in business or whatever, the one thing you can always guarantee is that, when there is light at the end of the tunnel, someone will say, “Let us build more tunnel . ”
Yes, or “What the hell is driving towards us?”
Yes. Let us just say that talks are ongoing.
But no negotiations.

Q373 There was a meeting yesterday of the UK side of the Parliamentary Partnership Assembly, which is a new structure between the European Parliament and Westminster. There were concerns raised about some joint working programmes, which were nothing to do with Northern Ireland . They were about the Horizon project, which is on joint participation in research and development—we contribute to that and then bid for some of the projects—Euratom and others. Are you aware that the Commission is deliberately linking the protocol negotiations to these other unconnected issues? Is it doing that to up the ante and to raise pressure, or is it just because within the Commission there is not that ability to work in multiple streams?
The European Commission is a big administration, so I am sure it has the ability to work in a myriad of ways. I have heard the same conversation take place, but I do not know the honest answer.
Q374 I just want to get something in the diary. Will the election be on 8 December or 15 December? It is either a six-week or seven-week campaign. What are we looking at?
I would like to think it would be a relatively short campaign, but I am wary of any days that might have some sort of religious connotation to them.
They all have religious connotations.
Q375 Are you thinking of Remembrance weekend?
If we get to the 28 th and I have called the election, I will be naming the date very quickly afterwards.
Q376 Will it be the 8 th or the 15 th ?
I am not going to say yet, Ian, but you are in the right zone.
Q377 You can confirm it would be before Christmas.
Yes.
What could be nicer than campaigning in Belfast—
We had a 12 December election.
Yes, indeed, and the general learning from that was that we would never have a general election in December again, but there we go.

Q378 Some 68% of households in Northern Ireland use heating oil, compared to about 3.2% of houses here in the UK mainland.
